The beleaguered bankers and secretaries of Yasuda Holdings were busy individuals, with better things to do than become the minder of some mysterious contraption.

Only a small group of ten accompanied the machines - Fujitsu's FACOM-222 mainframe computers - to their destination, before sitting at the seats assigned to them and thumbing through the provided instruction manual.

Most wore expressions of deep puzzlement, at a loss of where to begin reading the two-hundred page document. But this was their job now - and nobody wanted to lose it.

Over the coming days, the Yasuda men were guided through the ins and outs of computing by their Fujitsu instructors. Data entry, operations, outputs, storage - what had required a myriad set of discrete tasks in pen and paper before, was all possible with a single interface.

Bafflement was replaced by awe, followed in short order by a voracious curiosity. Even if many of them believed their abacus proficiency sufficient to calculate at speed, they were not so arrogant to believe they could retain more information than a machine, and in a workplace where knowledge was power -
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.6.a: - knowing where the skeletons were buried was an ace unlike any other.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.7.desc:
There was nothing unusual in what the Hitachi computer was capable of.

Under the watchful eye of their Manchurian instructors, the insurance actuaries quickly picked up the basics of operating their new mainframe computers. Inputting data, sequencing operations, command syntax, storage hierarchies, and displaying outputs. The magnetic tape storage units were - despite the intimidating size of the entire machine - remarkably easy to remove and service, if one was so inclined.

Nobody disputed the power of Hitachi's creation - crunching insurance numbers was hard enough by hand, and every second saved by the HITAC-201 was a second needed elsewhere. But some of the men had overheard the executives talking:

“Who needs a Fujitsu mainframe, when Hitachi's willing to sell an equivalent device at half the cost?”

How was that possible - materials? Unlikely, given the quality finishing and capabilities of the device. Guangdong's lack of tariff rates? That only answered why the HITAC-201 wasn't more expensive than its contemporaries.

It was the most unusual element of all - unless, of course, one thought of the labor costs. In which case, there truly was nothing unusual about Hitachi's creation at all.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.8.desc:
“Traffic's a bust - again.” Kawada balled his hands into a fist, fighting the urge to smack the truck's dashboard in misguided frustration. “And if we're going to be late, I wish the radio had something decent.”

“Heard the top twenty songs twenty times each, that's for sure.” Maehara grunted, tapping his cigarette's ash out the window before reaching into the glovebox. “Why don't we do something different, for a change?”

“I've got my own smokes,” Kawada started, before his voice trailed off as Maehara placed a metal box on the dashboard with a thud. “I don't need a super-sized ashtray, either.”

“Not an ashtray.” Maehara carefully pried a metal antenna loose from the metal casing, making sure it pointed skyward before pressing a switch. “Wonder what's on television.”

“You can't -” Kawada stopped mid-sentence as the box came to life with a click, a grainy, black and white image projected onto the glass screen - with several figures scurrying about on the five-inch screen.

“Don't get too excited,” Maehara chuckled. “Even if I can bring the TV with me, it doesn't mean anything if there's nothing good to watch.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.8.a: That, at least, wasn't Sony's problem.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.9.desc:
The best place to hide something is in plain sight.

Day in and day out, a steady stream of notables - executives, managers, employees, and 'other' acquaintances - made their way into a thoroughly unassuming office in Honkon. The full set of golf clubs, a wall of bookcases stuffed with meticulously-labelled binders, the neat stacks of paper stacked high on the desk - everything spoke to the overall importance of the room's occupant, fifteen stories above ground.

It was a space to speak freely. Promises, agreements, and contracts were haggled and agreed upon; no creed or loyalty was too sacred to be won over. Through honeyed words or cold cash, that office had borne silent witness to the best and worst of Guangdong in equal measures.

And so had the unassuming device of white plastic, nestled strategically under a pile of books that never seemed to be finished, a disused toy whose red button seemed to be permanently jammed in place.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.9.a: The tape reels were wisely hidden elsewhere.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.10.desc:
This is not a telephone.

How silly, one might say. It looks, in every respect, like a telephone, the likes of which have graced the world for over fifty years. A rotary dialling system and a sleek black plastic casing - in fact, many would say that they had seen one or a hundred more just like the Type 600.

But appearances can be deceiving.

What? Yes, what - the words spoken by anyone struggling to hear words spoken over the scratchy, tinny white noise so common in existing phone systems.

Except the Type 600.

When a listener hears the voice of their counterpart coming through the Type 600's receiver - crisp and clear, as if they were standing beside the listener - that was when the word 'impossible' would be used. A purchase would, more often than not, follow.

This is not a telephone -
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.11.desc:
The cutting edge, sometimes, is overrated.

Putting the pinnacle of technology on a pedestal is often an exercise in rarified elitism - that perennial haunt of Ibuka's sneering gaze. Trying endlessly to create bigger and clearer screens for television viewing - what does that really do, beyond creating an engineering arms race far beyond the reach of the average man?

Neither, however, do people want to feel cheap.

Pandering to the masses with plastic and cheap construction - like Matsushita and Morita do - is oftentimes an exercise in testing your customers' patience. They'll accept it so long as it's cheap - but if they had the means, you know they'd want something different.

Enter the ST-3500. It doesn't promise a revolution - black and white television, after all, has been present for years - but it doesn't insult the tastes of our customers. A tasteful finish of polished wooden panelling, with every dial tested for that satisfying tactile click, and a picture quality no worse than any of its competitors - and all at a price level that can't be beaten.

Hitachi promises a future where technology ceases to be extraordinary, or a cheap gimmick - it promises a lifestyle.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.12.desc:
The beauty of transistors was not so much what they could make possible - everything worth doing, essentially, had been done once before - but that it could be made smaller. Calculating machines could be shrunk from an entire floor's worth of space to a single room; multiple records' worth of songs could be fit onto magnetic tape.

Now, one could bring the technology of a recording studio into the home - in a wholly unobtrusive package. Though it would be hard to call the mass of knobs and dials on Sony's TA-1120 amplifier 'user friendly', any audiophile - those who were Sony's premier customers - would immediately recognise the value of an amplifier small enough to fit on a dresser.

Those who didn't recognise its intrinsic value would find aesthetic value in the polished chrome finishing of the entire package - and be metaphorically blown away by the amplified sound of whatever the owner wanted the listener to hear, whether that be a song - or a surreptitiously recorded conversation.

It was a statement to the owner's technical proficiency, wealth, and power - in a way that only Guangdong made possible.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.12.a: Sony stands apart from the crowd.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.13.desc:
“Experience unprecedented clarity of sound and fine reception through the nine-transistor, T-100 radio - the latest from Matsushita Electric! Listen to your favourite programs when and where you please - ”

“Everyone says the same thing these days,” muttered Chen. “Weren't they releasing nine-transistor radios a few years ago?”

“Yeah, but did you hear the price?” Mak said, fiddling with the dial on the break room's T-100 to a rising din of static. “Keeps on going down and down. Matsushita's just the latest one playing this game - at a thirty percent discount, no less.”

“Whatever. Even for the Chinese radio stations it's all government-approved programming, right? Radio plays, the latest baseball scores from Japan - can't say it interests me, even if I hear it from every house on the street these days.”

“Still faster than waiting for the morning paper. And listen to this.” Mak twisted the dial once more, and the static faded away - to a scratchy faint voice in Chinese, an amateur speaking a language they understood, and a message they both held dear.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.13.a: The people speak in the space between the noise.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.14.desc:
Everyone talks about miniaturization, but what does that actually mean?

Human society has, traditionally, relied upon information - on wood, papyrus, or paper. Information recorded on reams of paper, filed meticulously in rows of cabinets stacked from floor to ceiling - our world is built on libraries of information, both deeply profound and profoundly trite, flinging a light into the future.

The speedy replication and physical preservation of information has always been a problem. The Great Library of Alexandria burnt to the ground, taking much of what we know of antiquity with it - and all we know of our ancestors even a hundred years ago relies on what information has survived, in mildewed pages and torn pages, to this day.

And if that doesn't strike a chord with you, gentlemen, it should. Our treasured processes, manuals, and trade secrets are one fire away from being lost forever - and making more copies, as it were, creates risks of its own.

The 603-F does away with those concerns. A single loop of tape can hold an entire warehouse's worth of critical records, housed in a metal casing resistant to fire and resistant to water damage, and can only be accessed from dedicated Fujitsu interfaces.

As users of the FACOM series of mainframe computers - the choice should be obvious.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.15.desc:
In business, there are no mistakes. There are errors, mishaps or flaws. But not mistakes. Mistakes imply a fundamental disturbance in the “bigger picture”, as it were, that their underlying plan wasn't what it should have been. But the KH-920L isn't that. If one drowns out the half-whispered sneers in the background, Hitachi's new product shares but passing resemblances to Matsushita's...design.

Powered by nine transistors, the KH-920L isn't content with merely giving sound out, like a crumpled leaflet to a passerby. It bellows, so even the half-deaf and the elderly can hear the crisp, clear quality from Hitachi's trademark design. Instead of devoting a portion of the front to the speakers, their speakers dominate the KH-920L. Percentage to surface wise, few others can match Hitachi's immensity. Perfect for any noise, any sound or any frequency that may come their way. When these features are all put together, it would be a mistake to say that Hitachi copied Matsushita's vision. Matsushita's vision is some fleeting glimpse into the future. But Hitachi...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.16.desc:
Necessity is the mother of all Invention, as the saying goes. An authorless and dateless phrase, part of it still rings true; after every single leap and bound that mankind makes. Part of it. Because, Invention's biological mother is crueller, darker and more widespread than anyone would like to admit. It is Competiton. Necessity brings about change, but the eternal drive of humanity - that inner mechanism that drives us forward to pole position - is what perfects it.

This is why, faced with such powerful enemies, Sony cannot afford a misstep. The TFM-110 is many things, but it is certainly not a failure. Packed with a record Eleven transistors, all connected with a mesh of integrated circuits, the TFM-110 shows off Sony's prized values. Efficiency. Power. Talent. All contained within a gossamer, aluminium case. Some may lament the age where a product's quality was decided by what it was; rather than who made the design. But to the Zhujin who make up Sony's customers, the only thing that matters is that their home has borne fruits of their own. Morita's origins matter little.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.16.a: After all, he isn't what's for sale.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.17.desc:
It's not perfect. It's not realistic. It's not even pleasant to look at. Yet, it's the future and you would be a fool to think that the future was a warm and comforting experience. Just as the Transamurian steppes - with their frozen silence and unpromised lack of resources - face a challenge for our settlers, so do the virtual frontiers of technology. Do not be fooled, colour is a frontier, and every frontier must be tamed before it's settled.

The...disappointing screen size betrays its promises. Contrasted to its monochrome adversaries, it is, admittedly, pitiful. Matsushita doesn't expect the TC-96G to be a wild success. It is far too expensive for the commoner to purchase and far too small for the affluent to consider switching their behemoths to the design. Maybe the design's only purpose is to crawl and perish in the elephant's graveyard of historical novelty. Yet, if it does, its sacrifice will not be in vain. This is only the beginning of a new age. Matsushita's enemies will look at the TC-96G with envious eyes. Within days, they will work on their very own design, promising to outdo them in grander ways. But it won't matter because by then, Matsushita will be one step ahead. For every feat reached by Hitachi or Sony, Matsushita achieves three. Because the TC-96G isn't a television - it's a promise.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.17.a: A promise to tame the unknown.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.18.desc:
The scene is set. Slits of the Hong Kong afternoon sun peek through messily closed blinds. Inside, a crowd of faceless, nameless individuals gather around a colossal, wooden pillar. On the front, a slab of metal displayed a constellation of red and green lights blinking lazily in the dark. To the salarymen, the FACOM 230-10 was an unknowable machine. A man on a desk tore a piece of paper and peered at it intently. Muttering to himself, he nodded and beckoned for another worker to come. After a short while, the partner turned to the crowd and said only two words.

“It works.”

Over the coming months, more and more pillars wheeled themselves into the workplace. Many failed to notice or care that where human calculators once sat - pouring over hellish sums and monstrous equations - now there was the FACOM 230-10. They were shrines to a new era of business, where men could rely less on the fruit of others but the whirring and turning of millions of intricate parts assembled into a machine. The FACOM 230-10 did not ask for breaks. It did not unionise nor did it ask for raises. The boss would praise Fujitsu's new strategy of a “rental” system - where machines could be paid per month for a fraction of the cost and would order more. Eventually, the machines came to dominate the office, and one could barely find a place where a computer didn't reside. Some complained. Some embraced the new devices. Most went on with their day. But the computers paid little heed either way.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.18.a: The only existence they ever knew was their job.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.19.desc:
The executive circled the device, inspecting every contour. Work? If Hitachi had settled for simply “working”, then they would have been shut down in their infancy. The RA-189 needed to dominate. Matsushita's time in the Sun was coming soon. They knew it. Hitachi knew it. Even the partisan in North-Western Manchukuo knew it. The question is, when the Sun's rays fade and the entire market falls into the shadow of speculation, what eclipses it? This.

“It's definitely cold, sir. The rate of temperature decrease is exactly to your liking. ” As if to prove himself right, the assistant put his hands over the grill, before quickly recoiling and limply shaking it. Everything about Matsushita's design was put into theirs, except better. Better because they had learned from the mistakes of their adversaries. Where switches and lights were needed to have any sort of control over the settings, Hitachi had replaced it with a simple control dial. Where minutes - if not hours - were used up just to control the temperature of the room, Hitachi made sure it took seconds. Where customers were thinking of replacing their conditioners with newer, smarter devices, Hitachi would be there to greet them with open arms. Yes, Matsushita may be king...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.19.a: But every king must die sometime.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.20.desc:
As home television sets have become more common in Guangdong, and the Sphere as a whole, people have become familiar with a very modern frustration: missing your favorite show. Your bus is late, or you have to work overtime, or you just oversleep, and now you have to scour the TV guide hoping to catch a rerun.

Sony plans to make that a thing of the past. Their new CV-2000 VTR, once attached to a TV, can be set to record a certain channel at a certain time, for up to an hour. The content of the broadcast will be encoded onto a strip of magnetic tape, which the VTR can then play back at any time the user chooses, allowing viewers to make sure they never miss their favorite programs.

The new device has already drawn concerns from several major film studios, who worry that people will record TV broadcasts of movies and sell them on a black market. They've even already coined an appropriately alarmist phrase: 'video piracy.' Nevertheless, the general public seems eager to be able to watch their favorite shows at a time of their choosing.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.20.a: Don't be a prisoner of the programming schedule any more!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.21.desc:
Most people in the twentieth century wash their clothes in much the same way that their ancestors did for millenia, scrubbing by hand with soapy water. For all the ways that technology has revolutionized daily life this is one area where change has been hard to come by. That changes now, with the release of Matsushita Electric's new automated washing machine, the NE-7000.

No more will housewives be forced to spend hours doing nothing but washing, scrubbing, and rinsing. Instead, they can simply put all of their clothes into the machine's large drum, add soap, and turn it on. The machine then goes through all the steps of washing automatically, leaving the user free to do other things. There are even settings to make sure that the machine applies appropriate force to different types of clothing.

While this may not offer the level of precision to each individual item that hand washing does, the hours of time saved are surely worth it.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.21.a: Another labor saving technology of the future.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.22.desc:
While largely invisible to the average user, the telephone network enjoyed by the citizen's of the Sphere is built upon an enormous infrastructure. It is this infrastructure that Fujitsu hopes to transform with their latest product, the PCM-24, which can convert ordinary, analog telephone signals into digital signals using a process called Pulse Code Modulation. This will not only give users a cleaner signal, it will also cut in half the amount of power necessary to provide that signal, greatly reducing the cost of running telephone infrastructure.

The world is growing more connected, and Fujitsu plans to be on the frontlines of building and improving the technology that makes those connections possible.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.23.desc:
Up to this point, most innovations in computer technology have focused on increasing raw processing power. But Hitachi's latest release, the HITAC-8100, has a different main selling point: user-friendliness. The new computer will automatically detect input errors and warn the user about them, as opposed to earlier models that would simply run them and break, leaving the user to struggle to figure out what happened. The systems architecture is also designed to be more responsive to inputs and more flexible overall.

In addition to a general improvement in user experience, this also means that companies won't have to spend nearly as long training new employees on how to use the system. This should serve as major incentive for business to convert their old computer networks to use the HITAC-8100.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.24.desc:
With the rise of home stereos, it's not uncommon to hear music blasting out of apartment buildings late into the night. But for those of a more reserved nature who would fear drawing the ire of their neighbor's, Sony's new DR-4-A headphones allow music to be enjoyed in complete privacy.

Fully-enclosed, the headphones provide excellent sound quality while ensuring that only the wearer hears anything, allowing them to be fully absorbed in the music without outside distractions and to listen to any genre of music without embarrassment or annoyance. This is especially valuable in divided societies like Guangdong, where playing Cantonese music in a Japanese neighborhood, or vice-versa, carries a serious social stigma.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.25.desc:
The power of the atom threatens to destroy the world, and for most people, the word 'radiation' conjures images of nightmare scenarios, of horrific cancers and mutations, of a world made unlivable.

But what if it could also cook you dinner? That's the premise of Matsushita Electric's new NE-700 Microwave Oven, using microwave radiation to heat food faster than any conventional oven ever could. This technology has already seen widespread use in the restaurant industry, but the ovens they use are far too large to be used in a home kitchen. But the NE-700 is small enough to fit on a countertop, and promises to make cooking faster and cleaner than it's ever been.

As the job market heats up, and especially as more women enter the workforce, cooking elaborate meals everyday is something fewer and fewer households have time for, and eating out for every meal is prohibitively expensive. The NE-700 aims to meet this need, and allow working people to cook for themselves cheaply and efficiently.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.25.a: A new additions to kitchens everywhere.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.26.desc:
With each telephone line having an individual number, it would seem simple to have directly dial that number to connect with the line they want. However, practical realities have made that impossible, due to the sheer amount of memory and power that would need to be allocated to such a task. Instead, an army of switchboard operators are employed to connect calls manually.

But with the dawn of transistor computing, that could become a thing of the past. Fujitsu Limited hopes to be the first to capitalize on the application of transistors to telecommunications with their new telephone transmission system, the CPM-12M, which uses transistors to handle the calculations necessary for automatic dialing, allowing it to be put in place on a large scale.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.26.a: The next stage of the telecommunications revolution has arrived.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.27.desc:
For most of history, a private bath on demand has been a rare luxury for anyone but the ultra-rich. The average working person simply does not have the time to spend hours heating water to bathe in, so hot baths in the home were reserved for those who could afford to hire servants dedicated to that specific purpose.

With their new HM-110 Home Bath, Hitachi plans to change that. A small enough to fit into an average home bathroom, the HM-110 includes 200 liters of external water storage and an onboard heating unit, drastically reducing the labor necessary to heat a bath.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.27.a: There's more than one way to clean up a city.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.28.desc:
The basic technology for color television has existed for years, but various obstacles have stood in the way of its widespread adoption, namely poor picture quality and small resolutions. But with the launch of Sony's latest product, the Trinitron, color TV may finally have its moment.

Using aperture mask technology, the Trinitron is able to show full color at a much higher fidelity and greater size than ever before. Blowing the competition out of the water in both picture quality and screen size, at an impressive 13 inches, the Trinitron stands to bring the magic of Technicolor into the world's living rooms.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.28.a: Enter the wonderful world of color!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.29.desc:
Vacuum cleaners have been on the market for some time, but they have been bulky, unwieldy, and primarily used by professional cleaning companies. The result is that the average middle-class housewife would never be caught using one, as they're generally viewed as a tool for 'the help.'

But with the release of Matsushita Electric's MC-1000C, that may change. Designed to be small enough to maneuver around corners and light enough to carry up stairs, the MC-1000C also comes in a sleek, stylish design that makes it look more like a household appliance than a piece of industrial equipment. With these innovations, Matsushita hopes to make the vacuum cleaner an essential tool for every housewife.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.30.desc:
Fujitsu Limited has introduced the latest innovation in computer technology with the latest in their FACOM line of computers, the FACOM 230-60. By utilizing a full suite of integrated circuits across multiple processors, the 230-60 promises to improve processing speed over currently available models by a factor of four to ten.

Even more impressive, it manages to do that while keeping the overall size almost unchanged, meaning that companies that choose to upgrade will get the greeting processing power without having to sacrifice any additional storage space. The introduction of integrated circuits promises to revolutionize computing, and Fujitsu will be on the front lines.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.30.a: It seems Gordon Moore is right.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.31.desc:
As governments of the Co-Prosperity Sphere attempt to develop their rural areas, they repeatedly encounter endemic diseases ravaging the population; chief among them being tuberculosis, which only become more of a problem as people shift from working isolated in fields to packed close together in factories. This has increased the demand for diagnostic and treatment tools, a demand that Hitachi intends to fill with their new Mobile Televised X-Ray Station.

These x-ray machines, unlike older models which were both bulky and delicate, are designed to be lightweight and hardy, able to be operated in underdeveloped areas that lack an established medical infrastructure. Combined with specially made transport trucks, manufactured by Mangyō in Manchukuo, they are ready to be shipped out across the Sphere, putting Hitachi on the front lines of the fight to improve public health.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.31.a: Detection is the first step to treatment.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.32.desc:
Computers are, as the name implies, designed to handle complex computational problems. Their widespread adoption in government and business has made the complex bulk calculations necessary to the function of a modern economy much easier, but the kind small calculations that accountants and stockbrokers make dozens of times everyday, calculations still have to be done by hand.

That changes today with the launch of Sony's new ICC-500 Electronic Calculator. While still somewhat bulky at 6.3 kilograms, it can fit on an average office desk and handle calculations up to 14 digits nearly instantaneously. This will be a necessary tool for anyone working in finance, or any other arena that requires regular calculations.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.33.desc:
While color TVs have recently overcome the image quality barriers that had previously prevented their widespread adoption, with Sony recently releasing a line of high quality color TVs, these models remain prohibitively expensive, lying well outside the price range of many working families. This leaves an opening in the market for a downmarket alternative, something that may sacrifice a little bit of size or picture quality, but that makes up for it buying much cheaper than the high-end models.

With their new TH-30PU, Matsushita plans to fill just that niche. Using the same basic technology as Sony's models, but made cheaper, and with only a minor tradeoff in quality, Matushsita enters the color TV market ready to compete.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.33.a: Only snobs will notice the difference anyway.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.34.desc:
It's become commonplace for any decent sized office building to have a designated computer room, where massive banks house the computers necessary to run a modern business or government department. The idea of a computer smaller than that, one that can fit on a desk, seems like science fiction, but Fujitsu is promising just that with their latest product, the FACOM-R.

Using the latest integrated circuits, which can back hundreds to thousands of circuits into the space older computers set aside for a single vacuum tube, it can fit comfortably on a typical office desk, while having a storage capacity for 4000 words. They are first step in Fujitsu's ongoing project to make computing more distributed and move it away from big central hubs.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.34.a: Sure to become a fixture of offices everywhere.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.35.desc:
The dawn of the integrated circuit continues to advance compute technology at lightning speed. The latest innovations comes courtesy of Hitachi, the H-7830, a television screen that, when attached to a computer, displays a live feed of both the inputs and outputs of the computer's processing. This eliminates the need for printed outputs, and makes coding much easier, as errors can be spotted in real time.

With so much added efficiency and ease of use, they will surely see widespread adoption in no time.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.35.a: A computer with a screen? Who would've thought.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.36.desc:
After the days of bulky vinyl records and tape reels, the advent of cassette tapes allowed hours of audio to be stored in a desk drawer, quickly making them massively popular with the public. Their main drawback up to this point has been the fact that audio must first be recorded on some other medium and transferred, as there is no way to record audio directly onto a cassette.

Sony now has the solution in their TC-1010 Tape Recorder. Using a cassette input and an electret microphone, it allows for the recording of crisp audio with minimal static - perfect for journalists and police interrogators.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.36.a: A recording studio in your pocket!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.37.t: The SP-10 Technics Direct Drive Turntable
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.37.desc:
While audio recording technology is evolving, the primary way of physically storing music, especially older music, remains vinyl records. So, the market is out there for a record player that incorporates the latest technology to deliver high quality sound in a compact package. Matsushita plans to deliver just that with the SP-10. By spinning the receiving plate, rather than relying on a belt, the SP-10 can deliver consistent, high quality sound.

It also allows for the curious new practice of deliberately stopping the record while it's playing, producing a scratching sound that, bizarre as it may seem, some people seem to find appealing.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.37.a: Spinning records has never been so much fun.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.38.desc:
The dawn of integrated circuits continues to revolutionize computer technology at an ever faster pace. The latest product of this revolution is Fujitsu Limited's new FACOM 230-75. With processing speeds up to 7 times faster than Fujitsu's previous 230-60 model, it also boasts a much larger memory capacity. That greater capacity allows the 230-75 to store error detection and correction code, allowing the system to retry or recognifigure code automatically if it encounters an unexpected error.

This brings us closer to the day when computers can truly 'think.'
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.38.a: This should make debugging less of a hassle.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.39.desc:
The first computer to be truly portable, Hitachi's new HITAC-10 Microcomputer takes advantage of advancements in integrated circuits to pack the power of a basic mainframe computer into a package small enough to be easily transported by a single person.

While it does need to be attached to a large system of machines or processors, which limits its commercial appeal to industry and research uses, the fact that a functioning computer can be made at such a small size represents a serious step forward. It is also the first computer built to support SHOGEN, the Sphere's first widely available simplified programming language. This allows the HITAC-10 to be customized to meet each individual user's needs.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.39.a: Soon we'll be putting them in our pockets.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.40.desc:
Home stereo systems have become commonplace, allowing their owners to listen to the tapes and cassettes of their choice with clear, high quality sound, in the comfort of their homes. But only in their homes, as the only available portable music players remained radios, which were at the mercy of whatever was on the airwaves.

That all changes with the release of Sony's latest innovation, the CF-2500 Portable Stereo. It packs four speakers producing genuine stereo quality sound and a cassette tape input into a package small enough to easily be carried by hand. Now you can take your music anywhere!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.40.a: Now if those damn kids would just turn them down!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.41.t: The SD-1802A Electric Rice Cooker / Mochi Maker
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.41.desc:
Cooking rice is fairly easy and non-labor intensive, as it has been since time immemorial. However, the process of making rice cakes is more difficult, requiring two people, one to pound the rice into a paste and one to turn it into a thick mass, and taking several minutes.

Matsushita Electric plans to change this with their new SD-1802A, which uses integrated motors to allow one to both cook rice and make rice cakes at the same time. Just add the rice, turn it on, and after a few minutes and some rattling noises, you can enjoy Japan's favorite snack.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.42.desc:
Fujitsu Limited has announced their latest entry into the microcomputer market, the FACOM U-200, a 16-bit microcomputer intended to control industrial processes. While its use cases are limited, it still represents a major advance in computer technology, able to carry the processing load of a large mainframe computer of a decade ago and oversee the kind of complex industrial processes that used to require teams of ten or more, while being small enough to fit on a desktop.

It won't be long before computers like this are standard at every office workstation.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.42.a: They just keep getting smaller and smaller.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.43.desc:
In a move to reinforce their dominance as the Sphere's primary manufacturer of high end computers, Hitachi has released their most powerful computer yet, the HITAC-8700. Sporting the most extensive use of integrated circuits to date, packing thousands of transistors onto a single circuit, an order of magnitude greater than any competitor, the 8700 offers unprecedented processing power.

In addition, Hitachi has moved beyond the use of magnetic tape for memory storage, instead moving to fully digitized memory, allowing the computer to boast 512KB to 8MB of memory while remaining affordable. The 8700 is fully backwards compatible and can be linked with existing Hitachi mainframes.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.44.desc:
Recording audio on magnetic tape has been widespread for a long time, and for the last several years it has been miniaturized, with cassettes replacing large tape reels. It was only a matter of time before someone found a way to do the same with video, just as television followed on the heels of radio. Sony has stepped up to the challenge with their new VO-1700, which records video data from a television, with space to record hours of programming, in color no less. Using their new U-matic video cassette format, this promises to allow viewers to record, pause, and rewind their favorite shows as they see fit.

There is already a renewed surge of concern from film and television studios about the epidemic of 'video piracy' this new technology will usher in, but the public response is so enthusiastic most pay them no mind - and several studios have decided that if people are so excited to pirate their programs, they might even pay for an official copy of their own.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.44.a: Finally, I don't have to worry about missing the big game!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.45.desc:
With color television losing much of its novelty, and more models coming on the market every year, manufacturers are all looking for something to give their product a unique selling-point that will give them an edge over the competition. Matsushita Electric have settled on user-friendliness as the draw for their latest color television model, the TH-6600FR. Using a system of infrared signals and receivers, the 6600 can be controlled remotely, from a sitting position a comfortable distance from the set, which eliminates the need to get up to change channels or adjust the volume.

The so-called “remote control” unit is itself rather clunky and awkward, and requires its own power supply, but Matsushita spokesmen assure that these inconveniences will be ironed out in later versions.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.45.a: Great, a way to get even lazier.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.46.desc: Most mainframe computers up until now have been limited in their storage capacity because of their reliance on magnetic tapes, with the amount of information they can store dependent on the amount of physical space set aside for the tapes. This has been a necessity as long as circuits remained too weak to reliably store data directly, but Fujitsu hopes to surpass this problem with their latest computer, the FACOM230 '8'. Using large scale integrated circuits, the 230 uses full digitized virtual storage, directly within the circuits themselves. In addition to being convenient, it will cut costs for users, who will no longer need to set aside storage space for reels of magnetic tape.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.46.a: The computer becomes more and more like a brain.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.47.desc:
Description: “It seems that every week computers become exponentially more powerful. But Hitachi has proposed something new: what if, rather than building a more powerful individual computer, what if we could get more power by linking several computers together? The product of this experiment is the HM-1201A Modem, which can link two computers together via a transmission line, usually a telephone line, which allows exchanges of information at up to 120 bytes per second, much faster than a person could physically transfer the data.

Modems are already in use, but only for limited, mostly military purposes. The HM-1201A is the first one efficient and affordable enough to hopefully see widespread adoption for research and business use.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.47.a: Computers that talk to each other?
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle.100.a: No more free money printer sad
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.0.desc:
Chief Executive {leader_name} poured over mountains of economic and market reports that littered his desk. Each one hammered the same idea home: that the Yasuda Crisis had unleashed tremendous damage on the Japanese and Chinese markets. Those markets made up the overwhelming majority of revenue for all of Guangdong's companies, with the requisite realization that only the diversification of Guangdong's exports markets could salvage the economy.

Chief Executive {leader_name} flipped open the thick report on his desk; a dossier, detailing the markets with the greatest opportunities for growth - detailing the future of Guangdong.

'Latin America and the Mediterranean markets are best suited for expansion. Neither region has close ties to Germany or America yet, reducing the threat of embargo. Additionally, investing in these markets may also deepen ties between them and the Sphere, reducing American and German influence by proxy.'

“It's a start,” {leader_name} said to himself, flipping through the remaining pages of the document. “Preferences, proclivities - we can handle the research. After that, the companies are on their own.
strings.GNG_post_yasuda_opening_up_markets_tt: After the £GNG_Yasuda_texticon Yasuda crisis shook the entire Sphere, we can now look towards £GNG_target_market_texticon new foreign markets to sell our products to.
strings.GNG_market_exhausted_events_5_percent_pr: Because we have exhausted special opportunities for this £GNG_target_market_texticon market, the £GNG_target_market_texticon market's £GNG_product_profitability_texticon product profitability will decrease by 5%.
strings.GNG_america_opening_up_markets_tt: After successful negotiations between the Sphere and America, we can now look towards the American £GNG_target_market_texticon market.
strings.GNG_germany_opening_up_markets_tt: After successful negotiations between the Sphere and Germany, we can now look towards the German £GNG_target_market_texticon market.
strings.GNG_begin_sales_operations_USA_tt: The lifting of the American embargo enables £GFX_GNG_Guangdong_texticon Guangdong to sell their products to us.
strings.GNG_begin_sales_operations_GER_tt: The lifting of the German embargo enables £GFX_GNG_Guangdong_texticon Guangdong to sell their products to us.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.1.desc:
The Chief Executive sat back in his comfortable office chair, the ghost of a smile on his lips. He had just received a call from Tokyo, informing him that negotiations with America had concluded and measured trade with the OFN would now be allowed. The opportunity this presented Guangdong was incredible: the market of one of the world's superpowers had just opened its doors to goods from Guangdong.

Everyone would benefit from this; Sony, Fujitsu, Matsushita, and everyone else were salivating at the prospect of their sales figures skyrocketing in America. The prospect was so promising that one might be tempted to say that it was too good to be true.

That thought would not be entirely incorrect. While it was true that the American market presented tremendous opportunity, it also promised great difficulties. The scars of the Second World War were still very apparent, and many Americans bore grudges against Japan for their defeat. Surely, the mere passage of the trade deal was already becoming a political issue, and the entry of goods made in Guangdong and other members of the Sphere was sure to create a backlash that could lead to boycotts and protests that threatened any investments in America.

Yet the great men of Guangdong were no stranger to adversity. America was a stagnant market, waiting to be disrupted by new ideas and new products, regardless of where they came from. The greater the challenge, the greater the profit.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.2.desc:
Morita Akio was conducting a telelphone meeting with one of the ranking executives of the newly formed 'Sony of America' - discussing the nature of the American market, what consumers responded to positively, and what they did not care for, and to better tailor Sony's marketing efforts to break into the American market.

“Our current efforts are centered around the West Coast. As we continue to expand our operations and look to provide services and products to other regions, we must be ready to take into account differences in regional culture and necessities,” the executive explained to Morita.

“This has all been very encouraging news,” Morita began, “but every new venture has its fair share of obstacles. What difficulties have you experienced thus far?”

“Well,” the executive said, his voice showing the slightest bit of discomfort, “there are many consumers on this side of the ocean that are not happy to see any Japan-linked businesses setting up shop in their neighborhood. The nationalist sect of the National Progressive Pact has been inciting dangerous stunts in cities with Sony of America locations. They're demanding that we be expelled from the country, or leave voluntarily.”

“I see,” Morita said. “Stay the current course and monitor the protests closely. Our sales matter, but we can't ignore the safety of company assets or employees - especially when replacing anything in America is so difficult.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.3.desc:
Once again, Morita Akio was meeting with an executive of Sony's American branch, except this time the two men sat face to face. The executive had flown all the way from San Francisco to personally inform Morita on the Sony's progress in the American market - a matter of personal interest to Morita since he'd heard about the hostile reaction to Sony's arrival.

“Things have actually improved significantly since our last meeting,” The executive told Morita. “The nationalist demonstrations have decreased in frequency and severity, while our electronic sales have continued to rise. If I were to guess, consumers are waking up to the quality of our products. They're buying our televisions, listening to music on our radios - slowly but surely making us part of their daily lives, with less and less reason to join anti-Sony rallies. For the average American, convenience trumps anger.”

“It's good to hear that they've come to their senses,” Morita said. “Hopefully, it'll be easier expanding into the other parts of America.”

As the executive left, Morita felt a swell of pride - in his company, and in his products. If this was the power of Sony quality, then it wouldn't be long until all of America watched TV on Morita's televisions.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.4.desc:
Morita Akio read the most recent report on Sony's expansion into America with a sense of pride and accomplishment. The report was full of glowing numbers, and devoid of worrying news - Morita could tell when a report was hiding negative information, and this report had no such omissions.

Sony now dominated the electronics markets on the West Coast. In California, Sony outsold every American electronics company by a significant margin. The public trusted that Sony, regardless of where it was based out of, provided better quality than anything else in America.

Elsewhere in America, Sony was making inroads, with deals signed to establish regional headquarters in the Midwest and New England. Extensive research was being done on market preferences, and soon batches of Sony imports would be hitting the shelves in Ohio, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania - bringing the storm that had swept California to the rest of America. If Morita had his way, the Americans would be so busy buying Sony products that its origins in Asia wouldn't matter - the ultimate symbol of the free market trumping politics, even in the heart of America.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.5.desc:
Matsushita Masaharu sat at the end of a long table, its sides crammed by Matsushita executives discussing the company's plans to expand into the American market. As soon as they got word that the American markets would be opening up, all they could talk about was how Matsushita simply had to be the first to stake its claim to the wallets of such a vast and wealthy population.

But beyond that, the executives were stumped. How could Matsushita properly harness the American market? How could a company, with a name as classically Japanese as Matsushita, ever hope to claim significant share in the American market? The wounds of the Second World War were still raw in America, and japanophobia was not uncommon in the United States - which could prove to be a death sentence to Matsushita if handled improperly.

It was then that one of the executives had a breakthrough idea. “What if we simply renamed our American branch to something else?”

“That's actually a pretty good idea,” Matsushita Masaharu said, breaking the silence that had fallen over the boardroom. “And what would we call ourselves?”

“America has that airline carrier - Pan-American?” The executive stroked his chin. “And we make radios. What about Panasonic?”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.6.desc:
Matsushita once again sat at the end of the long table, savoring the surprised looks that were written on the other executives' faces. The representatives of Matsushita of America had just delivered their yearly sales report, and the results were astonishing. The Panasonic label had taken off like a rocket in the American market, with sales particularly strong in the West Coast and Southwest - ever in need of air conditioning. Despite this region being by far the most Japanophobic, its inhabitants had put comfort over prejudice.

Matsushita felt a great sense of irony in this victory. The explosive growth the American “Sun Belt” had experienced over the past two decades had been driven primarily by the presence of the military-industrial complex. Now, Matsushita had turned the guns of the Western imperialists against them. In the end, the company's superior engineering and competitive prices had once again triumphed.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.6.a: Can we give even GE a run for their money?
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.7.desc:
Sitting at the conference table, Matsushita allowed himself to drop his composure slightly, the expression of joy on his face visible to everyone else in the room. The Matsushita of America yearly sales report had once again turned the heads of every executive in the rest of the company. Thanks to competitive pricing and an unprecedented outreach campaign, the Panasonic label was now competing with American consumer electronics manufacturers such as General Electric on a broad range of fronts, from washing machines to televisions. Matsushita's goods could now be found in the homes of millions of Americans, and its market capitalization was growing more and more dominant by the year. Inevitably, their American competitors were now loudly complaining, raising the usual excuses for uncompetitiveness such as “currency manipulation” or “unfair trade practices.” Ultimately, the invisible hand of the free market would make fools of them.

With all the praise he expected - and more - being heaped on him, Matsushita took a moment to enjoy his victory. How many in the company had felt he would never amount to anything? Now, he would forever be remembered as the one who cracked the American market and planted the Rising Sun on the American heartland. This was his achievement, his triumph. Nobody could deny his preeminence. And that was what mattered most.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.7.a: Matsushita wondered how many more lands there would be to conquer.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.8.desc:
Ibuka moved quickly to open the new report from Fujitsu America. He read excitedly, hoping that the America market had yielded untold profits, but what he read gave him pause.

Just as he'd hoped, the Americans had been very impressed by the efficiency and processing power of their new FACOM computers, but their awe had quickly turned to suspicion. It seems the American government simply couldn't believe that the Japanese would allow them to have such cutting edge technology for so cheap a price without some strings attached, and had become convinced that the computers were part of an espionage operation. The report described how the Americans had demanded that the new models be inspected by NSA agents and IBM engineers before they could be sold, and how Fujitsu America were forced to consent, lest they fall behind in the American market. The paranoid bastards didn't find anything, of course, but it was still troubling that people from a major rival were able to see the inner workings of their new machine before it hit the market.

Ibuka was perturbed, but heartened to see that after all this troublesome business was over and the FACOM was actually released to customers, it sold very well, slightly outperforming expectations. It seems the American people did not share their government's reservations.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.8.a: Didn't anyone ever tell them not to look a gift horse in the mouth?
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.9.desc:
“We've hit a bit of a stumbling block,” the Fujitsu America representative said.

Ibuka's eyes narrowed. “Of what sort?”

“IBM. They're pushing aggressively against us in the American market. We think their government's backing them, and they've caught up with us in technical capability faster than we anticipated.”

“But can they match our prices?” Ibuka asked. The representative shook his head. Ibuka shrugged. “Then we have nothing to worry about.”

The representative sighed. “If only, sir. It's true they can't price their computers as low as we can, but they've launched a serious PR war against us. They say we're only able to sell so cheaply because we use slave labor in China, and that they've dug that business with the NSA to claim that the Japanese government can see any data stored on one of our machines.”

Ibuka removed his glasses and rubbed his eyes.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.9.a: “Well, Americans have always excelled at playing dirty.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.10.desc:
Ibuka smiled as he read over the latest report from Fujitsu America. In spite of IBM's competition, it seems that Americans just can't resist a bargain, and the FACOM has outsold all competitors as the most in-demand high-performance computer in America.

The administration of whole American cities is now run on Fujitsu computers, with any irresponsible talk about spying apparently disregarded. IBM and Fujitsu's other domestic competitors are scrambling to catch up, but they have a long way to go.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.11.desc:
Komai frowned at the newspaper in his hand. The headline read “POLITICIANS WARN AGAINST JAPANESE GOODS”. Under it was a picture of an American congressman, one of the rabble-rousing leftists that America apparently didn't know how to handle properly. The article detailed how several prominent politicians and business leaders had come together to warn against buying from certain Japanese companies, chief among them Hitachi. They claimed that the production methods used in Guangdong and Manchukuo were “inhumane” and displayed photographs of destitute Chinese workers.

Komai frowned. Hitachi had been making headway in the American market recently, launching a fresh wave of products suited for corporate offices, such as computers and air conditioners. A boycott right now could kill their momentum. Komai put down the newspaper and reached for his phone.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.12.desc:
“It's important we don't respond to this boycott directly,” Komai said to the Hitachi America representative. “Even a complete denial would only bring attention to the allegations and make us look more guilty. Where are we with the new product launches?”

The representative looked at the sheets on his lap. “They're doing well sir. Our household products have been particularly strong this year. If this boycott has had any effect, it isn't measurable in the numbers yet.”

Komai nodded, satisfied. “You see. I want next quarter's marketing campaign expanded. Let them know that no one can beat our prices, mark them down even more if you have to. We'll starve this little tantrum of oxygen.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.13.t: Just a Bump in the Road
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.13.desc: Komai smiled as he looked at the latest American sales figures. Hitachi products had become fully integrated into the American market. With their vast diversity of products, it was now hard to find a middle-class American household that didn't contain at least one appliance manufactured by Hitachi. The boycott movement carried on, but it grew smaller every day. Americans' wallets spoke louder than their consciences, and no products could beat Hitachi's for both price and quality. Komai chuckled and shook his head. He felt silly that he'd ever let such a foolish thing worry him.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.13.a: “I know it's wrong, but it's just so darn cheap.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.14.t: From the Silicon Delta to the Steel Curtain
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.14.desc:
The business halls and stock brokerages of Guangdong have exploded in activity following the announcement of trade renormalization between the Empire of Japan and the German Reich. While relations between the former allies remain shaky, the prospect of a thaw in a previously incandescent Cold War is too precious an opportunity to ignore. Already, the corporations of Guangdong are preparing their campaigns to conquer Europe.

With a population of more than a hundred million, metropolitan Germany by itself represents a vast and untapped market for consumer electronics, and that number does not include the other members of the Einheitspakt. While German electrical engineers pioneered many aspects of computer science and Siemens remains at the forefront of electronics research, the German electronics sector revolves around the needs of the military-industrial complex and heavy industry, leaving ordinary citizens behind. This deficiency has become especially apparent following the economic boom caused Minister Erhard's market liberalizations, which has raised the fortunes of Germany's middle class but left domestic manufacturers unable to meet its newly-raised demand for consumer electronics.

If the corporations of Guangdong are nimble enough, they might be able to corner the German consumer electronics market for the foreseeable future. Of course, some have expressed concern that Erhard's reforms may eventually create German competitors and entering the Reich's market will only make that possibility more likely, but the vast profits that could be made in the near-term outweigh such fears.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.14.a: Let's be careful that we do not create future rivals.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.15.desc:
Morita had been warned of this place: it was once the site of Albert Speer's Sondergericht, where gavels struck sound blocks and the enemies of the Führer were sentenced to death. But he had seen its facade, walked its hallways, and found only an old building he could give a new heart. This was now the home of Sony Europe, the beachhead of their interests in the Reich and beyond.

His plan for Europe was simple and familiar. Just as he had made connections among the local tycoons of Guangdong, so too would Morita Akio make himself known to the local tycoons of Europe. He would show them respect, he would show them products - and in exchange he would open up their networks to Sony.

Today was to be the first plenary meeting of its board. Morita watched the line of cars parking outside his new building. They were BMWs, fine German automobiles that would soon be found all over Asia. He tried not to think of their factories in the east, the malnourished hands in the Rhine that built these cars, the look of concealed disappointment on Li's face as Morita told him he was going to Germania, as he practised his 'guten morgen' and 'wie geht's' on his European partners.

Two limousines pulled up. Morita walked down the stairs to introduce himself directly. Out of the first limo stepped Helmut Schmidt, Reichsminister des Auswärtigen, an esteemed observer of these proceedings and a fan of Morita's reforms in Guangdong. Out of the second stepped a smiling man, a pipe stuck between his lips. Morita shook his hand, thanked him for his support. Hermann Josef Abs - chairman of Deutsche Bank, CEO and board member of a dozen European companies, richest and most connected man in the world - took Morita's hand and shook firm.

“Herr Morita,” he said, “it's a fine day for business.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.15.a: Morita smiled, and tried not to think about the factories in the east.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.16.desc:
There are naysayers, even in Morita's own clique, who question their growing connections with the Reich. In quiet moments, comparisons are made between Moskowien and Manchuria. Li tries to gently broach the subject, but his friend won't listen. Morita could point to growing profits from Sony Europe all he wanted, but it could not stop the accusations of hypocrisy, profiteering from the very exploitation that they sought to ameliorate at home. Sometimes, even Morita had sympathy for these arguments.

But now that he's back in Sony Europe HQ, its immense profits laid out for him in earnings statements and line charts, he knows he's made the right call. Abs' connections with German wholesalers, distributors, and media outlets have carved out a fine niche for Sony to inhibit, and media campaigns drum up interest to match this supply. Across the Pakt, Sony is rapidly becoming a familiar sight in department stores and consumer electronics shops. Not even the home-grown Siemens can compete with Sony's quality goods at affordable prices - a fact which Abs seems to relish in reporting, for reasons Morita will never be allowed to understand. 'An Abs-olute success!' calls out the headline of a local paper, and Morita couldn't help but chuckle.

On the way back, Morita was given a translated copy of this week's front page interview in Die Zeit to read on the plane back home. There was a picture of a portly man in a suit, a lit cigar wedged between his fingers. It was an interview with Reichswirtschaftsminister Ludwig Erhard, on the repatriation of slaves in the Reich. Morita read the interview with interest. They were taking active, if measured steps to repatriate and reparate their indentured workers. This Erhard did not seem to mince words: he was open about how it was a drain on the state, how it was only good economic management to free up German jobs for German workers. If only such a man existed in Manchuria! Less people working for free, more people working for a wage.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.16.a: And more people working for a wage meant more money with which they could buy Sony products.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.17.desc:
This time, Helmut Schmidt and Hermann Josef Abs came to Sony. In the sea of lights and haze of smoke that covered the cabaret club, they brought Morita excellent news. From Sankt Petersburg to Strasbourg, Sony products were flying off the shelves. The earnings statement Abs brought with him almost caused the Chief Executive's eyes to pop out of its sockets. Morita smiled, and apologised that his friend could not be here to see their bright future. Even though this was a purely Sony meeting, Li Ka-shing still made it a point to excuse himself. But at least he had stopped trying to convince Morita to cut this relationship off, ever since Cheung Kong's exports found a small niche in the Zollverein.

“Gentlemen!” Morita called out over the big band on stage. “I want to thank you all for your contributions. WIthout your support, Sony Europe would not be the success it is today. Let all the people of Asia and Europe share in our success! To Sony Europe!”

Schmidt raised a glass so quick and so high the liquid sploshed around the glass - the man was drunk on wine, lights and success. Abs was more muted, yet he called out “To Sony Europe!” as loud as Schmidt did.

By the end of the night, more promises had been made. Schmidt was so overflowing with praise for the Chief Executive (who had rendered an invisible yet important service to his cause) that he pledged to let Albert Speer himself know of Morita's brilliance. Abs even left Morita with a little gift, 'a symbol of Asian-European unity.' It was a BMW Glas 3000 V8, part of their new luxury fleet. Even though he was tipsy, Morita still crawled into the driver's side - just to have a look. It was a beautiful interior, but his eyes lit up when he saw a light cast from the dashboard. They had installed, at Abs' request, a Sony TV5-303. It showed a news report on the last LegCo session, announcing further trade links with Europe.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.17.a: Morita had forgotten all about the factories in the east, the malnourished hands that built this car.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.18.desc:
Sitting before the Führer was a nerve-racking experience at the best of times. Sitting before the Führer and the entire Gang of Four was even more so. Kurt Kiesinger, at least, looked friendly. Matsushita shifted his collar and locked eyes with Ludwig Erhard, who was puffing away on a fat cigar. They observed each other impassively for a moment. Helmut Schmidt did not look happy to be here - Matsushita knew that he was in favour of closer trade relationships with the Americans. Speer himself was, of course, inscrutable as ever.

Suddenly, the Führer began to speak, and all Japanese eyes turned to his interpreter.

“The Führer would like to know what the precise benefits of this equipment are.”

“Temperature and humidity control are key drivers of productivity increases,” Matsushita replied. “A comfortable environment, particularly in the context of an office, is very helpful to maintain morale and workrate.”

As he waited for the interpreter to finish, he motioned for one of his engineers to switch on the unit. Cool air flowed through the room, slightly ruffling the Führer's thin hair.

“The equipment is perfectly safe,” Matsushita continued, knowing full well that the RND had already disassembled the unit well before it reached the Führer's office.

Speer remained quiet for a moment, before turning to Schmidt, who gave him a begrudging shrug. A small smile broke across the Führer's face, and he began to speak again. Once again, Matsushita's eyes swiveled to the interpreter.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.19.desc:
Matsushita sat alone in his office, staring at the phone. A single drip of sweat ran down the back of his neck - the company's Europe office had been due to make its report three minutes ago. Though the rational part of his mind told him it meant nothing, Matsushita knew only too well that Germany's business environment was somewhat less than ideal. You never knew when the RND might come knocking.

The phone started to ring, shocking Matsushita out of his thoughts, and he grabbed for the receiver with one hand while retrieving a pen with the other.

As he noted down the most important points, Matsushita's nerves gave way to something approaching relief. Sales were booming, particularly in the office sector - the endorsement of the German government had been a very useful boon for them in this regard. Matsushita air conditioners had even made moderate inroads into German households. More importantly, though, brand recognition was through the roof. Surveys taken by Matsushita's subsidiaries in Germany were recording an astonishing explosion in recognition - in Germany's cities, Germania in particular, Matsushita was fast becoming a household name.

After some encouraging words to his Europe chief, Matsushita hung up and started to dial the number for his father-in-law's office.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.20.desc:
The European sales team had called ahead to Matsushita, warning him that their latest report would most likely require a dedicated team of transcribers on the Guangdong end. This alone told Matsushita all he needed to know, but he couldn't help feeling a little nervous waiting for the secretaries to bring up the paper. His father-in-law, Matsushita Kōnosuke, had never been entirely on board with Matsushita's plans to expand into the Pakt - companies there had a disturbing tendency to be nationalized.

However, as reams of paper were placed on his desk, Matsushita's nerves vanished. Sales were continuing to rise at an explosive rate, most notably among the German urban upper classes. In the capital of Germania in particular, a city very concerned with projecting an image of modernity, their units were now almost ubiquitous.

Outside the capital, the outlook was still very positive. While rural areas remained aloof, the small towns that housed so much of the German population were also taking to Matsushita's units - their products were rapidly swamping the efforts of Siemens and other European companies.

A Matsushita fever was sweeping the Reich, and profits were streaming eastwards. The thought of a nice healthy bonus at the end of the year put a spring in Matsushita's step for the rest of the day.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.20.a: A gamble repaid many times over.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.21.desc:
Sitting across the table from Ludwig Erhard, the Reich's notably reformist Minister of Economics, Ibuka couldn't help but see a kindred soul. There was a bespectacled and unassuming man who nonetheless reached for the stars. The conservatives in the Reich had vigorously opposed the liberal social market policies Erhard had implemented, but the Minister had persevered and was now presiding over an unprecedented economic miracle. Perhaps these reforms would one day birth challengers to Fujitsu's commercial empire, but for now, Ibuka wished to speak with Minister Erhard as a partner.

Erhard's words came slowly but carefully, and the translator made sure to convey every nuance. The Führer had made the computerization of German society a top priority. While Siemens and the universities had their own initiatives, the Reich still faced a shortfall of high-end computing systems in the short-term, and needed a stop-gap solution. This was where Fujitsu could come into the equation. Erhard desperately needed a way to identify failures in the economy and set economic policy without legions of bureaucrats, and the unprecedented capabilities of Fujitsu mainframes in memory and processing speed could provide a solution.

Ibuka considered the offer carefully. What Erhard wanted was a custom-built system that combined multiple mainframe units into one whole, capable of finding order in the chaos of the market. Such a tool in the hands of the Reich could prove dangerous if relations between the two superpowers once again froze over, but the engineering challenge it represented was too tempting to pass up. Besides, it would be a fantastic business opportunity - if the planners in Tokyo were too afraid of Germany arming itself with silicon swords, they shouldn't have restored trade relations in the first place!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.22.desc:
Ibuka and the engineers of Fujitsu's export division celebrated the WirtSchaftNet's first week of error-free operation. The central supercomputer hadn't been too daunting to create, as it was simply a scaled-up version of an existing mainframe. The other components were another matter entirely. Computer networking was a field still in its infancy, and trying to get different mainframes separated by hundreds of kilometers to talk to each other without crashing from desynchronization was the cause of many a headache. However, Fujitsu had emerged from this having created a network that connected computers across multiple institutions and critical industries. The Berlin-Germania stock market, Deutsche Bank and its subsidiaries, and Siemens formed nodes on a web that all linked back to the decision-making center of the Ministry of Economics. Mr. Erhard would have all the data he and his economists needed at their fingertips, and would be forever in Fujitsu's debt.

Despite only just having entered operation, the WirtSchaftNet had already generated significant positive press. Already, many other German companies and even lower-level sectors of the Reich's government are lining up to purchase Fujitsu mainframes for forecasting and administration. Fujitsu appears poised to drive a German digital revolution.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.22.a: Fujitsu's empire of copper spreads to Europe.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.23.desc:
Ibuka could not contain his glee as he read the latest reports from Futijsu's German branch. Their products had permeated all sectors of the economy, securing a dominant market share of the computing market and leaving Siemens, their German competitor, in the dust. It appears the old giant could not compete with either Fujitsu's innovation, nor its price, all while the company became the public face of computing in the Reich. It seemed that every factory, office, and administrative building had a Fujitsu product installed in it, streamlining the previously stifling bureaucracy so characteristic of National Socialist economics.

This has of course provoked a great outcry from the more traditionalist and xenophobic citizens of the Reich, who have stoked fears of a “sinister Asiatic-Jewish plot” to undermine the hard-working Aryan with unaccountable machinery that secretly transmitted its users' data to Tokyo. These accusations have not found much purchase among level-headed German businessmen, though they are a cause for concern as long as the Führer's regime remains on unsteady ground.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.23.a: Mediocrity will always try to drag excellence down to its level.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.24.t: Building Back Better - The Hitachi Way
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.24.desc:
Komai Kenichirō forced a pleasant smile on his face as he watched Minister Erhard agonizingly review the more than a hundred pages of proposal Hitachi had submitted to the Reich's Ministry of Economics on the importation of construction equipment. After what seemed an eternity of silence, the Minister looked up.

“The Ministry will have to conduct further reviews of the proposal, but it appears sound from my initial inspection. However, keep in mind that all offered equipment will first have to be subject to independent qualification testing before they can be approved for use on state-sponsored construction projects.”

Komai struggled to hold his tongue. He knew very well that Hitachi's construction equipment exceeded the quality of their German counterparts on every possible metric, and the very thought that the Reich would doubt their handiwork made his blood boil. Still, he could not afford to let the mask slip this deep into the belly of the beast. With Germany in the middle of an unprecedented economic boom as a result of the Führer and Erhard's policies, her domestic construction industry was left unable to keep up with demand. Hitachi had a one-in-a-lifetime opportunity to enter the German market by selling its own construction equipment or even taking on construction contracts themselves.

Once again, Komai was needed to play the gentlemen. For the good of Hitachi, for the good of Guangdong, and for the good of the Empire.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.24.a: “Minister Erhard, it has been an honor to be granted this audience...”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.25.desc:
Komai's eyes narrowed as he examined the quarterly sales reports from Hitachi's German subsidiary. As expected, the company had effortlessly become one of the most sought-after construction firms in the Reich, with their low prices and modern technology putting them a step above their German competitors. With the Speerian economic miracle continuing unabated, Komai felt confident enough to make his next move.

He would expand the beachhead Hitachi had acquired into a fortress by purchasing uncompetitive German construction firms, by agreement or by subterfuge. Once acquired, they would be consolidated together with Hitachi's existing subsidiary firms to forge a construction empire that would prove unassailable as long as Minister Erhard's free-market policies continued. This strategy seemed blunt and obvious, but he was confident it would deliver Hitachi a dominant market share in Germany's construction industry.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.25.a: He stayed awake into the wee hours planning the Empire's latest conquest.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.26.t: An Empire of Concrete and Steel
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.26.desc:
“...in summary, Hitachi now possesses a controlling stake in fifty-three Reich subsidiaries, and has purchased shares in more than a thousand European construction firms.”

Komai felt dizzy for a moment as his brain processed the full meaning of that statement. His gambit had paid off. Hitachi was now unquestionably the face of the construction sector in Germany. Hundreds of hospitals, offices, railroad and metro stations, stadiums, and even monuments of Adolf Hitler had been built by their hands. The Hitachi logo could be found along every boulevard in every German city, and it was indelibly pressed into the psyches of the German population. This had proved the perfect advertising campaign, as millions of Germans were now pouring into stores to purchase Hitachi-branded consumer goods. What had started as a construction empire was rapidly transforming into the most diverse corporate enterprise in Europe.

Komai could not help but see history repeating. Germany had borrowed the Manchurian System's planning to build a war machine that brought Europe to its knees, and now, they would import the corporation that was bringing the Manchurian System its second era of greatness.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.26.a: He would make sure the Germans would never forget what Manchuria had done for them.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.27.t: From the Silicon Delta to the Steel Curtain
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.27.desc:
The business halls and stock brokerages of Guangdong have exploded in activity following the announcement of trade renormalization between the Empire of Japan and the German Reich. While relations between the former allies remain shaky, the prospect of a thaw in a previously incandescent Cold War is too precious an opportunity to ignore. Already, the corporations of Guangdong are preparing their campaigns to conquer Europe.

With a population of more than a hundred million, metropolitan Germany by itself represents a vast and untapped market for consumer electronics, and that number does not include the other members of the Einheitspakt. While German electrical engineers pioneered many aspects of computer science and Siemens remains at the forefront of electronics research, the German electronics sector revolves around the needs of the military-industrial complex and heavy industry, leaving ordinary citizens behind. While the Führer has paid lip service to promoting innovation, German consumer electronics will likely remain moribund for the foreseeable future. The slowly-revitalizing Mittelstand wants a new deal, and Guangdong is poised to service their demands.
