Given the pathetic state of their competitors, it is all but certain that the corporations of Guangdong will corner the German consumer electronics market for the foreseeable future. The conservatives in the Reich may grumble about “autarky” and “national pride” as foreign electronics fill the supermarket shelves, but Guangdong will sell its products no matter what they think.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.27.a: We shall see who truly is the “master race.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.28.desc:
Friedrich could feel all eyes in the room on him as he lugged the burlap sack into the room. His friend, Mark, instantly walked over. “Do you have it ready? Is that it?” he asked.

Friedrich nodded, gently placing the sack onto the floor, trying desperately not to drop it too hard. Unwrapping it gingerly, the contents of the bag were revealed to be a bulky, black cuboid with a silver plate on the front. On this plate were various knobs and dials, with the word “Sony” proudly emblazoned in black typeface at the top. A TA-1120 Amplifier.

“Fresh out of Guangdong. Frau Matthews could've killed Fritz with the look she gave him when he handed it over to us, but I doubt she'll tell. Now, if this could just work...”

The boy fiddled with the back of the item, as Mark produced a disk and popped it into a smaller cuboid, used to play music. Having plugged the Amp into the wall, Friedrich quickly connected the two devices. “Alright people, it's the moment of truth.” Dramatically, he leant down and turned one of the knobs of the amp up as Mark pushed the “play” button on his device.

And suddenly, the room was filled with a peppy tune not unlike the blues in America.

'You're the devil in disguise,' crooned Elvis Presley from the amp. The entire room cheered loudly, as they began to dance in tune with the music. Mark jumped up too, equally happy. “Yes! We did it! Speer Jetzt!” he said, high-fiving his friend. Whether Herr Bormann liked it or not, the students would be having one hell of a party that night.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.29.desc:
Hans reclined backwards on his chair, allowing the stress of the day to gradually ooze out of him like water from a sponge. It had been a long day at the office - writing down memos, passing papers around, and performing otherwise mundane tasks all day was never good for the soul. Nonetheless, it was vital work for the Reich so he carried on.

Checking his wristwatch, the bureaucrat noted what time it was. He quickly scrambled around, looking for the remote to his television. It was 7:45PM and the new film would be broadcast in roughly 5 minutes, and he did not want to miss it. When Olympia had been released all the way back in 1936, he was a young man, but even then he was enraptured by the work of Leni Riefenstehl. The woman was able to capture the noble spirit of the German people He had even met his very own wife at a screening of Triumph des Willes.

As the television flickered to the film, Hans reached for a device that his son had gotten him for his birthday a few weeks ago. It was called a “CV-2000”, apparently, which was a type of VCR. It came from Guangdong and recorded things, letting you play it back. He had tried it a few times and it worked fine enough before.

As Riefenstahl's newest film began to play on the television, views of rolling African hills coming onto screen, Hans clicked a button. He wanted to be able to watch this with his family whenever they pleased.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.29.a: It was one of her better works, definitely.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.30.desc:
Joachim Funk raised his eyebrow as his fellow project manager plonked a large television set in front of him, his face like thunder. “... may I help you, Walther?”

Walther nodded. “Look at this, Funk. Do you know what this is?”

Joachim nodded. “It's a television set. One that you have nearly dropped on my desk with little elaboration. Is there anything wrong with it?”

Rolling his eyes, the other man walked away, head in his hands. “You don't know then. Very well,” he said, beginning to pace around the room.

“This is no simple television set, Funk. It is what is called a trinitron, made in Guangdong. Do you see it?” he asked, gesturing to the trinitron. “This... box... it is making us look like clowns. Do you know how many of these have been sold in Germany in the last week alone?”

Joachim shook his head. “Please, Herr Kopp, enlighten me.” he said, taking a sip of his coffee sardonically.

“750,000.”

Upon hearing this, Joachim almost spat his drink out, choking. In all his time working for Siemens, they had not sold that much of anything in the span of a week.

“But why?!” Joachim asked, honestly confused as to how they were hammering them so badly.

Walther shook his head. “Plug it in, you'll see. The picture's immense. It makes our stuff look like it's been dragged through a field of static and barbed wire.” And sure enough, the picture was some of the crispest he had seen in ages. The figures of the colourful people on the television were crystal clear.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.30.a: So much for superior Aryan engineering.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.31.desc:
The new washing machine was a lot more intimidating than it had any right to be. Gerthe knew she had no right to be anything other than pleased about the damn thing - she had practically begged her husband to buy it for her, and it wasn't like Matsushitas were cheap. But regardless, she worried. What if she accidentally shrank the entire family's clothes by pressing the wrong button?

Shaking her head, she tried to dismiss the silly thoughts. Max would be home in about an hour, the children were only barely entertained by the television, and dinner was barely prepped. She had to get this over with. Hesitantly, she knelt down with her basket of dirty clothes, loading them into the drum of the machine. Closing the door, she pushed the button at the top and the machine began to whirr.

Her eyes widened. That whirring couldn't be good. She looked down at the manual to check if she had done it right. Apparently, all she needed to do was wait... 20 minutes? That couldn't be right.

Squinting, she reread the manual again. She had done it exactly right, and in 20 minutes she would be able to unload the washing and hang it out to dry. Well, that made things a lot easier. Putting the manual down, she checked the time. 5:15PM. The dinner could wait, she supposed. Perhaps she could finally get started on that Mann book she had been meaning to read for a while...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.32.desc:
As it turned out, getting the new washing machine would lead Gerthe into a world she hadn't previously imagined herself even dipping a toe into. The machine itself didn't contribute to this, of course - it wasn't as if washing machines held the key to enlightenment, or anything. But no, it had helped her get a better understanding of who she was in one key way.

Time-saving.

Popping the new micro-oven made by the same company as the washer on, she leisurely strolled over to the kitchen table, having made sure that it was set half an hour ago. Now that she was less tied down by menial exercises such as washing and cooking, there was time to look elsewhere. She sat down, producing a notebook and pen. She fiddled with the knob of the nearby radio. It was almost time for the news - something that she had been eagerly trying to keep up with.

The box crackled to life, a staticky voice coming through. As it spoke, Gerthe studiously wrote down everything it said. She had made a habit of doing this over the past few weeks - at first it was out of curiosity, but after hearing what was happening to other women across the country, she felt compelled to educate herself. After all, if not her, then who else?
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.33.desc:
“Frau Babler! Come in, come in.”

“Ah, Frau Adelberg! How are the children?”

“Yes, just put your shoes there Frau Helborg, it's fine...”

The inaugural meeting of the Southwest Ulm Women's Rights Association had gone swimmingly, Gerthe mused. Months upon months spent learning about the situation of other German women had given her a lot of time to reflect on what she actually wanted to do with her life. Of course, she didn't hate being a housewife - and god knows that if she did, she'd never say it aloud - but the knowledge that opportunities for her to make something of herself were deliberately being kept out of reach was maddening.

So, deciding that she'd had enough, Gerthe decided to start hosting little get-togethers for the other women in the neighborhood to come to, where they could talk about these things freely. Curiously, they all seemed to agree that as life became easier - thanks in no small part due to all the new Cantonese devices - they wanted more from life. And as more and more women showed up, she began to wonder - why not make it official?

Her husband had said that it was just a glorified sewing circle, of course, but he was always going to say that. And when she looked across the room of their local town hall and saw all the strong-minded, courageous women that filled it, Gerthe knew damn well that he was wrong.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.33.a: I'm sure Bormann will love this...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.34.desc:
Dr. Horst Zuse watched as test printouts emerged from the Fujitsu FACOM230-50 that had been installed in Riga's Palace of Justice. The local Reichskommissariat office in Riga had been one of the first administrative centers in the Reich to purchase the system following the normalization of trade relations between Germany and Japan, and as the son of one of Germany's esteemed pioneers in computing, Dr. Zuse had been assigned to oversee it.

The system was bought with two goals in mind: to assist in the reconstruction of Ostland and to track vital economic and demographic statistics in a region that hasn't had a census since the Civil War. It seemed a steep task to a layman, but Dr. Zuse was not daunted. The Reich's “model colony” had kept detailed and organized records with the help of native collaborators, and while some had been lost in the Civil War, there was plenty left over to fill in the gaps. All that was needed was to feed them in via punch-card and voila! The Reich's grip over Ostland would be restored.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.34.a: He wondered if it would be this simple for the others.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.35.desc: Dr. Zuse groaned in frustration as he went over the latest batch of pre-Ukrainian Civil War census data - or, more accurately, the lack of it. With the success of Ostland's pilot program, Fujitsu mainframes were now being purchased in administrative centers all across the East, and Dr. Zuse had been brought in to oversee the record digitalization process in Kiew. While the technical aspects of the job were simple, everything else about it was not. Ukraine had been a significantly more restive Reichskommissariat than Ostland. While there were some collaborators the Reich could rely on, the vast majority of the populace remained hostile to their rule and partisans still infested the countryside. When the Civil War erupted, insurgents had destroyed countless documents during their reign of terror, turning the RK's already spotty records into a nearly-unusable mess. It would take plenty of detective work to put Ukraine's government back together again, and Dr. Zuse couldn't help but wonder if the Reich had hired the wrong man for the job.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.35.a: He silently cursed Koch away from prying ears.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.36.t: -Couldn't Put the Reich Back Together Again
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.36.desc:
Sitting at his desk still awake at 2 in the morning, Dr. Zuse felt the dam in his mind holding back despair finally burst. He had pulled heaven and earth to get the digitalization project in Ukraine to a state where the local administrators could make proper use of the Fujitsu hardware, but this hard-won success had only been rewarded by the assignment he had been dreading most: extending digitalization into Moskowien. The out-of-touch bureaucrats in the Reich Chancellery were under the impression that a computer science professor could somehow shed a light on the Reich's black hole in the East, and Dr. Zuse did not yet have the courage to tell them the truth.

The Fujitsu computers worked just fine, of course. With unparalleled processing memory and processing power, they made administrative calculations and data tabulation a dream. No, the problem was in the utter lack of quality data to use them with. It had been only two weeks since they set up the system, and the team was already on the verge of giving up entirely. Moskowien always had a poor reputation, but Dr. Zuse had just seen how deep the rabbit hole went. Entire regions had somehow misplaced all but the most basic and least useful census data, and much of what they could find had likely been distorted or even entirely fabricated by unscrupulous administrators.

It was abundantly clear that no technology on Earth could help Moskowien. It had already perished decades ago.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.36.a: “Damn Globocnik, damn Kaminski, damn them all!”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.37.t: Out with the Old, In with the New
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.37.desc:
The Reichswerke steel plant's decision to purchase a Hitachi 8100 Series mainframe had been an obvious one. When the company from Guangdong had first made their pitch, the plant's managers could not believe their ears. Hitachi had managed to do away with punch cards entirely and instead was using a magnetic disk-based storage system that promised to vastly increase usability and reduce labor costs in one fell swoop. Who could fault the managers for seizing the opportunity?

Of course, the operators who had maintained the previous mainframe told a different story. Their replacement with a small contingent of well-educated computer specialists would no doubt do wonders for the plant's efficiency and throughput, but that would do nothing to feed their hungry bellies and put a roof overhead. The managers had insisted that finding new jobs would be a simple task, but the Reich's employment statistics betrayed this hope. A few enterprising operators got it into their heads to launch a formal complaint to the manager's higher-ups, but it inevitably fell on deaf ears. Faced with an uncertain future back in the city, the operators had no choice but to hang up their employee badges and take what fate had dealt them.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.37.a: Another class of humans rendered obsolete.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.38.desc:
Hermann felt a wave of relief wash over him as he sat down on his tattered bunk, savoring the wonderfully cool air of the dormitory. His coworkers had thought that lobbying the management for one of those cheap Hitachi air conditioners had been a long shot, but it appears the higher-ups had finally realized the value of the purchase. Now, the laborers would have some respite from the grueling heat of the steelworks and a few precious minutes to recharge their batteries. After all, an exhausted worker could not be productive.

Hermann stared at his blackened and calloused palms. Ever since he graduated Hauptschule, he had labored in this plant for ten hours a day and six days a week. For two decades, he had known nothing but endless toil, suffocating heat, and toxic fumes. The air conditioner had only thrown his and his coworkers' misery into starker relief. Hermann had heard the occasional complaint come down the grapevine. Perhaps he could find some others to talk to about his problems.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.38.a: A small comfort in a cruel world.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.39.desc:
Hermann huddled around the table in the dormitory commons with fourteen of his colleagues, straining his numbed ears to hear the news from the cheaply-bought Hitachi radio sitting on it. The announcer calmly and professionally announced that a whopping five hundred thousand jobs had been created in the past year, along with an unprecedented 10% rise in Reichswerke's stock price that demonstrated the great success of the Führer's policies.

At that moment, Hermann felt something snap in the psyches of those around him. One of his coworkers, a middle-aged man named Joseph, suddenly broke the silence.

“It's all cowshit!” he blurted out. “Just yesterday, the bosses threatened to cut our pay by 10% if we didn't go past last year's numbers! Where are all the profits going to, anyway? To us, or to the suits? When's the last time we've seen a pay raise? I can barely afford to pay rent as it is!”

Hermann felt his heart alight upon hearing these words which all of them knew. For all the talk of a new era for the Aryan worker, Hermann felt just as destitute as ever. They had told him that he was uncountably lucky to be blessed with Aryan blood, but all he could feel was the boot of the German Workers' Party on the faces of German workers such as him.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.39.a: The mask slips; the illusion shatters.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.40.desc:
Lorenzo thought that he might have made the smartest purchase of his life. When Sony had launched their new five inch TVs in Italy, he'd been there on the first day to pick one up for his limousine. Lorenzo's wife had balked at the price, but he knew a little entertainment would make the drives to work go much faster. His guests were certainly impressed, the three expensively dressed businessmen gazing at the technological marvel before them like children. It was playing some soap opera; Lorenzo didn't watch them himself, but his compatriots were enthralled.

“So, what do you think?”

One of the men, a balding fellow named Andrea, responded “It's ingenious,” without taking his eyes off the TV.

“I meant about the new arrangement for oil exploration rights.”

Another of the men looked at him confused. “Oh? Is that what we were talking about?”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.41.desc:
Alonzo paused to catch his breath, in the moments before one his waiters brought him another order. Business at his pizzeria had picked up in recent weeks, ever since he had installed the new Matsushita air conditioning unit. People were flocking to it in the afternoon, when the summer heat was at its worst. Alonzo was happy for the customers, and their money, but the extra work was putting a strain on him. His son, whose idea the air conditioner had been, had been telling him to hire another cook for a while, and maybe now he would.

When a waiter came to him with another slip of paper, he sighed and turned to his oven. As he did, a blast of cool air hit his face. The air conditioner at least had the added benefit of making his hot kitchen more bearable.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.41.a: Good for business and good for you.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.42.desc:
Giuseppe let out a sigh as he leaned back in his chair. He found himself at something of a loss. As a bureaucrat in embattled and dysfunctional Zara, his day would normally be full of reports and complaints to file and send up the chain, more than enough to keep him occupied from morning to evening. But last week his office had received some of the new Fujitsu computers that the government had purchased, which had made his work more efficient by a factor of at least a thousand.

He looked around at his coworkers, several of whom seemed to be in a similar boat to him, unsure of what to do with themselves with the days work made so much shorter. Giuseppe reflected on the possibilities that this could bring. Maybe a more efficient administration could make the Balkan territories at least slightly less of a mess.

Or maybe not. He'd be happy if it just made his workday easier.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.42.a: “I'd rather get paid to be bored than paid to be busy.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.43.desc:
“But where do we put the punch cards?”

The overseer sighed before embarking on his explanation for the tenth time today. “It doesn't use those.”

“Then how do we use it?”

The overseer felt a headache coming on. He closed his eyes and reminded himself how much these new Hitachi computers would increase efficiency. More efficiency was what the company desperately needed. The Italian shipping industry was growing faster and faster, and keeping up technologically was a necessity.

If only he could get his employees to understand it.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.43.a: “But how do you turn it on?”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.44.desc:
The teenagers in the urban football field clogged around the newly imported Sony radio. They were all attempting to configure it, to find a source for music. They hoped it would play songs they would come to know from the concerts they went to when they were young. One teenager grabbed the instruction manual from the packaging, torn apart considerably from excitement. From what he saw, however, he could not understand the instructions as only English, German, and Japanese were in the manual. Another teenager grabbed it and quickly found the Spanish and Portuguese sections of the manual, which in turn led to the first teenager ridiculed for missing something “obvious.” They began to argue with each other and placed bets on whose team would lose.

The other teenagers twisting the knob of the radio were in amazement as the radio began to produce the songs some appreciated. The Spanish teenagers were elated hearing “Y Sabes Bien.” But the Portuguese teens were displeased at the music, thinking it wasn't including them. So they twisted the knob until they found a Portuguese song that would please them. Turning the knob twice, the Portuguese teens found “Mas, Que Nada” on the radio. The faces of the Spanish teens as they were getting ready for their football match became displeased hearing the songs changing. They looked back at the radio and saw the Portuguese teens happy with their decisions.

The Spanish teenagers changed it back to the music they liked. After that, the Portuguese teens changed the radio to the music they liked. Soon, all the teens were fighting for the radio, changing the station back and forth. The Portuguese teens grabbed the radio and began to hog it while the Spanish teens tried to grab it off him. However, after one of the Spanish teens had successfully got ahold of it, the radio slipped out of their hands and fell into a broken state.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.45.desc:
The sun rose upon the worn-down Iberian government building of Tangier, but the money they received from Iberia wasn't much to fund anything except a few repairs. The cracked windows showed the exotic coastline, just barely out of reach. Getting sent here was like a fate worse than hell, repeating the same action while burning under the intense heat. The only thing to battle the heat was a simple water dispenser that was half-empty most of the time.

Today, the small office was cramped with a construction crew, installing a new air conditioner labeled: “MATSUSHITA ELECTRIC INDUSTRIAL CO.” It was from the lands of the far east, from Guangdong, a new weapon for the battle against the raging heat of Morocco. The office was quiet, without conversation to drown out the laborers' small stamping sounds and footsteps, but no words were needed to show what they were thinking. Where the bureaucrats once looked miserable, with distraught expressions and sweat pouring down their bodies, they now look more at ease, slightly more relaxed in the breeze from the air conditioner. They would still sweat in the heat, but it didn't show through their shirts.

In the weeks that followed, the efficiency of this office rose along with the employees' newfound second wind. It was a rise in productivity that wouldn't go unnoticed by the Iberians on the continent, who all found themselves thinking:
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.46.desc:
The AAS in Iberia had the most important job: locating, countering, and ending terrorists. The majority of the AAS' job was sifting through hundreds of reports, sifting through hundreds of reports to decipher the exact location of their base of operations. But the terrorists continued to change their base of operations; otherwise, the terrorists would already be in jail. Humans couldn't discover where the base could be, so the Iberians had to use something new to find the terrorists.

The new computers from Fujitsu were going to be a gamble from the Iberians; however, they were willing to try anything. The machine roared to life, tasked with finding the most discreet and hidden terrorists. The computers showed “FUJITSU LIMITED” text on a white screen, slowly fading into nothingness, showing nothing but a flashing white rectangle ready for input. Hurriedly, the AAS laborers grabbed thousands of documents from their registry and hurried to see what the computers would do next with this newfound information. After the grueling hours of getting the documents registered onto the computer, the computer projected the map of Iberia. This map contained all the terrorist attacks, reported the possible bases of operations, and even predicted potential targets.

The computers showed where the CNT-FAI bases could be, generalized in a specific area. Yes, sometimes the computer was wrong, with incorrect data. But it still saved lives through their outputs, stopping the terrorists dead in their tracks. And the Caudillos, looking at the successes, wrote a letter to Fujitsu: “The Iberian government is grateful for the assistance of the Fujitsu computer, and the successes it has caused for the AAS. Our gratitude is indebted towards your company.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.46.a: “Fujitsu condemns all terrorists, at home or abroad.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.47.desc:
The Miranda Dam was the pinnacle of Iberian unity. It stood between the internal borders of Spain and Portugal. It began construction in 1955, and only recently has it been finished. As the Iberian market began to expand, it was only natural they needed more advanced components for their dams. The Iberian government would seek the Hitachi Ltd. Company for their advanced computers. Their technology should hopefully erase the problems within the dam's energy output.

The Miranda Dam awaited the Hitachi computers. Its bulky exterior barely fit through the door, and the plug with its wires dragged across the floor. The technician's desk had the computer put on it, with its complete exterior filling the desk halfway. The technician stared at the screen, filling in the data from the electricity gathered, then finally, routing the plugs and hooking up the cables to the dam proper. Now, it was time to see the fruits of their labor.

It was successful in this opportunity, and the dam saw a 23% increase in the total hydroelectric energy withholding power outages in the Northern Portuguese and the Central Spanish regions. The Iberian government couldn't ignore such a dramatic increase in energy and saw the source of this increase. Immediately, this caused orders of Hitachi computers on a nationwide scale. Soon, the dams in Iberia were running on Hitachi engineering.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.47.a: The magic hand of Hitachi blesses everyone.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.48.desc:
The first cord entered, and a crack emanated as the machine came to life. Adnan's ears were pierced by the screeching of the machine, and after a few moments of tampering with the dials, he managed to get the buzzing to halt. The noise gave way to silence, before suddenly roaring to life once more. “HOW HAPPY IS THE ONE WHO SAYS I AM A TURK!”

Adnan jumped and clapped with glee. The Sony amplifier was sent directly to the small party office in Tunceli from the CHP's headquarters in Ankara. It had arrived late, and he spent the last hour of his shift fidgeting with cables in an attempt to unscramble the machine's function, but he had finally done it to astounding results: the sound was so pristine that he was taken aback. With that done, he left the office, marching back home to rest for the day after an exhausting and tiresome shift.

As morning came anew, Adnan awoke to a city abuzz with conspiracy. He passed by his neighbour, Cemal, a bearded man whose build seemed intimidating were it not for his passionate eccentricity, with a new legend to tell for each day. Some were amusing, some were nonsensical, but Adnan would always listen; today's legend struck him as extraordinary odd, even when compared to the rest. Cemal told him that the Ghazi was still alive, hidden somewhere here in Tunceli and that his voice could be heard emanating within the city.

Adnan laughed and carried on with his trek to work, but to his surprise, the small party office in Tunceli that sat isolated and undisturbed within the city's exterior was now surrounded by a sea of men. The truth suddenly came to him: he had forgotten to unplug the amplifier last night and the sheer quality of the sound had deluded many into believing Atatürk himself was now walking among them.

With a gleeful smile forming on his face, Adnan took to the masses to clear the misconceptions.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.48.a: “We cannot revive the Ghazi, but we will forever carry his ideals!”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.49.desc:
At times, it felt like there was nothing in the world that could alleviate the overbearing Syrian heat. Mehmet felt the brunt of it most days - going on patrol in the middle of the desert at high noon in full military uniform made a man feel as if he had left the living world and entered some grand, cosmic oven.

And yet, as he re-entered the military base, Mehmet was met with precious, cold respite. A few weeks ago a new air conditioner from Matsushita had been installed, and it had made a world of difference to him and the other troops. The cold was limited to one room alone, granted, which made it something of a haven for scorched troops after a patrol.

Throwing off his headgear, and heavy vest, Mehmet collapsed onto one of the nearby benches, savoring the chill. He knew that historically, poor conditions had been the death of older Turkish soldiers. It would be back out into the heat tomorrow, but he had the advantage of the aircon that they never had. As long as he had a nice, cool base to come back to, then Mehmet would be fine.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.50.desc:
“An incident has been reported 3 miles north of Sulaymaniyah. Activity has increased amongst rebels in that area by...” The administrator tapped a few keys on the computer, before a number popped up on screen. “...30% in the last few months.”

Bogdan nodded, a severe expression on his face. “Very well. Is there a specific pattern in their recent attacks?”

“Hold on a moment. If I just...” He clicked a few more buttons, before a few boxes popped up on the screen. “They all appear to be localized around the northern and eastern half of the city. If we increase security around those areas, we stand a greater chance of catching them out.”

The other man nodded, genuinely impressed. These new Fujitsu computers were well out of his understanding, but he would be damned if they weren't useful in catching the terrorist bastards.

“Very well. I'll have 3 more officers on patrol per area and 2 more patrol cars. Anything else that magic box has for us?” he joked. The administrator shook his head, not seeming to understand.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.51.desc:
It brought great pleasure to Mohammed to no longer have to sift through mountains of paperwork every week. Before the new Hitatchi computer arrived at the mill, he would end up sitting in the office for hours on end, looking at the driest possible reports on steel output, worker productivity, and costs. As the general manager for the mill, such a task would fall to him if all else failed.

Now? With a few pushes of a button, he could simply let the computer take care of the accounting. And by god, was it needed.

Packing up his supplies for the day, Mohammed looked out of his office window below, seeing the many workers toiling away. He nodded to himself, satisfied. They were working at the exact level local Turkish businesses like his needed to be at to compete with the German competition in Reichwerke.

As he left the factory and felt the hot Turkish air on his skin, Mohammed smiled. The future would be bright for him and his workers if technology kept progressing at the rate it was.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.52.desc:
“One more thing,” Ramón said, as he reached into his pocket and tossed Juan a bundle of American dollars. “Now get going, you're wasting the morning.”

Juan started his truck, and began traveling towards the border station. The drive from the Mexican warehouse in Nuevo Laredo to its American counterpart in Laredo only took about fifteen minutes, twenty on a bad day. Juan glanced through the back window, happy to see that all of the goods had survived the many potholes littering the roads. Arriving at the border, he squabbled briefly with the border officer, who demanded twice the usual rate for his “services,” forcing Juan to hand him an even more extortionate bribe than usual. Upon arriving at the Texan warehouse, Juan disabled the engine and leaned over the window to greet the American manager.

In broken English, he communicated, “Same as always, Sony electronics, fresh from Japan.” Juan hesitated a moment. “Border is tighter now, our rate just went up 30 percent.”

“Fine, this had better be good.” The American scowled, before directing a half-dozen American men to unload the truck, bringing the boxes, brightly marked SONY, into the warehouse.

Juan started his truck and began traveling back towards the border station. This run had been fairly smooth, all things considered.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.52.a: Only a few dozen more to go.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.53.desc:
Javier sighed in relief as the newly installed air conditioner finally began working, blanketing him in a blissful, soothing cold. Not every minor official was getting one, especially not those stationed in a minor city surrounded by the Sonora desert, but not every official had connections with the shipping industry. Matsushita got their cut, his people got their cut, and he got a brand-new air conditioner. He didn't make deals this clean very often.

Glancing outside, Javier felt the smallest amount of pity, noticing that not a single window that he could see held an air conditioner unit. All of the shipments, Javier reflected, were going to the men in suits, not the ones in the streets. He was lucky to get one at all, he thought.

Javier sat at the desk and cleared his mind. He did important work; it only made sense that he be rewarded in kind. If someone wanted cool air, he thought, they could come work for him. And hey, it was a lot easier to manage papers at twenty degrees Celsius.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.54.desc:
“And this, people,” David paused for a moment, “this is what it's all about.”

David typed a command into the display computer, and a list of names and faces streamed down the screen. The security ministers attending the conference gasped, as the images were intimately familiar. The faces of one of the most active terrorist organizations in Mexico, covered the screen, accompanied by their names, known aliases, and latest recorded locations.

“As you can see, computing technology is good for more than just accounting. This machine can compile all known information about every terrorist in the country, in a fraction of the time it would take a human,” David explained. “By offloading menial labor to computers, we can dedicate more manpower and resources to bringing these radicals down.”

The audience began murmuring, much to David's delight. The officials seemed to be hooked. An elderly man in the front discussed potential uses with his neighbor, and an officer in the back grinned, imagining the possibilities.

“This is your chance to get in on the ground floor,” David proclaimed. “This is your chance to be the vanguard of Fujistu computing. If this is what they can do now, who knows what they'll do in ten years? What about twenty?”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.55.desc:
PEMEX headquarters in Mexico City could often be a quiet place. There were always many employees taking trips out to one oilfield or another, leaving a skeleton crew to hold the fort. When the annual production reports came in, though, you could hardly walk ten steps without bumping into someone.

The CEO of PEMEX sat at his office, tapping a pencil against the side of his head and listening to the cacophony of ringing phones. This was the worst time of year - not the production reports themselves, but presenting his own report to the President afterwards. He and his ministers would invariably demand another impossible increase in production for next year.

As secretaries began to carry papers into his office, he took a moment to flick through a few pages. An odd figure caught his eye - surely there was a missing decimal point there? 12% annual growth in net operating profit? He grabbed the papers and took a closer look.

It was true, and the culprit, it seemed, was Hitachi. The computers the government had ordered imported that year were making waves at the rigs, making possible a massive streamlining effort in the company's logistics department. The CEO hesitated for a few seconds, before rushing to the phone and dialling the President's appointments secretary.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.55.a: Perhaps he might even be happy with this one...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.56.desc:
Pedro shouted for the ball, making a run past the midfield line, and João fired a quick pass through to him. Sprinting down towards the opposing goal, a beefy center-back stood in his way, crouching, ready to dart to either side. Pedro grinned at him, made to pass the ball around his left side, but instead chipped it over his head and darted past him. Other forwards were running up on either side, but Pedro had it covered himself. He switched the ball onto his favored left foot and sent it rocketing into the back of the net. The keeper never had a chance.

“GARRINCHA!” yelled Teodoro from the sidelines, holding a bottle of beer in the air. He took a deep swig and sauntered over to Lila, who was noticeably not celebrating her boyfriend's goal. Instead, she was fiddling with some strange device Teodoro had never seen before.

“The fuck is that?” Teodoro asked her, trying his best not to slur his words, and hiccupped slightly.

“Radio,” she replied, wrinkling her nose in concentration. “It's from Japan, some company called Sony. Mother bought it last week. I just don't know...”

She hit a few buttons, and suddenly Ronnie Cord was blaring at top volume across the beachside of Rio de Janeiro. Cheers went up from the guys playing football, and some of the bathers were even coming along to see what was going on. Lila patted her radio, and she and Teodoro began to sing along in raucous harmony.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.56.a: Hi, hi, Johnny, hi, hi, Alfredo!
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.57.desc:
After what seemed like an eternity, the lunch horn sounded, and Henrique threw down his shovel. He stretched his back, groaned as joints and bones cracked, and wiped rivulets of sweat off his brow. The heat of the jungle lay across him like a wet cloth, and in the distance the city of Manaus shimmered. Even the trees seemed to be sweating, moisture pouring off them and spattering the workers below.

As he trudged over to their temporary camp, he spotted the rest of his fellow workers on the Trans-Amazonian Highway crowding around a corner of the mess tent. Curious, he walked over to them. As he tried to muscle through the throng to see what was going on, he was met with complaints and grumbles.

“Hey, come on man, I've only been here five minutes,” one guy complained as Henrique shoved past him.

As he broke through into the front of the crowd, cool air washed over him, and in that moment Henrique could think of no other sensation he had enjoyed nearly as much in his forty years on earth. The air was coming from some strange machine that had been bolted down to a corner of the tent, and bore a logo reading 'MATSUSHITA.'

“My God,” someone next to him said, “I never want to leave.”

Laughs and a chorus of agreement greeted that statement. Henrique couldn't help but smile. He'd been planning on quitting this shitty job within the next few weeks, and knew for a fact there were others in the dorm who were going to do the same.

Maybe they'd reconsider. Summer was hot anywhere in Brazil, after all. And it wasn't like any of them would ever be able to afford this machine on their own.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.58.desc:
Brazil was a big country. Too big for its government. All the numbers and graphs and various other pieces of paper the people at the top demanded were, quite frankly, impossible to supply. It had all started with Kubitschek, and only gotten worse from there. None of the politicians seemed to have any idea what it actually took to get the data they wanted. Right now, Afonso and a staff of five were engaged in the task of compiling the year's economic data from the state of Minas Gerais. Impossible - they'd take some real numbers, make some 'estimates,' and call it a day.

At least, usually. But today, a special consignment had been flown into Brasília from the port of Rio de Janeiro. Afonso was currently staring at one of the items in that cargo, a Fujitsu FACOM 230-10 computing system.

Hesitantly - he was still getting used to this novelty device - he punched some numbers into the system, and glanced at the hefty manual he'd been provided. He flicked through the pages until he had found what he wanted, and slowly typed the commands into the machine. The printer growled, and spat out a neat graph that would have taken him hours to make on his own.

Despite himself, Afonso grinned.

It was slow going on account of his inexperience, but the computer seemed to make up for his human deficits a thousandfold. By the time he left the office that day, he'd finished nearly his entire work for the week - no 'estimates' required.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.58.a: The price of progress is paper.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.59.desc:
Yasuoka hated Brazil.

Guangdong was hot and humid in summer, absolutely. Japan could be too, if the weather was particularly unforgiving. But nothing there compared to the absolute hell that was the Amazon at midday in high summer. He scrubbed his face with a handkerchief for the millionth time that day and stared up at the massive bulldozer. Toyoda, that lucky bastard, was up there in the air conditioned cabin, helping some Brazilian worker figure out the controls. Hitachi had shipped this monster over a few days ago, promising the Brazilian government that it would help double construction speed on this section of the road.

As he watched, the bulldozer lurched forward unsteadily like a drunk. A few workers had to dive out of the way to avoid it. Slowly, very slowly, the bulldozer's blade lowered, and it charged into a large mound of dirt. The blade was stuck in there for a while, but eventually Toyoda was able to back it out, carrying a huge chunk of dirt in the bulldozer's blade.

The assembled workers cheered, seeing the bulldozer do an hour of work in just a minute or so. Yasuoka produced another handkerchief from his pocket and swiped it lamely across his forehead. Hopefully the Brazilians would have this figured out soon, and they could all go home. There was another monster coming in soon - a crane, assembled by parts in Guangdong and shipped over to be assembled in Nowheresville, Amazonas.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.59.a: Hopefully it had air conditioning too.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.60.desc:
Maria was burning the bread.

She growled and took the crisped loaf out of the oven, which stuttered and belched smoke. Waving the smoke away out the open window, she placed the loaf on a cutting board and tried to slice away the most charred parts.

Behind her, a small Sony radio foretold doom and gloom. Roberto had bought the damned thing last week, and it had done nothing but cry apocalypse ever since. Political instability, army units in Buenos Aires, the lira falling, and always Perón, Perón, Perón. Every so often, she wished it would just shut up.

Outside, a horn blared, and Maria looked out to see her four children scurrying out of the path of a passing car. She scowled, and hollered at them to come inside. Her eldest went to pick up the football they were playing with, but the bastard in the car drove over it and burst it.

As the children stared forlornly at the broken football, Maria sighed, and twisted the knob on the radio. As luck would have it, she managed to find a jazz station. She took a moment to sag back against the countertop, savoring the brief quiet as she listened to her children's footsteps pattering closer. No doubt they were about to demand she buy a new ball for them.

Didn't they know the lira was unappreciated, or whatever they were saying it was?
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.61.desc:
The kids were getting restless. Felipe clearly didn't know what he was doing, crawling around all over the big silver box with a screwdriver. Juanita shushed them all, slapped the youngest son when he decided his tongue was too big for his boots, and sent concealed glares Felipe's way. He'd spent almost their entire disposable income for the month on this little gadget.

As Felipe played with the antennae and consulted a manual he definitely couldn't read well enough to understand, the TV suddenly flicked on, and the children cheered. 'Titanes en el Ring' was on, and in glorious color!

Juanita had been skeptical, she had to admit. What was wrong with good old black and white, she'd asked Felipe. They already knew what color people were, didn't they? But no, this really was different.

As the wrestlers pummeled and slammed each other to the ground, extravagant outfits displayed in vibrant hues on the TV screen, Felipe and the kids shouted and egged on their favorites. Juanita sighed, smiled faintly at the whole spectacle, and went to enjoy a nice cup of tea.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.62.desc:
Keeping track of different army units might have been merely a routine procedure in countries like the United States, but in Argentina, where the army thought quite highly of itself, the task gained a certain urgency. The Ministry of Defence was nothing if not old school, relying on phone transcripts and reams of hand-drawn maps to figure out where everyone was. So it had been for decades, and so it would be for decades more.

At least, until the government had decided it wanted some of Fujitsu's toys. A shipment of Fujitsu computers had arrived at the Ministry's Buenos Aires headquarters that morning, and a horde of clerks were currently engaged in inputting huge quantities of data into the machines.

Given that Fujitsu's hefty manuals had to be consulted at essentially every step of this process, sometimes multiple times, this was not a quick endeavor. At least the computers themselves weren't prone to such deficiencies.

Little by little, as the grand picture of Argentina's military infrastructure was fed into the network, the computers generated huge tables, containing the location, equipment composition and current status of every military unit in the country, down to company level. The army of printers roared, spitting out tables and charts that would have taken weeks to plot out by hand, all ready to be sent up to the Ministry bigwigs.

Now they'd just have to figure out how to make them do strategic calculations.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.62.a: A slow but irreversible tide of change.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.63.desc:
Every dictator worth their salt knew how to make the trains run on time. Apparently Argentina, a supposedly liberal democracy with an occasional side job as a military state, did not possess such knowledge. Breakage along the country's freight networks was high, unacceptably high, and it was throttling Argentina's investment potential. You never knew how long a shipment was going to take, even if the rail trip was only supposed to take a few hours.

Hitachi and Mangyō, though - they knew how to make trains run on time. In Manchuria, they'd proven it, and now they were over in Argentina to tackle the gargantuan task of bringing the modern railway to a country that seemed to make a fetish out of antiquated infrastructure.

Their vehicle was Hitachi Rail, a specially created subsidiary company. Hitachi Rail shipped engines from Guangdong and personnel from Manchuria, as well as masses of manual laborers to change the country's rail gauge from their previous system based around the British Indian model.

Hitachi's help didn't come cheap, of course - the bastards seemed intent on swindling the government at every opportunity, adding triple digit markups on engines and signal infrastructure. But, even as Argentina poured money into Hitachi's open mouth, the rail network slowly ground forwards into the modern age.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.63.a: And that, really, was all that mattered.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.64.desc:
The sun was setting behind the Andes Mountains. Arturo fumbled with his keys as he locked up his store, a secret smile across his face. If he had a few more days of business like this, he might be able to keep this store afloat.

It all started when the government began an effort to sell televisions in a campaign to improve Chilean lives. Soon, everyone wanted a television, and every store in the nation was competing for that sale - from the largest of retailers to humble Radio Arturo.

But Arturo had a trick up his sleeve, something the department stores couldn't touch. When the government drive was announced, he had already bought a shipment of Sonys. Now, they were flying off the shelves. It was as if every man in Santiago was rushing to Radio Arturo, and each was buying the same thing.

Arturo turned to stare at his display television - a Sony, of course. It was remarkable the extent to which Chileans admired that machine. Its picture quality was certainly remarkable, but Arturo knew things were never that simple. Perhaps it was simply the legend of it, the mystique. This product had been shipped from some far-off province of China, a land only known for the quality of its goods. Now, it could sit in your living room.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.64.a: Even a man like Arturo was transfixed.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.65.desc:
The Matsushita Tape Recorder was a truly splendid device, and undoubtedly one of the best recorders on the market. With an almost unmatchable clarity of sound, the Matsushita could store hours of conversation and reproduce their every word, preserving these complex discussions for time immemorial.

In other words, it was a politician's nightmare.

Yet in the Chilean Chamber of Deputies, where parties seemed to split like splintering wood, where arguments exploded over the simplest of topics, there was no method better for keeping track of the chaos than the tape recorder. Placed upon the desks of the chamber's secretaries, this new technology allowed for every debate to be scratched into polyester and sent off to the radios, for all of Chile to hear.

Certainly, many politicians hated it. As their limousines drove down the winding streets of Santiago, they'd listen to their car radios and hear their disagreements splattered into the airwaves like bugs on their windshield. Then, usually, they'd tell their driver to turn it off.

But the citizens of Chile loved it, so strongly that not even the most irritated deputy could disagree. From far in the north to the icy plains of Patagonia, the people found another window into the lives of their politicians, into that mess in Santiago that occupied everyone's attention. They knew just a little more about the nation - warts and all.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.65.a: A man in Chile knows more than a man in Guangdong ever will.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.66.desc:
From the corner of his eye, Gabriel noticed that the Fujitsu had begun blinking and buzzing, so loud that a thin layer of snow fell from the station's roof and past the dusty windows. Gabriel turned from his instruments to watch it. For the first time in weeks, something was printing.

In the last few years, this desolate Patagonian weather station seemed all but forgotten by Santiago. As military fears grew and the economy shrunk, there was no more demand for maintaining this vessel. Instead, it had been left to the elements, set to become another victim of the weather it was meant to detect. Yet even as the lights flickered and windows cracked, Santiago sent Gabriel this teleprinter.

A coil of paper spilled out of the Fujitsu like a film reel. Gabriel ripped it off at the perforations and began to read.

“Argentinian soldiers spotted at the border, near Los Lagos. Remain on high alert until further orders.”

Gabriel sighed, pulling a rifle from below his desk and his heavy coat from a desk chair. As he unlatched the doors and climbed onto the ceiling, he thought about that new computer Fujitsu Limited, titans of science, could have sold the Chilean government finely-tuned weather instruments, observing systems, a grand suite of tools to help Chile understand its geography. Instead, they bought an alarm system across the nation, and the guns to hide behind each printer.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.66.a: Even tools of science become tools of war.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.661.desc:
A sample computer sat on a table in a presidential stateroom someplace in La Moneda Palace, in Santiago of Chile. Next to it stood the President of the Chilean Republic, an interpreter, and the Chief Executive of the State of Guangdong. This was not what Ibuka Masaru was used to—but Salvador Allende had personally invited him to Santiago to personally explain the applications of Fujitsu computers. He obligingly accepted; the better to get away from Akio and all the other wailing idiots in the Legislative Council.

While two men, named 'Puratsu' and 'Reterie', chuckled at the computer, making a pun about 'com-puta-dora' that the interpreter declined to translate, Ibuka went off on a tangent. “See here, Mister President, I plan to have the economic control mechanisms and police deployments automatically delegated as I improve my computer systems.”

Suddenly Allende interrupted the interpreter. “Wait a moment, Chief Executive. Would you say that these marvellous devices of yours would also work for sending and receiving economic data and benefits for popular usage?”

Ibuka, a bit thrown, answered the interpreter, who was himself confused, saying, “Tell him, ... uh, yes.”

At that the Chief Executive swore he saw stars in his interlocutor's eyes. Allende called his finance minister and wrote out an order to him on official letterhead; the man nodded and handed the document to one of Ibuka's assistants, whose eyes boggled. As that happened the President turned to Ibuka and said, “I'll buy your entire stock. Deliver them at once!”

Ibuka stammered out, “Y-yes, I can see to that at once,” and began to bark out orders to his men in the room. Unbeknownst even to Allende, this meant the beginning of a new system of governance based on computers.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.661.a: And Fujitsu processing was to serve as the foundation for it.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.67.desc:
The technicians' trucks kicked up the dirt as they pulled off the main roadway and towards the foreman's office. They roared past Arturo's head, and he saw the Hitachi logos emblazoned on their car doors. Must be here to install the new computers, he thought to himself.

Arturo tried to ignore it. He needed to focus on his work - one incorrect detonation, and he'd find himself back on the streets, searching for work with a few less fingers. Yet as his face grew caked with dirt and sweat, as he loaded more and more ore into his truck, he could not help but think about it. What on earth had motivated the foreman to purchase such a thing?

He thought about the copper in those computers. Arturo may have been a miner, but he still prided himself in keeping with the news. He knew where this copper was going. Once he slung the dust and rock into his truck and drove it off to the refinery, it was processed and rolled into fine metal wires, and sent off to the electronic developers of the world. One such place was Guangdong. There was a real possibility that metal from this very mine was currently knocking around the foreman's new computer.

Arturo turned away with a bitter frown. The foreman's office seemed to get nicer and nicer. Through his window, a pit into the earth's crust only grew more and more vast.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.67.a: Workers of the world, united in misery.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.68.desc:
“It's just not enough,” Morita sighed, letting the report he was reading fall back to the table. “This country is huge, but there's no money here. Even if we sell at prices that just barely break even, practically nobody in China will be able to afford our products. We'll have to market to the wealthy coastal oligarchs, at least for now.”

“In a purely monetary sense, yes,” Li replied, “but we have other priorities that China can help us achieve. If we are seen to help bring modernity to China, we will gain favor with the Chinese population back home. The occasional promotional campaign and giveaway, I think, will help us out tremendously in this regard.”

“Our investors won't like it. They're already skeptical enough of China as a business proposition - we need to find some profits somewhere.”

“We can adopt both strategies. China is poor but growing quickly. We'll secure the area around the Yangtze delta first. The investors will get their dividends, and we'll get points with our workers.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.69.desc:
In Shanghai, a small restaurant owner has run out of money. People just aren't buying his food anymore, and the rents are only getting higher. As he locks his doors for the last time, he turns and is surprised to see a man with a briefcase and a gleaming suit greeting him. He is from Sony, he says, and he'd like to buy out this establishment. A few months later, the man passes by his old store to see it replaced by a sleek dealership, packed with radios and audio recorders.

In Nanjing, the bottom floor of a luxurious hotel has been transformed into a showroom of the future. Wires snake across the floor, criss-crossing and darting around each other as smiling salesmen show curious guests around the rooms. Sony's audio systems are everywhere, and the wealthy Chinese guests ooh and aah over the latest technological innovations.

Outside the big cities, in the towns of Suzhou and Nantong, armies of junior Cheung Kong men descend on the marketplaces and town squares. They loudly peddle modern audio-visual systems at deeply discounted prices - sometimes, when they have surplus stock, they can even be persuaded to give them away for free.

The Yangtze delta is now saturated with Sony, and everyone from the lowliest villager to the wealthiest oligarch knows of the scrappy entrepreneurs out of Guangdong.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.69.a: If you're going to announce your presence, do it loudly.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.70.desc:
As Li and Morita got off the phone with their respective Chinese offices, they immediately arranged to meet each other at Sony headquarters. They exchanged notes on profit margins, demographic targets, and local commercial networks. Then the discussion turned to the wider aims of the whole ordeal.

“We're unbeatable in the delta,” Li proclaimed. “Our logos are everywhere, and the urban core of Nanjing and Shanghai are swallowing up our products as fast as we can ship them out there.”

“And the rural areas?” Morita asked.

“Not so successful. They know of us, and we've had a few sales here and there, but overall the people out there are too busy trying to put food on the table. They're not going to be buying audio-visual equipment any time soon.”

“At least our workers are happy,” Morita said. “I've even gotten a few letters from our rank-and-file people, thanking me for giving something back to the Chinese mother country. I've been wondering if I should report them to the Kenpeitai.”

The two men chuckled, and clinked glasses. No, the police would not need to be kept informed of this. Happy workers meant productive workers - however that happiness might be achieved. Here in Guangdong, that was rare enough.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.71.desc:
In the best of times, inland China would not have been a very good vacation spot for a Japanese businessman. Apart from the suffocating heat and choking humidity, there was the additional health hazard of a bullet through the skull that could put a serious damper on the precious few days off they were afforded. Loosening his tie - an otherwise unforgiveable laxity in manners - Matsushita Masaharu's personal aide glanced at the green, rolling countryside and wondered why his boss chose to visit this particular bomb-cratered rural shithole rather than any other. But, of course, he voiced nothing - the boss knew best.

The heat was getting to the boss, too, and he was starting to regret coming with a subordinate. However, the part of his mind that was completely divorced from material circumstances was working overtime. There could be no one in the world that enjoyed weather like this - and while the average peasant might simply grin and bear with whatever stained teeth they had left, the portly warlords that had grown fat from the peace would not.

Once upon a time, Japanese military engineers produced machines that transformed the Chinese landscape into a boiling hell of mud, blood, and wasted souls. Now, under his leadership, her engineers would bring that most basic of industrialized luxuries - temperature control - to this savage land. A few muscles twitched near the corners of his mouth that once a long time ago might have produced a smile. It was almost poetic.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.71.a: Poetic nonsense can stuff itself. Time to send some letters.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.72.desc:
“Well? How has the product rollout fared?”

“Very well, sir. The customers - that is to say, the warlords - are immensely pleased with the product. A source of mine informed me that since his was installed, a certain one has not even turned it off a single time-”

“And the engineer's reports?”

“ -ah. Initially, they faced many difficulties with designing a model capable of handling the Chinese heat without itself overheating, but by adapting several features on our already existing models, they report that the current design should be easily adaptable for mass production shortly. In fact, we may now have a product for other tropical-”

“What about the rest of the people?”

“Beg pardon, sir.”

“The Chinese people - the millions of potential customers that have watched as we fanned and cooled their overlords and now probably wonder why they have to suffer in the heat. After all, I was the one that ordered the survey of them under your name. Did you not receive the result yet?”

“...I have, sir. The result is not... exceptionally positive. It seems we have contributed somewhat to a growth in social tension, with the product as a focal point. We may have to consider increased security.”

“Hmm. There is another way to consider this instead - that we have just received confirmation of very high demand of our air-conditioners by a very large consumer base. If we cannot sell to the customers, why not sell to the local governments that tax all their income away anyways? We can sell it to them as both a public service and a means of reducing local unrest.”

“...Local unrest that we caused, sir. ”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.72.a: After all, the best markets are the ones you create for yourself.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.73.desc:
Once upon a time, the princes and peasants alike of China's inner provinces - the heart and soul of the nation - found themselves boiling away in the humid summer heat, unable to do naught but pray for rain. Those with money spent it on fans, chilled water, cool stone houses and every means of making shade known to man. Those without continued boiling. One day, they thought, some wizard or genie would arrive and solve their problems for good.

Now, the new princes sat in offices that were almost freezing, shivering slightly as they sought to impress every visitor with their mastery of the weather. Outside these offices, in bus stands, tea stalls, and even sometimes just in the open, crowds of the new peasants congregated under the blissful cover of cold granted by the Matsushita air-conditioners as they thrummed away noisily, beating back the heat.

Meanwhile, Matsushita Masaharu himself stared at an accounts sheet that was certainly not anything from a fairy tale - it was better. The air-conditioning programme had proven so popular that even coastal provinces were sending in their orders by the hundreds. And this was no simple, one-off purchase either - they needed the machines, technicians, repairmen, spare parts, all of which he would be only too happy to keep providing. With this capital flow, there was now a sound footing to begin investigating muscling their way in to foreign markets. More importantly, however...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.73.a: Every man, woman, and child looks at the Matsushita logo, and sees a wizard that grants their wishes.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.74.desc:
China had been an investment.

It was an investment the Empire of Japan had paid for with blood, toil, and treasure. It had left millions of her sons dead, and though she had emerged the victor, the years since had shown that the nature of that victory was a slow strangulation with the laurels. Ibuka Masaru had grappled with the question of how to turn the black hole that was China into an opportunity to finally begin reaping the returns that should have come long ago - and, of course, for Fujitsu to take first picks.

It was with this mindset that he looked into the sunken face of Gao Zongwu, the President of China. He listened about how Nanjing could barely communicate with massive city centres like Chongqing, despite how important they were for tax collection and policing. He heard about how the Centre received reports of bandit attacks and unsurrendered soldiers - all these years later - days or even weeks after they had happened. Finally, the President decided to let him in on the big secret - despite China covering such a great span on the map, the reality was that the country was really just the coast and the cities close to the coast. Everything else was one great question mark.

In his engineer's mind, one thing became clearer and clearer. This was not a question of legitimacy, or force of arms - those things were important, but secondary. No, this was simply a matter of communications. And this was exactly what Fujitsu dealt with. Ibuka Masaru glanced at the interpreter, and began.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.74.a: “I trust you are aware of what a computer is, Mr. President?”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.75.desc:
In a dimly lit room guarded by a single man with a pistol at the door sat the most powerful man in China - on paper. This was an ad-hoc meeting, guaranteed only by Fujitsu's clout and reputation, and in the back of his mind Gao Zongwu could not rule out the possibility that this would be the pathetic way his death was going to be recorded in the history books.

His gloomy thoughts were sharply interrupted by a burst of glaring light from the projector. A map of China, with the major cities highlighted, stared back at him. As the presenter continued, lines like spiderwebs grew from the bolded names, connecting further and further - and obscuring the smaller names entirely. The true scale of Ibuka's plan became evident.

“Fujitsu's computer centres have been finished in Shanghai, Nanjing, and Beijing, and have already been interconnected. Contracts to process the import-export data from the major ports have also been finished, and currently the Nanjing office is able accelerate the process so considerably it has actually facilitated the export of more goods to the Sphere. Currently, we are also working on lines to Ningbo and Fuzhou, which may require extensions to the budget as outlined in the document given, and we have also begun computerizing the records of the police forces of the three cities currently active under the scheme. Additionally...”

The man went on and on. However, the President realized almost immediately what was really being offered here. The chance to see China whole again - if not politically, then at least in communications.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.75.a: “Please tell Mr. Ibuka that he will have my full cooperation in expanding the programme.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.76.desc:
It had started so well.

Nanjing, Beijing, and Shanghai had been interlinked and computerized almost as straightforwardly as it would have been in the Home Islands. Ningbo and Fuzhou had presented some difficulties, but they could be covered with the enhanced budget granted after the Port of Shanghai almost doubled its daily loading capacity in a matter of months.

But Chengdu and Chongqing had dashed those hopes to pieces. Apparently the damned barbarian warlords refused to understand that all they had to do was cooperate with the Centre, and it would help them reap more in taxes. Even if they cooperated, the question remained of how even to maintain the accounts - some parts of the country still used bookkeeping systems from the Qing era, whilst others simply adopted the Japanese method wholesale. In Yunnan, the question devolved even further to who was even in charge of the cities and towns - Taiyuan and Xian said one thing, Kunming said another, and meanwhile someone had already stolen the cables, wires, and computers.

Ibuka Masaru pressed his eyes shut, and once again reduced the problem to numbers, limits, and constraints. Focusing on inner China obsessively would be a total loss - but some advantages had been reaped. At considerable expense, Fujitsu had essentially become a key component of the government's administration - something that would certainly help in negotiations back at the Three Pearls. And one could always interpret this as an investment that could lead to more in the future. An investment...
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.76.a: Is that all China will ever be?
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.77.t: A Proposition, from One China to Another
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.77.desc:
The Chinese Minister of Finance was a diminutive man, thick rimmed glasses accenting his face - and the lack of statue. Komai took an immediate dislike for the man from his appearance, but he could stomach it for now. Zhou Fohai was known as a thoroughly corruptible man, which was why he now sat in the halls of Guangdong's great and mighty, gazing neutrally over his glasses at Komai himself.

“Do you have any idea why you're here?” Komai began with an equally neutral question.

“I think I have some idea, but I'd like to hear it from your mouth before I jump to any conclusions.” Good, he wasn't that dumb, at least.

“I hear that China is replete with unfulfilled construction contracts just waiting for the right bidder. Hitachi will take these contracts and will bring with it an arsenal of industrial equipment, both heavy and light, ready to be sold in bulk to any wanting governments. In exchange, you personally, will receive a cut of the profits and...” The check slid smoothly over the wooden tabletop, a sizable number printed clearly in firm strokes of black ink.

Zhou glanced down at the check with a hungry glimmer in his eyes before meeting Komai's gaze again. “I think the Republic would be quite amenable to such a proposition, one that is beneficial for China as a whole.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.77.a: The floodgates open, and capital flows north.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.78.desc:
Liao shuffled along the sidewalk, refusing to look up as he took his hour-long walk to work. Above hung an all-seeing eye, perched atop its ever-growing tower like a hawk, just waiting to strike its unassuming prey.

He couldn't understand what had prompted the government to agree to a deal with such a force, and yet the mancing eye now dominated the skyline of Shanghai, and he heard from a cousin that it was similar in Nanjing. Another cousin, one with roots in Manchukuo, had explained to him the symbol's full meaning. An involuntary shiver still ran up and down his spine when he thought about that conversation.

All over the massive cities, the eye of Hitachi encroached on rightful Chinese land, glaring down with menace and a million tiny grievances against perceived slights. It was a symbol and a promise: we are here, we are coming, and we are bringing a fate forestalled by your petty leaders.

Those leaders were receiving their fair share of complaints, and they knew of even more traded by bystanders, both on street corners and in secret meetings. Komai, in turn, knew that they could do nothing to stop the tide of Hitachi as it overtook their petty markets, for as he glanced at the gradually building numbers, he knew the truth.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.78.a: China would bow, would bend, and once broken, would open the doors to Hitachi's global dominance.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.79.desc:
It was a strange thing, Cao thought, that the eye only seemed more menacing when bathed in fire and casting malevolent, dancing shadows on the ground. Unfortunate, really.

One Hitachi construction site was in flames, but beyond the smoky bounds of the unfinished apartment complex, eyes loomed in every corner of the Yangtze River Delta these days. Nantong and Hangzhou were almost as bad as Shanghai and Nanjing, with new eyes popping up with nearly every new construction project issued from the Minister of Finance's office.

Komai was certain that Zhou Fohai was under pressure from other, less... flexible government officials to resist Hitachi's constant bidding out of any competition, and yet the Minister of Finance continued funneling incredibly lucrative deals out of China and into the pockets of Guangdong's finest executives. What Komai was uncertain of was whether Zhou did this out of genuine belief, personal enrichment, or some unknown factor. Likely a combination of the first two.

No matter why the deals went through, they did, and once they were completed, money rolled out of Chinese accounts and into Hitachi's. It was a monumental infusion of cash for the company as they tapped into a market rife with investment capital and lacking any competition that could stand up to Manchukuo's methods. Komai couldn't help but smile thinking back to his first meeting with Zhou. If only Guangdong itself was so easy.

Now, even as more and more reports of bombings and attacks on Hitachi assets in China emerged, Komai was content with his coffers. China was but a stepping stone, and it had provided the key to Hitachi's global future.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.79.a: The eye opens to the world.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.80.desc:
Mitsui. Sumitomo. Mitsubishi.

Names that conjured up old images in Morita's mind. Ibuka, Tokyo Telecommunications, and the horrors that came afterwards - the fear of the merciless bailiffs, the many nights he spent eating plain white rice on the floor of a dilapidated apartment in Honkon. He remembered selling his watch to a toothless peddler in an alleyway behind a restaurant for about half of what it was worth.

Yes, he and the Zaibatsu had met before. Now, with these men sitting before him, it all came flooding back. Neither Sumitomo nor Mitsui had bothered to show up, but Mitsubishi had sent some nonentity, and Toshiba had sent two - an audience for this farce.

Morita had to fight to keep his lip from curling. That bald man, the one with the ridiculous purple tie, Morita recognized him from long ago. One of Ibuka's lackeys, maybe? Whoever he was, he was currently flashing Morita a smile acidic enough to cut through steel girders.

“So...good...to see you again, Morita,” the bald man said, his rictus grin widening. How is President Li?“

The other representatives tried and failed to stifle their giggles. Morita ignored the bait. Once this meeting was over, the representatives would head back to their cars, and their chauffeurs would drive them out of the building's garage. As they turned the corner, they would spot a billboard advertising a TA-1120. It had just been put up this morning. Dozens more would join it over the coming weeks in major metropolitan areas, all coincidentally placed quite near local Zaibatsu headquarters.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.80.a: And that was something Morita would pay good money to see.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.81.desc:
Standing on the twelfth floor of the headquarters of Sony Japan, Morita gazed down with barely concealed satisfaction at the footpath outside the entrance to the building. A couple of photographers - young, by the looks of it - were scurrying around outside, taking pictures of the building from various angles. B-roll for a newspaper article. One spotted him at the window and quickly angled his camera towards him. Morita smiled and gave him a quick acknowledgement before turning away from the window.

The numbers were good. Very good. TVs, audio players, radios - all were flooding into the country at an astounding pace. Cheaper and better quality than the stale tripe offered by the Zaibatsu, the growing Japanese middle class couldn't get enough of Sony's products.

The image was clear as day in Morita's mind. Zaibatsu headquarters in uproar, interns dashing around and hiding to avoid the wrath of enraged senior executives. As Sony ate away at their margins, they would be forced to make layoffs, turf out the sinecures, trim the fat. Undoubtedly, many careers would be lost. It was all enough to make Morita's heart beat a little faster.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.82.desc:
No longer was Morita Akio forced to be content to deal with intermediaries and middle managers. Sony's success spoke for itself, loudly enough to send the bigwigs scrambling out of the woodworks. Across from him sat the chiefs of Mitsubishi and Toshiba, whose businesses Morita was currently attacking through a policy of ruthless, cut-throat competition. A trusted source inside Toshiba had even informed Morita that the repugnant bald man from his first encounter with the Zaibatsu had been made redundant some weeks ago. Needless to say, there were plenty of glowering faces in that room. Morita was enjoying it all immensely.

“Good afternoon, gentlemen,” he began. “I trust you all made it here safely. I understand it is rare these days that you make business trips personally.”

Morita's barb had the desired effect, immediately turning up the heat in the room by a few degrees. It was true - these men had not had to deal with serious competition for a very long time, particularly not the old walrus from Mitsubishi. Even if a potential rival did arise, the Zaibatsu's superior political connections were usually enough to squash the danger.
