But, despite all the artificial roadblocks the Zaibatsu were desperately throwing in its path, Sony was on the front foot. The simple, unavoidable logic of the free market ultimately triumphed - cheaper and better goods meant more for him and less for them.

“Indeed, Morita,” the Toshiba chief replied through gritted teeth. “Shall we begin?”

Morita nodded.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.82.a: Hard work pays, even in Japan.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.83.desc:
The office of Matsushita Kōnosuke in Osaka was often called the 'Eagle's Nest' within the exclusive club of Matsushita's top executives. From his inner sanctum, the elder Matsushita surveyed his empire with a keen eye. Also, the younger Matsushita reflected as he made the ascent, he made sure to keep his subordinates fit. Getting here was quite a climb.

Entering the office, Matsushita quickly saw that his father-in-law was in an agitated mood. The old warhorse was a mercurial man to most who knew him, but Matsushita Masaharu had been around him long enough to notice the little details - standing by a window, his jawbones were starkly outlined against his cheeks, his spine rigid, his lips a razor-thin line.

“Innovation,” the old man said, starting to talk before he had even turned around, “is where we will beat the Zaibatsu. They are old and slow, and have no ambition outside the Sphere. They have lost the edge that put them where they are now.”

“Agreed,” Masaharu replied, “which is why I asked to meet you today. We're planning on breaking into the Japanese market, and our weapons will be air conditioners.”

“The Zaibatsu already sell them here,” Kōnosuke replied dismissively. “Where is our benefit?”

“Cost. The Zaibatsu sell to the wealthy - their units are too expensive for anyone else. Ours, however, are far cheaper, and maintain top-of-the-line quality. We will market ours to the middle class. A huge and growing market that the Zaibatsu cannot reach.”

A smile broke across Kōnosuke's face at that.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.84.desc:
Summer in Japan had been abnormally humid this year. The scientists had some explanation for it, something about ocean currents in the western Pacific, but, whatever the reason, the population of Japan was sweating out enough to fill a dam. Putrid armpits and wet backs were everywhere - and so, increasingly, was the Matsushita logo. Desperate for a bit of relief, middle class salarymen were flocking to appliance retailers and picking up W-31 air conditioning units in unprecedented numbers. The manufacturing Zaibatsu couldn't keep up, with their clunkier and more expensive models. And so Matsushita Masaharu found himself once again ascending to the Eagle's Nest, his climb mercifully cooled by a newly installed army of W-31s.

He found his father-in-law examining his own model, put in this morning at his request. Even up here, far above the bustle of the streets, the heat was heavy and oppressive.

“Marvellous, isn't it?” said Matsushita Kōnosuke, turning towards him. “You have truly outdone yourself, Masaharu. What are the numbers?”

“Sales of W-31 units are up by over 500% over the past four months,” Masaharu reported. “Investors are practically breaking down our door, as I'm sure you've heard. The papers are singing our praises.”

Kōnosuke beamed and switched on his unit. The blast of cool air nearly made Masaharu sigh with relief.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.85.desc:
The view from the Eagle's Nest was intoxicating, Matsushita Masaharu had to admit. Standing together at the window, he and his father-in-law could look out across the Osaka skyline. Cars passed by below in their hundreds, and swarms of people crowded in and out of office buildings. As the two watched, a bus pulled up outside their own building and disgorged a horde of white-shirted workers. Most had only been hired within the past year or so, so exponential had been Matsushita's growth in Japan.

“Innovation triumphs,” said Matsushita Kōnosuke, offering him a glass of red wine. “You always seem to outdo yourself.”

The younger Matsushita bowed slightly in response, and the two stood together for a while at the window, gazing silently at the activity below them.

“We have the Zaibatsu running for their lives in this country,” Kōnosuke said eventually. “So, what next?”

“We go out,” replied Masaharu. “Past the Sphere. America, Europe, South America - we'll have Matsushita products in all of them within the decade. You have my word on that.”

“Sounds like a difficult task,” Kōnosuke said, looking at him thoughtfully.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.86.desc:
The smoke in the room was so dense that Ibuka Masaru could barely see the bureaucrats and politicians sitting across from him. Typical for these Yokusankai-linked veterans. Most had been in government for decades. All were devoting much more attention to filling the room with cigarette smoke than they were to Ibuka's sales pitch. He wouldn't have been surprised if this was one of the little games they liked to play instead of doing work.

“Overall, you can expect productivity increases of at least 30% within six months of implementing Fujitsu systems throughout the administrative departments. Potentially even up to 70%, depending on how fast your workers take to it. Our engineers have been working on specialized administrative programs to further smooth out the process.”

The bureaucrats exchanged glances among themselves. Ibuka wrinkled his nose slightly as he was assaulted by a fresh wave of noxious gases.

“And how many bombs can we expect in these computers?” one bureaucrat asked, causing the morons around him to start cackling loudly. “They are made by Chinese hands, are they not? How long will it take for them to break down? A week?”

Ibuka had, naturally, planned for this scenario - openness to change had never been a strong point of the bureaucracy, or the YSK.

“Of course, I understand your concerns, gentlemen,” he replied, doing his best to keep the irritation out of his voice. “That's why I have taken the preliminary step of making deals with private accounting firms and Tokyo Stock Exchange analysts. Believe me, they will vouch for the efficiency of my products.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.86.a: Change, one exhausting step at a time.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.87.desc:
Even for a hard-headed businessman like Ibuka Masaru, well accustomed to paper, the quarterly reports of the Tokyo Stock Exchange could be a challenging read. By the five hundredth page, all the numbers had a tendency to blend together into a meaningless jelly. This time, however, Ibuka was active and alert, pen at the ready. Those companies Fujitsu had struck deals with to provide state-of-the-art computing technology were marked with an asterisk. Those Fujitsu had approached and been rejected by were underlined. As pages flew by, Ibuka was starting to notice a definite trend.

The asterisked companies were doing well. Almost uniformly well, in fact. There were stubborn holdouts, as there always were in the business world - one particular group of unfortunates Fujitsu had sold to didn't seem entirely clear on what a computer actually was - but, by and large, Fujitsu was proving its worth. The underlined companies, by contrast, tended to be stagnating.

He also did not fail to notice that one of these underlined companies was run by a certain Oguda Ichiro, a brother of one of the faceless Yokusankai men he had met with to pitch his products. The Oguda family doubtless would be distressed to find that their business was losing money at the hands of Fujitsu-equipped competitors.

Ibuka allowed himself a self-satisfied smile, and picked up the phone. Perhaps he would make a second offer.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.88.desc:
These bureaucrats and their damned cigarettes. Couldn't they go a few hours without them?

At least Ibuka could be satisfied with their expressions. Those patronizing half-smiles were gone now, replaced with something much more businesslike - and, dare he say, humbled. By now, the competitive advantage to be gained from Fujitsu's computers was universally known. Major companies on the Exchange were begging for deals. Ibuka had made it known to the government in no uncertain terms that he was being indulgent by granting them a second opportunity to work with him. He did not expect too much resistance this time around.

One of the bureaucrats cleared his throat and leaned forward over the table.

“Ibuka, I have to say, we have all noted the benefits your products have brought. Your claims of extravagant productivity increases seem to be well founded. The government believes it can make a deal with you.”

Ibuka duly adopted a grateful smile, but this display of bravado fooled nobody, and everybody in the room knew it. These poor fools would be kneeling at his feet right now if that were appropriate behavior for a government official.

“I am glad you have come around,” Ibuka replied. “Fujitsu is, as always, eager to serve. I believe you have already received the necessary papers.”

The bureaucrats nodded vigorously, although Ibuka did notice that some were less keen to meet his eyes than others. He clapped his hands, sending a few bureaucrats jolting out of their chairs, much to his amusement.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.89.desc:
“The essence of our proposal is this,” Takasaki Tatsunosuke said. “We have Manchukuo. You have Japan. A mutual relaxation of our respective grips over our territories would be, I believe, very beneficial. Mitsubishi recently lodged a development application for several plants in the outer regions of Xinjing - these could be sped to approval.”

The Mangyō director was deploying all his legendary charm, but Komai couldn't help but notice that the Zaibatsu heads weren't convinced. Yes, Mitsubishi wanted their cheap plants, but could they really be expected to give up their stranglehold over the Home Islands for that?

“And therein lies the issue,” the director of Sumitomo said, taking a long puff on a cigar. “You have Manchukuo. We have Japan. One, I must say, is a much greater prize than the other. I'm sorry, Takasaki, but I don't see any way we can make this deal acceptable.”

“So, Komai,” Takasaki continued once the conference room had cleared out, “the Zaibatsu stick their heels in the ground, as expected. You said you had a backup plan?”

“Indeed, Director,” came the reply. “We'll use their heavy hand against them. There are many companies with significant plant investment on the verge of bankruptcy, thanks to our friends' intolerance of competition. Hitachi will buy them up, establishing ourselves as a major player through ruthless efficiency.”

“Wonderful,” said Takasaki. “Mangyō is right to believe in your abilities, Komai. I'll wire whatever you need for this scheme down to Kōshū. Get us those assets.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.89.a: If they don't take the carrot, use the stick.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.90.desc:
Business success, Komai reflected, meant more than just pure greed. The Zaibatsu had that in abundance, but Hitachi was snapping at their heels all the same. No, there had to be a certain drive, a determination to succeed, and a willingness to do whatever it took for success to come. A willingness to work for days straight - and to make unwilling Chinese factory workers do the same.

He surveyed Hitachi's latest figures. Slowly but steadily, they were creeping up on the Zaibatsu in Japan, with the help of established capital and plant provided by the unfortunate companies they had taken over. The fact that the Zaibatsu were sowing the seeds of their own destruction by carelessly stomping over potential competition was a source of tremendous satisfaction for Komai.

The insistent buzzing of the telephone on his desk shook him out of his thoughts. He put the papers down and picked up the receiver. He was greeted by the crackly, distorted voice of Takasaki Tatsunosuke.

“I saw this morning's release. Excellent work as ever, Komai. Mangyō has taken notice of your success. Continue as planned.”

Hearing the click, Komai chuckled slightly. Takasaki could be terse at times - however, what many of his quaking subordinates didn't know was that this was, strangely enough, a sign of his approval.

Without further ado, he returned to his work.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.90.a: There was still a long way to go for Hitachi Limited.
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.91.desc:
As soon as Komai entered the conference room, he sensed the extraordinary tension. It had an almost physical presence, like a thick blanket. As he sat down, he nodded to Takasaki and smiled innocently at the Zaibatsu chiefs at the other end of the table, and got a host of glares in return.

“The dog has left the kennel,” one of the chiefs snarled before Komai even had a chance to find a comfortable sitting position. “You want Hitachi to stand on the level of Mitsui, eh? Well, we have an answer to that. We will crush you upstarts like the insects you are. Your Chinese slave laborers might have given you the edge for now, but we have ways of overcoming this. Do not expect to be let off lightly.”

“I'm terribly sorry you feel this way, Directors,” Komai replied, his smile unwavering. “Should you wish to drive Hitachi out of Japan, you will have to beat us honestly, in the free market. I wish you luck in this endeavor - you'll need it.”

With much grumbling and a frankly unprofessional number of obscenities, the Zaibatsu chiefs quickly filed out of the room, leaving only Komai and Takasaki.

“I think that went quite well,” Komai said, taking a sip from a glass of water.

“You've certainly thrown down the gauntlet,” Takasaki observed. “Can you beat them?”

“Of course,” Komai replied. “Our model has been vindicated. We'll export it to other markets. Hitachi will be the jewel in Mangyō's crown soon enough.”
strings.GNG_Product_Cycle_Market.91.a: And the old Zaibatsu will tremble.

After trial, error, frontstage deals, backstage deals, as well as fanfare, whistles, and electric bell rings to boot, the results for the one hundred days' tribulation upon Guangdong's chosen crown jewel of the year has rolled in at last - for better or worse. Obvious political repercussions for all parties concerned aside, the outcome of this year's Product Cycle decides whether gold will flow into or out of our coffers, and as such whatever impact it may have upon Guangdong's growth and sustainability throughout the following year cannot be overstated.

Such is yet another testament to our technological expertise, another stroke upon the annals of a state that is still coming to be.

Excellence, ingenuity, and efficiency. The benchmarks Guangdong has strived towards on all fronts, new ways to murder people included. The arms industry is yet another one that demands innovation, and innovate we did, by hook or by crook. Or perhaps it'd be more apt to say by burnt batteries or by thrown-away soldier lives.

Then again, every single novel discovery in human history is made of copious amounts of trial and error with just a healthy dose of human trauma thrown into the mix, and the only thing different with the Product Testing Research Group's latest harvest is that said trauma tends to lean toward the physical. Let us wish our next client a luckier time with the gun - you never know when the failsafe is off.

strings.GNG_Hitachi_Growth.1.desc:
As {gng_getleader} sat in his office, listening to a report from his factional whip, he felt trepidation rise from somewhere deep within him. That grinning wretch Komai had been busy with Hitachi's money, it seemed. The whip was reporting many late night meetings and brown paper bags changing hands, with Hitachi representatives entering the offices of high-ranking Kenpeitai officers and not coming out for hours. According to the whip, this had been going on for weeks now with no sign of abating.

The results, as far as they could tell, consisted solely of an uptick in Legislative Council seats, and an emerging pro-Hitachi sentiment among the military. Hitachi was getting favorable amendments tacked onto routine ordinances - but seemingly nothing more.

Long after the whip had left his office, {gng_getleader} found himself wondering what it all meant. Hitachi was putting some serious money into this, whatever this was, and Komai was clearly bringing all his unsavory talents to bear. But why? Were they going to propose an ordinance? Make a bid for IJA contracts? Surely, whatever they were planning, it could not possibly justify the lengths they were going to in order to make it happen.
strings.GNG_Hitachi_Growth.1.a: The rats come up from under the floorboards.
strings.GNG_hitachi_each_year_growth_tt:
£GNG_Hitachi_texticon Hitachi will grow in power through acquiring votes and expanding their power by spending £MAN_manchukuo_texticon Manchurian and £GFX_MAN_mangyo_texticon Mangyō funds, as well as splurging on the £GNG_kenpeitai_texticon Kenpeitai.
We should monitor their movements, to ensure that they do not entrench themselves in the £GNG_legco_texticon LegCo.
strings.GNG_Hitachi_Growth.2.desc:
High ranking military officials were driving around in expensive new Mitsubishi Debonairs. Legislative Council members were sporting new watches. As {gng_getleader} entered his office in the Council chambers to start the day's work, he was greeted by a wide grin from one of the policemen guarding his door, revealing a golden tooth where last week there had been nothing. Money was in the air, like ozone before a thunderstorm.

Unsurprisingly, the first report of the day came from his whip. Hitachi was at it again, flushing money into the country at an alarming pace. Where before it had been only a stepped-up instance of the usual horse trading that went on in Guangdong, by now it had reached proportions suggesting something deeper was at play. The money was targeting Guangdong's top military men and influential Legislative Council members, yes, but also the colonels of the garrison regiments surrounding the capital, as well as senior bureaucrats in the government departments. Bribery on this sort of scale could not be the work of Hitachi alone, the whip concluded - most likely, Mangyō were assisting.

As the whip left the room, {gng_getleader} puzzled over the possibilities. These were hard-nosed businessmen who spent every day wringing dimes and nickels out of destitute Chinese factory workers. It wasn't in their nature to be so profligate. But, whatever their ultimate aim, Hitachi wasn't the only company with money here in Guangdong.
strings.GNG_Hitachi_Growth.2.a: Time to bring out our own wallet.
strings.GNG_Underworld_Changes.2.desc:
In Kōshū, yakuza counted their earnings from the street: protection, fraud, and a hundred other crimes. In Honkon, bags of opium flowed through the streets like water in the Pearl River, bringing poisonous comfort to the masses. In Makao, millions changed hands in seconds with the reveal of a single tile.

With the Silicon Years in full swing, business in all sectors of Guangdong boom. A careful dance is played between the forces of order and crime, as Triads and Yakuza dance and fight in the underworld. Below the feet of law-abiding citizens, from the lowly laborer to the Chief Executive himself, there lies corruption.
strings.GNG_underworld_each_year_changes_tt: Every year, the £GNG_yakuza_texticon Yakuza and £GNG_triads_texticon Triads of Guangdong will increase operations, in response to £GNG_police_texticon Police control growth.
strings.GNG_Underworld_Changes.3.desc:
In Kōshū, protection rackets turned into a proper industry as yakuza escort the Japanese through streets increasingly hostile to them. In Honkon, the police held aloft shields and batons against protests as the flow of opium marches uninterrupted behind them. In Makao, there are fewer players in the back alleys and the mahjong parlours, leaving only the dedicated and the desperate, looking to win freedom from the Oil Crisis with one hand.

Tensions rise in the streets. Common citizens and workers march for their rights, for their frustrations, for anything and everything. All the while, Yakuza and Triad continue their sordid trades with even less scrutiny. Anyone who would care what they were doing is too busy holding back a tidal wave of protestors.
strings.GNG_Underworld_Changes.3.a: But they can only stay out of this impending chaos for so long.
strings.GNG_Underworld_Changes.4.desc:
In Kōshū, Japanese expats fleed the burning state flanked by yakuza, brandishing guns and nurturing hatred for the riotous natives. In Honkon, dealers sold opium to clinics and medics within the riots short on pain medication. In Makao, hidden mahjong parlours became safehouses and command posts for the GFT and CCL.

Hardened street fighters in the Triads teach blue-collar workers how to brawl, how to protect themselves from the batons and tear gas of the state. Yakuza run protection for expat communities and use their smuggler contacts to aid refugees fleeing a reckoning. What was once the perfect cover for criminal activity has now, for the moment, absorbed it entirely.
strings.GNG_Underworld_Changes.4.a: Triads and Yakuza alike find new roles to play in the Guangdong Riots.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.2.desc:
As Damocles was so memorably shown by Dionysius of Syracuse, power is never secure. It is an intangible thing, twisting and curling, planting itself in the minds of men and dissipating seemingly at random. It is the image of a fish refracted through water, never quite where it seems to be, never quite behaving the way you expect.

It takes cunning, ambition and drive to manage a touch at power.

It takes genius - and good luck - to capture it fully, to bend it to one's will in such a way that it remains unchallenged. Even then, time's ever-rolling stream will, at some point or another, wash it all away.

No such good luck has been afforded the Chief Executive. His three challengers, the barracudas circling him, have not given up their efforts to oust him and replace him with one of their own. With their seemingly limitless supply of funds, they chip away at the exterior of {gng_getleader}'s edifice, one nibble at a time.

With every piece that falls away from the monolith, the Chief Executive's abstract measure of authority over the Legislative Council weakens slightly. The will-o'-the-wisp darts away, perhaps providing an opportunity for one of his opponents to grasp it, should they have the wits to do so.

As favors are exchanged and opinions swayed on the Council floor, {gng_getleader} must intervene to shore up his position, or see his grip on history's coattails slip loose, leaving him at the mercy of time's cold, dark tide.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.2.a: To control minds is no easy task.

strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.3.desc:
As the chill winter wind howled around him, funneling through the streets of Kōshū, Murai pulled his coat closer around him and sighed. He watched his steaming breath dissipate in the wind, before the sound of a car engine alerted him to the arrival of his contact. A big Datsun pulled into view - a monstrous gas guzzler that could only have been made in the days of cheap oil. Despite everything that had happened, with the rioting and the inflation and the lines at the gas stations, this man simply could not abandon the high life he could no longer afford.

His contact was one Tsushida Miki, a Legislative Council representative originally for Matsushita. However, his loyalties had shifted as of late. Matsushita, staggering under the blow of the Oil Crisis, no longer had the money to subsidize this blowhard's extravagant lifestyle. Fujitsu - Murai's employers - didn't either, but Murai had been steadily drip-feeding Tsushida with small checks over the past few weeks, knowing that he was desperate enough to latch onto any hope of rescue from his creditors.

Tsushida stepped out of his car, shivering as a gust of wind hit him, and Murai walked over. Words were exchanged, then Murai handed him a paper bag, and then it was over.

Much different to the old freewheeling days, where Murai would be taking men like Tsushida to five star restaurants for a five hour marathon of feasting and negotiation. But he supposed it was more efficient this way.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.3.a: The Oil Crisis forces us all to economize.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.4.desc:
Outside, the masses roared. Marx's old specters once again stalked the streets of the world's industrialized cities, with banners of red and chants of revolution following in their wake. Against these old gods stood the governments, trying to hold firm against the tide. Their great duel was fought on the barricades, in the factories, in the plazas and squares and city halls, where the unstoppable force of the new met the immovable object of the old.

In Guangdong, the workers marched against the mindless cruelty of their overlords. Oil, too, was a knife in the heart of the body politic. Guangdong's middle class families first rationed gas, and then abandoned it altogether. The streets emptied, and yet the lines at the gas stations grew ever longer.

The tide had even breached the sepulchral chambers of the Legislative Council. The money which had once flowed freely between factions was now being tightly conserved, lest the next bank run lead to insolvency.

But even in a time of recession and revolution, the work of Guangdong's elites had to go on. Ordinances were passed, regulations were debated and amended and debated again. Even as the security detail around the Council chambers was doubled, private meetings were still held in the offices of representatives, as factions and sub-factions and prominent individuals traded favors and bargained.

One day soon, so the reasoning went, this crisis would end, and business as usual would resume. When that time came, those who had used the crisis to their benefit would have an insurmountable lead over those who had not. And so the companies quietly continued pushing their agendas in the Council, even as the tide of humanity outside threatened to swamp all they had achieved.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.100.desc:
As the session of the LegCo began, soft murmurs of panic spread throughout many of the Council's benches. Sony and Cheung Kong, long the underdogs within the chamber, had somehow achieved majority support. With Morita Akio as Chief Executive, the ascendancy of the state faction was impossible to deny. Naturally, Cheung Kong CEO Li Ka-shing and Morita saw this development as a victory and vindication of their reformist approach to Guangdong's problems and opportunities.

For the minority within the chamber, this was not a happy day. The Matsushita men were the least bothered. While they had their differences with Sony's approach their opposition was not a yawning chasm. The same could not be said for Fujitsu's representatives within the LegCo, all followers of Ibuka Masaharu's vision of a highly-efficient, if inhumane, Guangdong. Sony's pre-eminence was a firm challenge to their vision of the future and angry grumbles spread among their councilors.

Those loyal to Hitachi were the most upset. While CEO Komai Kenichirō was not present, his loyal underlings were. Progress was paramount for Fujitsu, but raw economic growth was Hitachi's priority. The Manchuria Model had no room for compassion for workers in its quest for a bigger bottom line and Sony and CK's new power threatened Komai's designs on the Pearl River delta.

Even as Morita and Li celebrated, just beginning to flex the muscles of their new legislative powers, the other corporations scrambled to react. An unchecked Sony was an existential threat so the conspirators spared no expense. Marginal members of Sony's coalition came under immense pressure, anonymous phone calls promising bribes, threatening blackmail and wheedling compliance.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.100.a: And as always, there were men waiting to name the price for their allegiance.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.101.desc:
When the press surrounded Matsushita after a dinner at Gaddi's, they asked him how he felt about Matsushita Electric attaining a majority in the LegCo. With characteristic slipperiness, he waxed poetic around the subject: “the future of the Three Pearls is truly bright with a forward-thinking Legislative Council shaping its destiny.”

But in the hallways and darkened corners of the LegCo, rival legislators whispered plots and schemes to save themselves from irrelevance. Matsushita's meteoric rise has come at the expense of the other tycoons, who have given tacit or direct orders to cut him down to size. Informal truces were made between the remaining companies as they sought out stragglers at the edges of Matsushita's empire. A bribe here, a takeover there; if Matsushita doesn't hold onto his newfound rewards, the corporate battleground might reach equilibrium again.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.101.a: The Heir takes the throne, but for how long?
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.102.desc:
All in all, Chief Executive Ibuka Masaru took the news that Fujitsu had just attained a majority on the Legislative Council rather coolly. He dispassionately thanked the aide who informed him, and asked her to leave him to his business. He had much to think about - namely, what to do next.

It was an inevitability that his company would be the one to ascend to the peak of power in Guangdong. For efficiency's sake, after all, would it not make sense for the business of the Chief Executive to be most exalted amongst them all? Alas, not everyone held his vision. He knew that even now, the stragglers and tycoons would be plotting to bring him and Fujitsu down.

But he knew they were plotting in vain. His vision was an inevitable victory, and he had come one step closer to realizing his destiny.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.103.desc:
A smile creeps on Komai Kenichirō's lips as his aide relays important news: with his latest acquisition, Hitachi has become the majority owner of the LegCo's representatives. He is sure that the other tycoons will hear the news in the next five minutes. He allows himself a small break in which he pictures the others scurrying around: Ibuka lashing out at his assistants, Morita and Li's panicked grovelling, Matsushita wandering his office in a daze. They will regroup, they will try to stop them - but they cannot stop the northerly wind blowing across Guangdong, carrying on its breeze Manchurian excellence to the Three Pearls.

All eyes turn to Hitachi, seeking weakness and loose appendages. War chests are raised, lawyers and negotiators are retained, contracts are scrutinised. The tycoons prepare for a fight to limit, halt and reverse Hitachi's growth. But Komai is unconcerned. Hitachi's system is the only one of strength in the Three Pearls, and even the combined efforts of its enemies is not enough to shoot them down. It will not be long before Hitachi is the undisputed ruler of Guangdong, and then the real work can begin: restructuring the state into a vertically integrated model, with Komai's domain at the top of this great pillar of power.
strings.GNG_LegCo_Changes.103.a: Manchuria's tendrils slither through the ground, dragging Guangdong into its care.
strings.GNG_3E_info_tooltip:
Even if the Chief Executive sits atop the food chain in Guangdong, there are three things that conspire to throw a wrench in their plan. Two that are outside the Chief Executive's direct control - and one that suffuses everything in Guangdong, formless but undeniably present.

The £GNG_japanese_nation_texticon Empire of Japan - the backer of Guangdong's security and its greatest investor - has expectations that must be met, lest a Chief Executive suffer their disapproval and open himself to attack by jealous peers. And the £GNG_chinese_nation_texticon Republic of China has never had a very high opinion of Guangdong - the 'state' carved out of its southern province - and certainly knows how to make life difficult, both for the Companies and the Chief Executive, if it is so inclined.

And beyond it all, £GNG_corruption_yen_texticon  corruption seeps into every crack and crevasse, locking up the gears of government with vice and apathy. Even if some would say such is the fate of a nation that worships the yen beyond anything else, nobody enjoys having to deal with  £GNG_corruption_yen_texticon  corruption - rotting away at souls, cheapening work, and crimping profits.

strings.GNG_purge_the_corrupt_officials_desc: The corruption in Guangdong is becoming unmanageable. No matter how concentrated our efforts are, there are still some officials dedicated to their lawless ways. We must purge them from our society.
strings.GNG_investigate_LegCo_member_finances_de: Several LegCo members are likely receiving “tea money” to push different corporates' agendas, who will continue to corrupt our legislature if they are not stopped. We must investigate members who might have these connections and reprimand them.
strings.GNG_investigate_corrupt_businesses_desc: Corruption in Guangdong isn't only regulated to the largest corporations. Small businesses especially are very prone to corruption, and this can not be allowed to continue. We must begin investigating them to prove their guilt.
strings.GNG_crack_down_on_underworld_connections: We have received concerning reports of members of the civil service having unsolicited connections with rings of the underworld, which corrupts our systems. These connections must be cracked down upon to eradicate corruption in Guangdong.
strings.GNG_anti_corruption_campaign_desc: The culture of Guangdong is a culture of corruption. Every day people aren't free from its influences, so we should direct funds into a mass-advertisement campaign to get people aware of its detrimental effects.
strings.GNG_audit_the_civil_service_desc: While corruption might have been mostly eradicated in the higher parts of society, the civil service is still open to unsolicited deals. We must audit civil service members, and ensure that corruption has been ended in all parts of our society.
strings.GNG_attack_white_collar_crime_desc: Corruption comes in many forms, and white-collar crime is one of the largest. Embezzlement is a huge issue, and tackling it is of utmost importance if we ever want to rid ourselves of corruption.
strings.GNG_target_the_ringleaders_desc: If we cut off the head, we can kill the snake. By targeting the ringleaders of several criminal organizations, as well as many increasingly disloyal senior officials, we will hinder their ability to sabotage our institutions.
strings.GNG_crack_down_on_petty_corruption_desc: Despite our many advertisement campaigns, petty street corruption is still very much prevalent in Guangdong. As other directives have proved inefficient, we must send a small police force to pacify it, at least for a while.
strings.GNG_investigate_rumored_yasuda_connectio: A wild rumor floating about, which Chief Executive Suzuki is very aware of, is that Yasuda and their representative Matsuzawa Takuji has some “secret” connections, which is corrupting their company. Having one of the four companies be corrupt is unacceptable, and Suzuki will make sure that they are investigated.
strings.GNG_strike_at_the_underworld_desc: During the chaos of the ongoing Yasuda Crisis, the factions of the underworld are running rampant on our systems, corrupting our civil service and rapidly seizing land in their ongoing gang war. We must strike them down swiftly.
strings.GNG_reforms_to_the_civil_service_desc: The Japanese-dominated civil service is currently very prone to inefficiencies and corruption. Chief Executive Morita and Chief Secretary Li have proposed minor reforms to the service, so that the system can be less corrupt and inefficient, which will also increase the people's trust in us.
strings.GNG_audit_the_police_desc: The Police of Guangdong is inefficient due to being particularly suspectible to corruption. Chief Executive Matsushita clearly knows of this, and has proposed doing a mass audit of police officers,to reprimand and fire the ones who have been engaged in corrupt activity.
strings.GNG_set_up_cameras_in_offices_desc: Every man in Guangdong who knows his trade, like Chief Executive Ibuka, knows that the corrupt deals happens between men exchanging power for money in highrise offices. By setting up cameras in these offices, we can catch corrupt officials and make an example out of them.
strings.GNG_use_the_kenpeitai_desc: The systems of corruption that permeates Guangdong is rotting its structure. Chief Executive Komai and his connections to the Kenpeitai shall strike fear into any who are caught dealing in illicit activities, to secure a prosperous future for the State of Guangdong.
strings.GNG_open_corruption_decisions_legco: To avoid the fate that befell on Suzuki, future Chief Executives can use £GNG_corruption_yen_texticon  corruption under the £GFX_GNG_three_evils_texticon 3 Evils £decision_icon_small decision category during ordinances to gather votes. They can also use £GNG_corruption_yen_texticon  corruption to buy up seats in desperate situations.
strings.GNG_sony_and_ck_less_than_35_seats: £GNG_Sony_texticon Sony and £GNG_Cheung_Kong_texticon Cheung Kong have less than 35 seats in total.
strings.GNG_desperate_measures_sony_desc: Due to mismanagement or being dealt a bad hand, £GNG_Sony_texticon Sony is at a backfoot in the Legislative Council. By using some connections, we might be able to rebound ourselves back and regain some influence.
strings.GNG_desperate_measures_matsushita_desc: Due to mismanagement or being dealt a bad hand, £GNG_Matsushita_texticon Matsushita is at a backfoot in the Legislative Council. By using some connections, we might be able to rebound ourselves back and regain some influence.
strings.GNG_desperate_measures_fujitsu_desc: Due to mismanagement or being dealt a bad hand, £GNG_Fujitsu_texticon Fujitsu is at a backfoot in the Legislative Council. By using some connections, we might be able to rebound ourselves back and regain some influence.
strings.GNG_desperate_measures_hitachi_desc: Due to mismanagement or being dealt a bad hand, £GNG_Hitachi_texticon Hitachi is at a backfoot in the Legislative Council. By using some connections, we might be able to rebound ourselves back and regain some influence.
strings.GNG_bribe_own_legco_seat_desc: To shore up more support for the current ordinance, we will bribe one our own seats, as support in every £GNG_legco_texticon LegCo faction is by far uniform.
strings.GNG_not_all_own_faction_seats_support_cu: Not all of our LegCo seats support the current ordinance.
