strings.GNG_meet_chinese_representatives_desc: We will ask to meet with the Chinese Consul-General to plead Guangdong's case, if they are available. Otherwise, we might meet with their security advisor... who may be less receptive to our entreaties.
strings.GNG_meet_chinese_representatives_tt: Fires an event with the Chinese Consul-General - or someone else...
strings.GNG_request_chinese_backing_desc: We will ask Nanjing to assent to and support our policy initiatives - but they will not be pleased.
strings.GNG_buy_chinese_radio_airtime_desc: By letting our companies program on Chinese radios, we can increase the interest for our products - though China would rather act as if we didn't exist.
strings.GNG_appeal_for_more_chinese_workers_desc: By appealing for the Republic of China to simplify the immigration process into Guangdong, we can get more workers to power our factories - though the Chinese would prefer if we didn't exploit their people.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.1.desc:
Thirty minutes. A full half-hour. That was how long {leader_name} had been sitting in the waiting room of the Chinese Consul-General for, and he was practically steaming at the sheer disgracefulness of it. He knew that Song was in there. Was he just sitting there and letting him stew? A businessman hardly ever has a half hour to spare, and a nation's leader certainly doesn't. Indeed, his watch was giving him increasingly dire warnings spelled out in ticking black numbers, each movement a reminder of the men he was eschewing so that he could sit in a lobby which was becoming uncomfortably stifling.

The door swung open, and the crisply dressed Consul-General emerged. “My apologies, Chief Executive. I was kept late by a series of complaints - I'm sure you understand.”

“I'll be kept late from my own meeting at this rate, Consul. I appreciate punctuality.”

“Oh, I'm sure of it.” Song replied. {leader_name} could practically feel the insincerity ooze from his words and drip onto his forehead. Maybe that was just sweat. Did they have a heater in here? “Regardless,” Song continued, “I'd like to speak with you about these complaints. I make a point of putting some time aside for reading the gripes of the Chinese here each week, and I found some today which were... particularly concerning. Please, come in.”

{leader_name} stood, checking his watch. “You've kept me waiting too long, Consul. My allies in the Legislative Council expect me to see them any minute. We'll have to find another time.”

The Consul-General sighed, adjusting his tie in a motion of disappointment so honest that the Executive was sure he had practiced it. “Surely they can understand one missed meeting. These are pressing matters, Chief Executive, and I would appreciate you treating them as such.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.1.b: “No, Consul, I must be going. Good day.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.2.desc:
“Hmm... yes, that certainly sounds agreeable.” Song finally replied, and {leader_name}'s jaw practically hit the desk.

What was this? What was happening? The Chief Executive had entered this meeting with folders in hand and no expectations in mind, as he had learned to do whenever he mentioned economic cooperation with the Chinese Consulate. There was always something that his opposite had to break up whatever line of attack he took - tariffs, or Chinese worker treatment, or some meaningless piece of bureaucracy back in Nanjing. The Consul-General had both an encyclopedic knowledge of delaying tactics and the skill to utilize them constantly. Yet, all of a sudden, it was as if he'd been replaced with someone who {leader_name} could work with.

It was too good, he realized suddenly, stiffening his chair as he watched the Consul's eyes flicker over the paper. There was something coming. “Do you have any more comments?” He mumbled quietly, hoping his gut was simply misjudging the situation. It only took a moment for the Consul to prove his instincts right.

“One thing, yes.” the Consul-General commented, straightening in his chair. “Your corporations - Fujitsu, Sony, Matsushita, the like - they enjoy generous subsidies to bolster their profits. If Chinese corporations are to compete in such an established market, it's only fair that we receive the same subsidies. Profit for Guangdong, profit for China, victory for us both.”

{leader_name} frowned. “You know very well that Tokyo backs our corporations. They expect me to maintain their dominance. Allowing competition won't cause too much trouble, but giving Chinese companies Japanese money is... a different question.”

“Yes, I imagine it'll cause some fuss.” Song replied in a genial tone. “But you're a businessman. Surely you see the opportunities for the Chinese market here - and you, too, could use better trade relations with China, yes? Hundreds of millions of customers just across the border, money in hand, waiting for products from Canton and Guangdong? Please, Chief Executive, consider my proposal.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.2.a: Perhaps I can see to some of these restrictions, if nothing else.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.2.b: “I'll have to consult with Tokyo first, I'm afraid.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.3.desc:
“Ah, Chief Executive, what a pleasant surprise.” Song smiled. “You've picked a wonderful time. Please, please, take a seat.”

{leader_name} warily took the plush seat on the other side of the table. Idly, he wondered whether the Consul-General even realized when he was smiling anymore. Endless diplomatic pleasantry couldn't be good for a man - though in comparison to the general, {leader_name} couldn't help but concede that the empty kindness actually served its purpose in moving things along. “Yes, it is... good to have such fortuitous timing. I brought-”

“My apologies, Chief Executive, but I must bring my own concerns to the table.” The Consul's voice seemed to slide off a cliff, finding some steel within itself. {leader_name} blinked - they were heading another direction, it seemed. “I mentioned your timing because just a few moments ago, I received a rather disturbing call from one of your Chinese citizens. You see, he had been going along his business some hours ago when one of your policemen took him aside and beat him senseless on some trumped-up charge. He was robbed, Chief Executive, by the very servicemen who you claim protect men like him.”

{leader_name} blinked, the gears spinning for traction in his head as he tried to recover. “Well... ah... that's terrible. A terrible thing, yes. We can begin an investigation-”

“No need.” Song cut him off again, and he felt a flash of anger shoot through his chest. By the Consul's expression, his counterpart felt the same - had he ever actually seen him angry? “I dispatched Attaché Wang and his detachment to find the culprit. We have a badge number and name. This behavior is unacceptable, Executive, and I strongly recommend that you punish the responsible officer. Is that clear?”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.3.a: “Rest assured, Consul, your concerns are mine as well. We'll handle the issue.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.3.b: “Perhaps you have too much time on your hands, running investigations in my country like this!”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.4.desc:
It was a beautiful map, {leader_name} thought. It was clear, detailed, precise and well-crafted. Someone had spent a lot of time on this piece of art, scratching in every street and every attraction. A visitor couldn't ask for better.

Unfortunately, in this instance, he'd prefer the visitor to have much worse.

“I'm not sure I understand your reticence, Chief Executive.” Song dictated, his voice making it apparent that he understood in full. “The delegation wishes to see some Chinese neighborhoods of Guangdong which have been left off of the official tour. Surely you would oblige these visitors and their humble request?”

“I would love to, Consul-General,” {leader_name} responded after a moment. “But I must ensure that the visitors are safe. The route we've given them-”

“You can't claim safety for diplomats in the center of your capital? That would be disconcerting news, Chief Executive. I can have Attaché Wang see to rectifying the issue-”

“Oh, cut the bullshit, please! How many times have we-” The words fell out before {leader_name} could catch them, frustrated little bits of embarrassing unprofessionalism that he'd finally lost control of. Damn that diplomat! He almost looked smug, the bastard. “...my apologies. What I mean is that, to be frank, we're uncomfortable with allowing them free run of the city. The Japanese citizens would be upset, they'd think it a snub. Our route pleases everyone. They see the sights, our citizens feel respected.”

Song steepled his fingers, light reflecting off the lenses of his glasses. “Understand, then, that the Chinese delegation is insistent. We will concede to the government here, but they surely would be displeased themselves if they were herded like cattle. It is up to you.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.4.a: “Alright. Fine. They can see their countrymen. Just get on with it.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.4.b: “Good, because we're doing it my way.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.5.t: The Most Irritating Man In The World
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.5.desc:
The only positive that came with meeting Song Zhiguang, {leader_name} had decided, was that he wasn't Wang Jingxu. Beyond that, there was very little that made him appreciate these meetings. It was unfair to the Consul-General - the man is an annoying bastard, and he really gets under the skin, but at least he was trying for an honest cause. Many men in Guangdong did worse deeds for worse reasons. {leader_name} had even caught himself respecting the man from time to time, much to his dismay.

At this specific moment, however, there was very little that kept him from reaching over the desk and strangling the glasses-wearing diplomat. Fugitives was the issue again. How he hated, hated, hated fugitives. How he hated this slimy bureaucrat across from him, the rat who delighted in harboring enemies of his state. He was talking now, the little bastard.

“I understand your frustration, Chief Executive.” The man began, the very tone of his words were like nails on a chalkboard. “However, there are procedures to inter-state extraditions. I would need to consult my legal staff to review concordance with Chinese laws, then refer the matter to Nanjing and wait for their response. I'm sorry, Chief Executive, but my hands are tied.”

“They're right across the border. You and I both know this.” {leader_name} seethed. “If you would simply arrest and return them, this whole escapade could end in thirty minutes, and you and I could never speak again.”

The Consul-General smiled. “That would be very simple, yes, but the laws of sovereign states must be respected - and Guangdong is a sovereign state, is it not?”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.6.desc:
“Consul-General, you must understand just how unusual the circumstances behind my visit are.” {leader_name} began, steepling his fingers on Song's desk. “I have received a complaint from all our major corporations about the present holdup of shipping. All of them.”

The Consul-General's face darkened as he settled in his chair, brow furrowed in contemplation. “I do not control the trade authority in Chinese ports, Chief Executive. Perhaps the corporate leaders can directly petition the ports, or the customs office.”

“No, that won't do at all. There are trade expositions, Consul-General, which the corporations cannot afford to miss.” Which I cannot afford to miss, he thought. “This is the very backbone of the economy we're discussing here. I cannot simply tell them to figure it out for themselves.”

Song shrugged his shoulders, taking his glasses off and setting them down. “I can only extend my deepest apologies right now, Chief Executive, and I mean it. I can send a notice to the ports myself if that would work, but my hands are tied beyond that.”

“Mmhm,” {leader_name} murmured, anger bubbling faster and louder with every word that reached him. “And would your hands be so tied if I involved the Japanese Consul-General in this dispute? Will they be so reverent towards your customs? These are their profits too.”

“You know there's no need for that.” Song responded immediately, leaning forwards towards him. “Please Chief Executive, don't make such a mistake. I promise you that you stand much more to gain from honey, not vinegar.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.6.a: “Then that'd best be damn good honey, Song.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.6.b: “I don't think I'm making a mistake at all. I'm going to make some calls.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.7.desc:
“That settles it, then.” The Consul-General concluded with a flourish, closing his folder emphatically. He was out of his seat within a second, his suit jacket straightened on his body a second after that. {leader_name} was in no such rush, and indeed he watched with surprised interest as his counterpart busied himself so suddenly.

“Where's the fire, Consul-General?” {leader_name} laughed. Song paused a moment as if catching himself, then returned to his tidying up with deliberate care.

“My apologies, Chief Executive. I have an outing with friends in the Chinese District. Old friends of mine. I suppose I'm excited to see them.”

Another laugh from the seated Chief Executive. “I would hate to be working in my free time.”

“What do you mean?” Song turned back to face him, smoothly buttoning his suit.

“Every time I see you in the papers, it's you meeting schoolchildren, or shaking hands with factory workers, or speaking to nurses. Always in the Chinese District, always for work.”

Song chuckled. “No, no, not always. I may be a diplomat, but I grew up here. It's a professional and a personal duty to see how my hometown is doing.” A moment's pause, then a grin. “Don't worry - I'll be sure to let you know of any complaints I hear. Good day to you, Chief Executive.”

With that, he slipped out of his office, leaving {leader_name}'s smile to slide off his face alone.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.7.a: At least he has a sense of humor.
strings.GNG_china_opinion_7_tooltip: This is a valuable clue about Song Zhiguang's character. We may be able to find more...
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.8.desc:
“If you'll excuse me, Chief Executive, I'll bring us some tea before we discuss the next point of business.”

“Please.”

Song stepped out without another word, leaving {leader_name} alone in his office. It wasn't long before his eyes began wandering, foot lightly tapping against the wooden floor. Loosely, his gaze fell upon the bookshelf to his left filled with academic tomes, then the window behind the Consul-General's desk, then the bookshelf to his right filled with binders marked by neat lettering, then finally settling on the desk before him. Papers, folders, pictures, some framed. One caught his eyes in particular - A group of men in fatigues, smiling before some village or another. The Consul-General's face was unmistakable.

He'd seen the picture before. It was facing him, after all, and it wasn't the only one like that. A number of pictures from the man's soldiering days had found a home on shelves and windowsills. He'd never been brazen enough to ask about it, of course - there were few Chinese men with many fond memories of the 40's, and the two were nowhere near close enough to touch that raw of a nerve. Still, he couldn't have fought for the Nationalists and surely not the Communists.

A soldier of Wang Jingwei. Yes, that must be it. How else could a Chinese man fight in the 40s and remain in the good graces of Nanjing? He mused over what the calm, contemplative diplomat would be like in war. He didn't seem like the type to fight. As with everything in Guangdong, {leader_name} concluded, there was more to Song Zhiguang than what meets the eye.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.8.a: The creak of the door and measured footsteps snapped him out of his daze.
strings.GNG_china_opinion_8_tooltip: There is more to Song Zhiguang than meets the eye. We may be able to learn more...
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.9.desc:
The tick of the clock on the wall was the only sound that cut through the silence in Consul-General Song's office. It was soon joined by the tap of {leader_name}'s fingers on the desk. His eyes turned to check the time - five minutes left. Five minutes of silence would be a decidedly awkward way to end an otherwise productive meeting, he decided, and so his mind spun through a few topics of light discussion before landing on one he liked.

“If you would indulge my curiosity, Consul-General, you've clearly had some experience with diplomatic matters before this. Surely you've been posted in a number of intriguing places. Which would you say is most memorable?”

“Most memorable... that's a difficult question.” Song's eyes turned to the ceiling in thought, his mouth drawing into a line. Finally, his focus shifted back to his counterpart. “I was assigned to the old united Russian front in the 50's, just before their invasion of the Germans. Most of my colleagues pitied me. The best were sent to Washington, or Tokyo, or Germania. Even the unlucky ones went to Bangkok or Jakarta.” A wistful smile spread across his face, seemingly without him realizing. “It was completely out of my depth. A country I'd not lived in which was colder than anything I'd known, speaking a language which I had poor grasp of and about to fight a devastating war. I certainly didn't build any connections like my colleagues did. But...”

“But?” {leader_name} tilted his head.

“I couldn't have asked for a more intense learning experience. And, in some way, being in those wastes with the soldiers and the cold and the shortages felt... familiar, almost comfortable. I've yet to feel that same way in any of my other posts.”

The clock twisted past the end time, but the Chief Executive didn't move, his brow still furrowed. Song simply smiled, took his jacket from its hanger, and made his exit.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.9.a: A modest man in a nation of excess.
strings.GNG_china_opinion_9_tooltip: We have learned much of Song Zhiguang's character.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.10.desc:
It was not the Consul-General who exited the Consul-General's office, much to {leader_name}'s surprise. Nor was the negotiator a secretary of some fashion, or even a diplomat at all. Instead, a short man in military garb with a receding hairline and a folder loosely held in one hand now regarded the Chief Executive the same way in which he might regard gum that had gotten stuck to his shoe. By all means, he was generally unassuming - the generic version of any military man - but it was that look alone which told {leader_name} that today was rapidly spinning off course.

“Good afternoon. I am Attaché Wang Jingxu of the Chinese delegation to Guangdong. The Consul-General unfortunately cannot make this meeting today, so I shall take his place - as I will in any absence of his from here on.”

“...it's a pleasure... General?” {leader_name} rose to shake his hand, but his extended arm met with no response. Instead, the Attaché glanced at the gesture, resoundingly ignored it, and raised his folder to read from.

“Lieutenant General, but call me Attaché. I have been instructed to forward anything noteworthy to the Consul-General that comes from our discussion on-” Now he squinted to read the agenda in his hand. “-tariff harmonization.” A quiet snort. “Not that I expect anything noteworthy from this meeting in the first place.”

{leader_name} could only regard his new companion with stunned silence. No, he realized, today was not going to be a productive day.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.10.a: At least the other man knows how to speak.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.11.desc:
{leader_name} liked to think of himself of a patient man, or at least a reasonable one. Who didn't? Few men out there please in thinking of themselves as rude or arrogant, and indeed it was a good idea in the world of politics to lend a little leeway to those partners of yours. It was especially a good idea when negotiating over a plan as tense and delicate as the one he had proposed. A joint training exercise between the RGOC and the Guangdong Police had never been attempted before, and it showed in the way that smugglers and criminals snuck across the border both ways with wild abandon. Both Nanjing and Guangdong were skeptical of the benefits, of course - when were they ever not? - so he'd have to tread carefully. Making a scene would do him no favors.

However, he couldn't help but feel some irritation at the fact that he had been mindlessly tapping his foot against the linoleum floor of the Consulate's lobby for the last thirty minutes, or that this was not the first time he'd been in such a spot. Which part of that got more on his nerves wasn't clear.

The Consul-General's door swung open with a flourish. Without even thinking, the Chief Executive was on his feet.. He took one step forward, his heart in his throat - then paused, then felt his heart drop back through his chest and through his stomach. Standing in the door was not the composed diplomat of the Consul-General himself, but instead was the sturdy figure of the attaché, arms free of notes and mouth drawn tightly.

“Good afternoon. I regret to inform you that the meeting has been canceled. Nanjing has scrapped the deal. The Consul-General wishes to inform you that he regrets that you were kept waiting for this.”

“Wait a second-” {leader_name} began, but his words were ignored as resoundingly as ever. His partner had turned around without a moment's pause, closing the door between them with a thud.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.12.desc:
It wasn't always that {leader_name} actually had a reason to talk to the attaché, rather than the Consul-General. Often, his meetings with the other man were born of accident and disappointment, the product of the Consul-General's busy schedule and the delight which the Chief Executive swore his counterpart took in torpedoing his plans. When it came down to police and military matters, though, there was no alternative but to head to the rather barren office of Wang Jingxu.

He really, really wished that wasn't the case.

“Reading these terms, Chief Executive, leads me to once again mention how lackluster the efforts of the Guangdong Police have been in gathering intelligence. Our agents and the Kenpeitai constantly outstrip their work. Your policemen get in the way far more often than they help.”

“That's an unfair attack,” {leader_name} responded, steepling his hands in an effort to keep them from clenching into fists. “The police are doing their best to maintain order in some of the fastest growing cities on the continent - without adequate help from either the Kenpeitai or yourself. I'd half a mind to commend them for even maintaining order in such a state.”

The attaché scoffed. “Explain, then, how my work mostly consists of cleaning up after your officers.” He remained unmoving in his seat, fixing {leader_name} with a cold glare. “China will continue to cooperate with your policemen, regardless of their mistakes. Our meeting time is up.”

A bemused stare in return changed nothing. Finally, the Chief Executive stood, allowing himself a shake of his head as he exited.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.13.desc:
{leader_name} contained a sigh as Attaché Wang, not Consul-General Song, stepped through the door of the Consul-General's office. “Where is he?”

“Good day to you too.” Wang replied with blunt detachment. “The Consul-General is indisposed at this time. I will conduct this meeting in his stead.”

“No, no, that won't do.” The Chief Executive scowled. “This is a matter of investment protocols. This is something which I must have the Consul-General's input on - not a lackey, not a stand-in, not a subordinate, him. And him alone. What's keeping him, anyways?”

“A bad bout of sickness, I'm afraid.” Another deadpan delivery of what was rapidly becoming a comedy routine.

“Is he here? I can see him regardless.”

“It's quite contagious.”

“And what do you know of investment protocols, hmm? I didn't take you for a banker!”

“I'm sure that I can grasp the basics of the subject.”

{leader_name} fumed, his grip on his chair the only think keeping him from launching himself from it in fury. Some gears clicked together in his head as his furious gaze bore into the Attaché's forehead. “He set you up to do this, didn't he? To avoid me, to waste my time? To give himself some time to think? Is he even sick?”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.13.a: “A man's health is nothing to ignore, Chief Executive. Shall we talk?”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.14.desc:
{leader_name} had some time ago learned to control the visceral reaction he felt every time Attaché Wang entered the office instead of Consul-General Song. A deep breath, a slow blink, and a personal reminder that the man just tended to be the way that he was. Now he went through that routine again, rising to his feet to weakly shake the man's hand-

“Good afternoon, Chief Executive. I have just received yet another report of your men's complete and utter incompetence when it comes to law enforcement. Have you not heard our complaints before?”

{leader_name} froze, unrequited handshake awkwardly extended in front of him. “Wh-”

“Once again, we are forced to clean up the mess which the Guangdong Police Force leaves behind it. Once again, another Chinese man has been arrested without cause - but this time, he was a Chinese national. A citizen of the Republic. That makes it my jurisdiction to handle, and I demand to know why a foreign citizen has been so shamefully treated by your so-called enforcers of peace. Furthermore, may I remind you that this is not the first time that your buffoons have brutally persecuted Chinese citizens who live within your borders. In fact, I receive weekly reports on the number of civilians who have committed no crime, have not been tried, have not been even credibly accused, and still are beaten bloody by nightsticks and batons - or they are thrown into prison without a second thought, like our subject here. A man cannot work from prison, cannot pay bills from prison, cannot feed his family from prison - and often he has not even been accused of a crime. Perhaps that crime is being Chinese?”

“...I-”

“I do not want apologies, Chief Executive. I want action. I no longer wish to have to track down police officers in the hopes that you will one day enforce the law upon the lawmen. I have a full list of officers who have committed crimes against the Chinese community in Guangdong which, perhaps one day, you would care to read. Until then, I shall be forced to compile that list further and hope that one day you will care enough about the plight of your own people to intervene against your very own police force.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.15.desc:
“...now, the Triads control these series of streets here. It's an advantageous position, I'm told. A base for smuggling illicit substances into the rest of the city at an exorbitant rate.” {leader_name} traced his finger across the map from one set of the urban grid to another, lazily circling a swathe of high-rise apartments. Across from him, Attaché Wang watched impassively, light from the desk lamp shining off his glasses. “The Yakuza would love to cut into that territory. I'm sure they would try it, should they gain the ability to.”

“Of course.” The attaché commented, taking a moment to adjust in his seat. “In the end, however, the priority would be to reassert government control in the area, yes?”

“Yes, yes. It would take quite the effort, though. If I ordered the police to try it today, they'd be shot to pieces. They would need-”

“More funding.” The two men spoke as one, then glanced at each other. The Chief Executive suppressed a laugh - a difficult feat, for as unprofessional as it was, this may have been the first time that he and Wang had ever actually agreed upon a course of action. Or on anything, for that matter.

“...very well, then.” Attaché Wang stood up. “I shall inform the Consul-General of our discussion. Shall we schedule a meeting for next week?”

{leader_name} resisted the urge to make a witty comment about how this was the first time in his life that he'd ever actually wanted a follow-up meeting with Wang. “I'll get my secretary on it at once.”
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.16.desc:
“That concludes our meeting time, Chief Executive.”

Unlike Consul-General Song, Wang Jingxu spared no pleasantries in his goodbyes. It was a blunt habit of his, borne of being a military man first, a policeman second, a pain in the ass third, and a diplomat somewhere around twenty-fifth. {leader_name} grumbled to himself as he stood - another waste of time that he could have spent productively. Maybe with the businessmen or in the Assembly or at home watching TV. Anything but this.

“Actually, Chief Executive, I have one thing I'd like to say.” Wang stood suddenly, marching across the room to block his path. “I'd like to say a few words about my role in Guangdong.”

“I believe I've gotten the gist of it, Attaché,” {leader_name} murmured, attempting to sidestep him.

“Yes, I am the Attaché. My job involves itself with the Army, the Consulate, and the Police - especially the Police. I am well familiar with their work. I am displeased by its incompetence.”

“Well-”

“Now I would like to make one thing very plain to you.” Wang cut him off again, his voice both flat and sharp. “I do not have much tolerance for incompetent policemen. They chose their careers as decisively as you and I have. In the end, we all chose to be here. Make sure your men can keep up.” And then he was gone, the door slamming shut behind him, leaving {leader_name} bemused, confused, and deeply unamused.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.16.a: That man knows more than he should.
strings.GNG_china_opinion_16_tooltip: This is a valuable clue about Wang Jingxu's character. We may be able to find more...
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.17.desc:
In comparison to the walk to the door which Consul-General Song seemed to enjoy conversing on, {leader_name}'s walk to the door with Attaché Wang was - as with most things applying to the man, it seemed - silent, uncomfortable, and tense. Wordlessly, he moved to open the door, pulling it to reveal the busy urban street outside. The Chief Executive adjusted his suit-

“Wang, sweetheart!”

{leader_name} turned around from his exit to see the Attaché embrace his wife, who seemed to have materialized from behind the both of them. Odd, he thought. He hadn't seen her before. On first glance, she seemed relatively unassuming, composed if nothing else - a perfect fit for Wang, he realized, cracking a smirk. The two conversed in amiable tones, exchanging menial news and relative pleasantries between themselves. The Chief Executive, now third-wheeling to some degree, considered that this was probably the least uptight he'd ever seen the Attaché. In fact, he'd almost say he looked like he had some emotion in himself.

...hmm. What was she doing here, actually? A workplace visit, conveniently timed - or a message to him that the Attaché was a little more human than he assumed? It was a little conspiratorial, sure, but this was Wang Jingxu. Conspiracy didn't exactly seem beyond him. Was making a point really enough to merit a workplace visit?

Well, {leader_name} conceded, he at least knew that even a hardass like Wang had family.
strings.GNG_china_opinion_17_tooltip: There is to Wang Jingxu than meets the eye. We may be able to learn more...
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.18.desc:
{leader_name} wiped his brow in frustrated weariness, eyes flicking over to the clock. “I don't think you understand me.” There were twenty seconds left to fill before he could leave another one of these useless meetings. “I know our experiences and opinions differ wildly - I'm sure you've noticed this as well - but we'll never find a compromise if you remain so rigid.” Ten seconds. The Attaché was staring at him with that same damn expression he always carried, the bastard. “In any case, I suppose we shall continue this conversation when we next speak. Tell your wife I sent her my regards. Goodbye.”

“Wait one moment, Chief Executive.” {leader_name} froze halfway through standing up, awkwardly posed against his chair. The attaché's glare practically scanned him. “I take offense to being blamed for this impassibility when you refuse to adjust your own views whatsoever. Why is it always our border police who must crack down on the drug smuggling, the trafficking, the crime which your syndicates bring? Why are my countrymen forced to carry the load while their compatriots here grow fat on dirty money and corporate kickbacks? Why is it that you refuse to even acknowledge it?”

“Attaché, these accusations-”

“You and I know it's true. So does everyone in the city. I know you need these companies to back you, but I'd at least like to hear you acknowledge it.”

{leader_name} glared, turning his nose up at the intransigent subordinate. “Acknowledge what?”

“That there is a problem. That you intend to solve it. Even though we both know you don't mean it, I demand that you at least direct your policemen to help my men when they put the work in.”

The Chief Executive picked up his folder in a huff, shaking his head. This rude little man had spoken down to him enough.
strings.GNG_ChinaOpinion.18.a: “I'll consider it. Good day to you.”
strings.GNG_china_opinion_18_tooltip: We have learned much of Wang Jingxu's character.
strings.GNG_meet_japanese_representatives_desc: We will ask to meet with the Japanese Consul-General to plead Guangdong's case, if they are available. Otherwise, we might meet with the IJA garrison commander - who may not be very receptive to our entreaties.
strings.GNG_meet_japanese_representatives_tt: Fires an event with the Japanese Consul-General - or someone else...
strings.GNG_request_japanese_backing_desc: We will ask Tokyo to assent to and support our policy initiatives - but they will not be pleased.
strings.GNG_solicit_financial_aid_desc: As our reserves are running dry, we might lobby Tokyo for an infusion of cash - but we will be seen more as a drain than a benefit.
strings.GNG_request_more_engineers_desc: To further our research initiatives, we must ask Tokyo for more scientists - though their brain drain will not please them.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.1.desc:
There wasn't really another way to describe the Japanese Consulate other than oppressive, ornately decorated as it was. The slit windows funneled light into beams which sliced through the Consul-General's office, illuminating the grey haze of cigarette smoke and the mahogany of the desk which the Consul-General sat behind - Takashima Masuo, a recent arrival to the city and a rather unhappy one at that, so {leader_name} had gathered. He couldn't blame him. Between an ambassadorship to China or Manchukuo or being shunted off to Guangdong, he didn't know a Tokyo bureaucrat who would choose the latter.

“Now this kid - he's one of those types who has more money than sense, yes?” {leader_name} continued, his mind drifting back to the topic at hand. “He drinks a little too much sake, starts a street fight, winds up putting a man in hospital. Frankly, a stay in a cell would probably help shape him up. Why don't you tell his parents that?”

Takashima returned a slight nod, the embers at the end of his cigarette flickering. “They won't hear it. Their son can't be thrown in jail, it's an embarrassment. Now there's nothing I'd like to do more than turn him over to you to deal with, but where do you think the kid got his money from?”

“It's an embarrassment to me if we let snotty children get away with assault because their parents blow their nose with yen. It's not like we'd give him a life sentence, anyway.”

“How about this.” Takashima snuffed out his cigarette, leaning back in his chair with a sigh. “I can hand him over to you, but you'll be responsible when they complain to Tokyo. You'll be responsible for when they take their business elsewhere. That will be your burden. Is that clear?”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.2.desc:
“Consul-General. I need to know why your government is delaying our exposition.” The Chief Executive didn't bother with sitting down, putting his briefcase down beside him with a thud that startled Takashima out of his smoky haze. “This is a critical matter for us - we can't afford to miss our deadlines, the way the market works. I need an answer and I need it now.”

“My apologies, Chief Executive, but I-” Takashima stammered, practically chewing on his cigarette, but a wave of {leader_name}'s hand cut him off.

“I don't need apologies, Consul-General, I need that exposition! If this is some meddling idiocy from Tokyo-”

“Well, let me speak, would you?” Now Takashima was the one cutting {leader_name} off, even if his voice seemed much less passionate and much more exhausted than his counterpart's. “Yes, it's meddling from home. The Zaibatsus, you see, they're worried about these expos. They think it's free marketing for your companies at this point. The Prime Minister agrees with them, too.”

“What am I supposed to do about that? We hold these expos for advertising in the first place!”

“I think it's rather simple, to be frank.” Smoke billowed from Takashima's mouth as he spoke in monotone, fogging up his glasses and wrinkling {leader_name}'s nose. “Tokyo says to let them share the stage with your corporations. To be quite honest with you, Chief Executive, they're not wrong that you're sidelining them, even if they're being petty about it. It's only fair to cut them in.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.2.b: “Let me find the world's smallest violin for them, then. We'll delay if we have to.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.3.desc:
“Cigarette?” Takashima offered one across the table, sunlight reflecting off his glasses. It was later in the day now, the sun at a lower angle and the light orange and slanted to reflect that, painting the wall in shades of color. If either man had taken a moment to admire it, they'd certainly have found some beauty in the scene. As it was, though, their thoughts were focused on more material things.

“No, thank you. Now, we can ascertain that Sony's transistors will pass through Nagasaki on their way to the international market. Taking our tariff situation into account, Japan will take a good 10% share and the rest will be moved into the open market.”

“... ah, one issue with that, Chief Executive.” Takashima murmured sheepishly, retracting the cigarette and slipping it into the pack he'd taken it from. “The electronic firms on the Home Islands have...taken issue with the tariff exceptions which Guangdong corporations are granted.”

“Oh, please.” {leader_name} exhaled. “Each time I talk to you, Consul-General, it always becomes about what the Zaibatsu are complaining about now. I can't cripple our exports to satisfy them.”

“I know, I know.” Now the bureaucrat put up his hands in resigned deference. “It isn't fair to you. But they have Tokyo's ear, Chief Executive, and Tokyo would like you to... engage in ”voluntary export restraints.“ They'll pay you for it, and they'd certainly be appreciative of your cooperation.”

{leader_name} frowned, staring daggers at the Consul-General. A thought clicked together. “That cigarette was your idea of an apology, wasn't it?”

“It seemed courteous.” Takashima mumbled, putting a hand on his forehead.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.3.a: “Well, tell them to take the courtesy of adding an extra zero to the check they'll send.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.3.b: “Well, can you take the courtesy of telling them where my shoe will go if they ask for this again?”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.4.desc:
It was Takashima today, a fact which made {leader_name} want to kiss the floor beneath him. No military men, no officers, no hard stares from soldiers who thought themselves better than their negotiating partner - just a bureaucrat, and a relatively reasonable one too. {leader_name} hoped his feelings didn't show through his expression. That would be rude, after all, even if he figured it was entirely warranted.

“Have you read through the report yet, Chief Executive?” The Consul-General's tired tone floated across the table and through the haze. {leader_name} nodded, taking a moment to sweep some of his hair back into place.

“We're in agreement. You, I, and Tokyo. How often does that happen?”

A muted smile creased Takashima's face. “Not often enough. Yes, the IJA will be available to contribute intelligence to your government when requested. Tokyo asked myself to deliver the good news and wished to mention that they hope such cooperation can continue.”

“And, ah...” The Chief Executive considered whether he wanted to risk continuing on this train of thought. “Where is General Nagano? I would have thought he'd want to be present at a meeting of this nature.”

“He's out on drills, I'm afraid. A scheduling conflict, very unfortunate.” Another smile from the Consul-General, this time more of relief than anything. “Trust me, Chief Executive, it's better this way.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.5.desc:
“They changed the itinerary?” {leader_name} practically choked on his tea, eyes bugging out of his head as his attention shot back to the wincing Consul-General. “What do you mean, they changed the itinerary? You can't be serious.”

“I'm dead serious, Chief Executive.” Rather than tea, Takashima seemed to default to a cigarette as his jolt to start the day - and starting the day they were. The rising sun hung low in the sky, beaming light through the other windows in the Consul-General's office for a change. “They'd like to see the rural parts of the provinces. The farms and mountains and such.” A breath of cigarette smoke caught the Chief Executive square in the face, to his murmured displeasure. “The beautiful scenery of the countryside and all.”

“Do you even understand how expensive it would be to secure all that? There are bandits out there, Consul-General. Thieves, robbers, communists. I'll be damned if a bunch of Diet legislators get captured by communists of all people, you hear me?”

“I do, and I know. They expect appropriate security nonetheless.”

“No, you listen to me. I control the security. I control where they go. Nobody goes out of the cities on a joyride without me saying so.”

Takashima sighed, extinguishing the cigarette in one smooth motion. “They'd be upset with you, but I doubt any would have the spine to risk it. It's your decision.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.5.b: “Tell them they'll enjoy the cities and that's final.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.6.t: A Formal Way of Putting It
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.6.desc:
“Chief Executive, I've been waiting to see you. There's another snag that's come up.”

“Sometimes I think all we talk about are snags,” {leader_name} murmured as he took his familiar seat in Takashima's office, breathing in the smoke and blinking in the haze he'd grown accustomed to.

“Yes, well, Tokyo's gotten themselves all twisted in knots about some of your corporate compatriots. There's no room for Japanese firms to compete in the Guangdong market now that the five corporations have gotten so entrenched.”

“I can't stop corporations from making money, Consul-General, and I don't know why you expect me to.”

“Of course I understand that.” Takashima rubbed his brow, snuffing out his cigarette. “But it's their complaint all the same. They want you to pay the corporations to make some space for them.”

{leader_name} stared incredulously across the table. “You can't be serious. You want me to pay my peers to allow competitors into the market? How about you tell the Japanese firms that they've got the whole rest of Asia to sell to?”

“Chief Executive, surely you of all people understand how... profit-driven these corporations get.” The Consul-General sighed, adjusting his glasses. “It's your call, but if you don't give them this, I wouldn't count on their investments coming back anytime soon.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.6.a: “Fine. Fine. I'll do it, damn them.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.6.b: “If they can't compete, I don't think I want those investments anyways!”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.7.desc:
“...and that concludes our agenda, Chief Executive.” Consul-General Takashima snapped his binder shut, taking a drag from his cigarette. “A productive meeting, all things considered. I'm sure you've other things to attend to, so I'll let you go early today.”

“”Oh, no, I have time. Surely we can talk about other things than business.“ A polite smile slipped across {gng_getleader}'s face as he reclined in his chair, sunlight beaming into his eyes. ”Tell me, Consul-General, how are you finding Guangdong? I hope it is suitable for your interests.“

”Oh, yes, it is an... interesting city, surely. Very active.“

There was a bit of reluctance in that answer, {gng_getleader} thought, and so he pressed a bit further. ”Active? Is it as active as, say, Tokyo or Nanjing?“

”Well, there's certainly much to like about it. The food is quite good, the weather is relatively good. But...“

”But?“

”I can't say I don't miss home. I suppose anyone would. And I do wish that I had the good fortune of some of my colleagues - a senior position in the Foreign Ministry or a good ambassadorship would have been quite nice, yes...“

{gng_getleader} let the man reminisce further, but he'd heard what he needed to. Of course the Japanese viewed Guangdong as a second-rate post, something that was beneath their talents. One day, that'd change, and they'd give this position the respect it deserved. Today, though, he'd have to grin and bear it.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.7.a: Disrespect is never easy to take.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.8.desc:
A man had to have hobbies in the professional world. Everyone did. For some, it was drinking or smoking. For others, it was women. For still others, it would be concerts, or operas, or gambling, or whatever else the Pearl River Delta could offer a man - and in that regard, the opportunities were truly endless.

{gng_getleader} had just discovered that Consul-General Takashima's hobby was golf, and he was beginning to seriously regret that.

“...there's nothing I would like more than to play a game at Augusta, but those Americans are so exclusive with their membership, to say nothing of their racial policy - of course, the Old Course in Scotland is a must-see which I hope to get to one day, but Kobe is a beautiful course in its own right - though I must say it is exhausting to lug yourself up and down those hills.”

“...I would imagine so.”

“Do you golf often, Chief Executive? You must - businessmen always love golf - how have you found it? You seem like the sort of man who would have a strong putting game, I'm sure of that. So many of my friends have struggled with putting - nothing more frustrating than missing a short putt, and watching them get red and angry with themselves is - it's hilarious, truly hilarious. Even Arnold Palmer misses those every now and then, and-”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.8.a: “Arnold Palmer? I heard he did quite well at the Scottish Open...”
strings.GNG_one_more_jap_riots_decision_tt: We will gain one more favor with the £GNG_japanese_nation_texticon Japanese Consulate should they become £GNG_japanese_frustration_texticon frustrated with us.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.8.b: “My apologies, Consul-General, but I have a meeting with the legislators. Good day.”
strings.GNG_tell_the_consul_no_tt: There are more important priorities than playing nice with the £GNG_japanese_nation_texticon Japanese Consulate.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.9.desc:
“Chief Executive?”

{gng_getleader} had just turned to leave when he heard Takashima speak again, catching him right at the beginning of the next routine in the long list of routines he had in a day - a quick walk out of the Consulate, down the stairs and to his chauffeur, and then a drive to a LegCo meeting to soothe whatever needed to be soothed next. He twisted his neck around to look back to the still-sitting Consul. “Yes?”

“If it wouldn't trouble you, I would quite like to extend an offer of goodwill. I have quite the impressive chef on the staff at my official residence, and I would quite like to continue our discussion over that - in a more pleasant and relaxed setting than this.”

“Ah. Well, thank you for the offer, but I'm quite afraid that I have a meeting with the Legislative Council that I must attend.”

“Well, Chief Executive, it is always your decision, but I will tell you that the tempura is to die for.” Takashima cocked his head to the side, taking a cigarette from his pack. {gng_getleader} considered his options - closer relations to the Consul-General meant closer relations to Japan regardless of the cuisine on offer, and that could never be downplayed, but he did have a schedule to stick to. Decisions, decisions. He always had too many of these.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.9.b: “My deepest apologies, truly. Have a good night.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.10.desc:
{gng_getleader} had always thought of Consul-General Takashima's office as an oppressive place, with its slit windows and prevailing smoke, but Takashima himself had never been that way. The Consul-General was, as you would expect from a bureaucrat of his kind, a relatively tired man with spectacles and the prevailing air of wishing he was anywhere more prominent. He was irritating at times, friendly at others, generally cooperative, but frightening? No, never.

Takashima was, in short, nothing like his military counterpart.

General Nagano Shigeto stood less than he leered over the desk, eyes like steel and a suit to match the color. Beams of light slashed across his silhouette, illuminating a face which had seen it all, the mouth drawn into a thin line of distaste. The Chief Executive, for once, squirmed a bit in his seat under the pressure.

“... General Nagano. I take it that the Consul-General is not available.”

“No,” Nagano replied, his voice flat. “We will discuss the topic of organized crime in Guangdong ourselves.”

“Organized crime.” {gng_getleader} could see where this was going already. “You have a proposal, I assume.”

“A suggestion. The IJA is more than capable of controlling this epidemic. Yet you do not allow our forces to aid your... overworked, let's say, police forces. Why?”

“Sovereignty, General.” Really, the answer was so much more than that. Like how stock prices didn't tend to like martial law, or how {gng_getleader} didn't relish in the idea of wading through blood to get to work. He knew Nagano knew that too - this time holding his posture as the other man leaned in.
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.10.a: “Pssh. Can't even speak your mind. You all really are roaches.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.11.desc:
“I have noticed something about these cities, Chief Executive. They are lawless under your direction. Without any sense of regimen or order. Contrast Guangdong itself to Tokyo or Kyoto, or even a city like Xinjing. Those are cities in which disorder and criminality is an object of the past, and those who violate the statutes of law are properly prosecuted. What, can you tell me, is the difference between the Home Islands and here?”

The staccato of the clock cut through the silence like knives through a blanket, drawing {gng_getleader}'s wary attention. Fifteen minutes into this impromptu interrogation, he realized. That left an hour to go, maybe more, for the General and the man besides him to needle at everything they could think of. A sigh. “The Kenpeitai's reach.”

“Got it in one.” Now it was Colonel Miyazaki's turn to speak, something he seemed to relish in. “Yes, you're understanding. My men, I assure you, are the best in the world - unceasing in their efforts to crush our enemies and protect Japan. Protecting Guangdong would be an extension of that effort. And yet, while our men are so proficient in China and Manchukuo - and, of course, the Home Islands - you remain reticent.”

{gng_getleader} had hardly opened his mouth when Nagano leapt back into conversation. “And we see now that your authority is undermined by criminals, foreign actors, communists, all sorts. Your police are not strong enough to contain them. Allow us to intervene.”

It was that damned tone of voice, he realized. That condescension. It made his blood boil. His hand gripped the armrest firmly as his jaw locked, finally coming apart to spit out-
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.11.a: “With all due respect, General, save the harassment for my secretaries!”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.11.b: “I hear you, truly. Please, continue with what you were saying...”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.12.desc:
“Where is Takashima? We are discussing a Japanese citizen's crimes in Guangdong and I don't have the consul to speak to?”

Nagano's face betrayed nothing as the soles of his shoes clacked against the floor. He came to a stop at the desk, looking down on {gng_getleader}. “We are discussing accusations against a soldier of Japan. This is my jurisdiction.”

The Chief Executive sighed, turning his chair to face the General. “Alright. Your soldier of Japan was accused-” - he mocked quotation marks in the air -“-of beating a citizen of Guangdong senseless. We have witness testimony, a man in the hospital, and a riot brewing. So, General, what is your plan?”

Nagano scoffed. “It is a matter of military discipline. We will handle it and nobody else. I have more important things to attend to.” With that, he turned away again, marching to the door.

“General, I can't just let you sweep this under the rug while a man is in the hospital-” The slam of the door was all the response that {gng_getleader} got. He sat in silence for a moment, then crumpled a random paper on the desk and hurled it into the trash can with a grunt and a clang. A moment's pause as he sat back down-
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.12.b: “Paper... something to cover ourselves could be written. Of course.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.13.desc:
Nagano's finger traced across a red line on the map, snaking through printed city streets and past blue circles. He came to a stop at an intersection, tapping it twice. “Chokepoint for ambush. Your men are out of position.” Onwards, to a bridge. “Chokepoint. No security detail.” Around a corner and to a park. “People will congregate here, and yet there are so few policemen stationed. Tell me, Chief Executive, did you draw this?”

{gng_getleader} fixed the General with a glare he knew the man didn't fear. “No. The police force submitted it for consideration.”

“Of course. Amateurs always have such passion for their work. But this is a delegation of Japanese executives and Japanese lawmakers, and so it is my responsibility to actually keep them secure. So here is what you will do.”

“General, I'm sure-”

“The IJA garrison will supplement your police forces in key areas. Similarly, the Kenpeitai will ensure that no trouble forms around the tour's route. We will secure the checkpoints which your men have ignored and create a safe passageway through the city.”

Another scowl escaped {gng_getleader}'s expression. He was being shown up. Again. By Nagano, the arrogant bastard. Letting himself be made a fool of for what felt like the hundredth time was unacceptable, but it would certainly take a lot of elbow grease to get the Police to create a plan that was up to standard - and at the end of the day, he did suspect that Nagano cared more about a good security plan than political showmanship...
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.13.a: “The IJA's help will be... appreciated. Certainly.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.13.b: “I will take your revisions to the Police and see what they adjust from there. How's that?”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.14.desc:
The embers of Takashima's cigarette flared yellow as he took a puff, exhaling as he read over the last paper which {gng_getleader} passed to him. “Tariffs.” He murmured. “Yes, that should be on the next itinerary we have. I'll make sure to look into it. Thank you for your time, Chief Executive.”

“Of course. The pleasure is mine.” {gng_getleader} rose to his feet, brushing a speck of dust from his suit jacket. That had been alright, all things considered. Now to the LegCo, and then home-

“Excuse me, Takashima. I have something to say.” Nagano's voice sliced through the air, stopping both men dead in their tracks. He had been sitting there observing all this time, filling the room with an unspoken dread as the two bureaucrats danced their way around him. Now he stood, his presence more than felt. “Our friend here has failed to note something of interest.”

“Mmm?” Takashima glanced over at {gng_getleader}, who could feel his stomach dropping to his shoes in real time.

“Earlier today, members of the Kenpeitai were called in to clear out an incident at the docks. Imagine, if you will, their surprise when they found that members of the Police had gotten into a shootout with smugglers in the middle of a crowded workplace.”

“They were armed smugglers, General.” {gng_getleader} noted, like a stick propped up against a tank. Nagano's eyes flashed.

“And your men saw fit to shoot through a crowd to get at them? Perhaps I should direct Consul-General Song's complaints to your office - I'm sure you'll find the number of casualties shocking as well.”

Takashima frowned as his eyes turned back to the rapidly wilting Chief Executive. “Is this true? Damn it, {gng_getleader}...”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.14.a: “I, uh, we will, ah, we'll look into it further...”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.14.b: “Gentlemen, ah, how about - perhaps some sort of liaison and training from your men to ours could work wonders...”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.15.desc:
“A ten percent uptick in robberies, twelve percent in stolen cars, fifteen percent in assaults, eight percent in murders.” Miyazaki cooly read the statistics from memory, standing to the side while Nagano looked on. “This is despite your orders of increased police presence in the area, Chief Executive. The evidence shows that they have not performed well.”

“It's a fluctuation in a difficult area to control.” {gng_getleader} countered, his frustration boiling as healthily as ever. These two were twin demons that he could never seem to shake. “Crime has fallen. A one-time increase should not be taken as a sign to throw the work of my men out entirely.”

“Will you tell the widow of a poor Japanese soul that her husband's murder was the result of a fluctuation?” Nagano remarked, not moving from his chair.

Another sigh from the Chief Executive. “Any Japanese man in this city should know better than to go walking alone through dangerous neighborhoods, particularly Chinese ones. We cannot fully account for stupidity.”

“Of course. I'd prefer they stay in the safe neighborhoods as well.” Nagano stood, crossing around the table. “And yet... I find shrugging your shoulders to be unacceptable as a response. The locals, seeing as your police cannot control other neighborhoods, have asked for the Kenpeitai to up their security around their own. If you find that unmoving, I'm sure Tokyo would feel quite similar.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.15.a: “Fine. Damn it, fine. Have your fun.”
strings.GNG_JapanApproval.15.b: “I will take personal oversight of the police's actions instead. Find something more important to do.”

strings.GNG_PTRG_flavour.1.desc:
Chief Executive Suzuki tried to not let his shortness of breath show as he entered his office, taking pains to slow his stride and mask his chest's heaving by straightening his tie. He made no such effort to hide his irritation at Prime Minister Ino, who stood languidly by the desk as if expecting a guest - in Suzuki's own office.

“I'm sorry to have kept you waiting,” Suzuki said dryly, “though I'm afraid my cabinet secretaries will need me back shortly.”

“A cabinet meeting? My apologies.” Ino dipped his head slightly, a formality without feeling. “I was just thinking about our conversation the other day, and I might be able to help you. You're aware of the Malayan problem, yes?”

“...Of course.” Suzuki had read the reports of the ongoing 'peace preservation' operations in Shōnan - for years, by now. “What about it? The IJA garrison reports to Tokyo, not -”

“The Army needs new rifles, Suzuki.” Ino barreled over Suzuki. “Standard issue isn't enough to flush out those guerrillas.”

“I see.” Suzuki digested Ino's statement. “You realize that the companies here make electronics, not weapons? Why not ask the Manchurians -”

“I'm asking you,” Ino stated firmly. “I can get the Army Ministry to request proposals. All you have to do is submit a design. We sign a contract, you get paid. I don't see what's the problem.”

Suzuki fixed his once-junior in the Tōjō cabinet with a wary eye. The Army he'd served was rarely so careless with their contracts to turn to first-time manufacturers. But Ino had always been a deal-maker - and Suzuki needed a win.
strings.GNG_PTRG_flavour.1.a: “I'll see what the Companies can do.”
strings.GNG_PTRG_flavour.1.tt: In 20 days the corporations will present their projects for consideration.
strings.GNG_PTRG.1.desc:
SONY - MODULAR RIFLE MK 1 - EASILY ADJUSTABLE - COMPATIBLE WITH MULTIPLE AMMUNITION TYPES

MATSUSHITA - SPECIAL FUNCTION WEAPON PROTOTYPE - LIGHTWEIGHT 'FLECHETTE' AMMUNITION, SUPERIOR PENETRATIVE POWER

FUJITSU - EXPERIMENTAL TYPE-1 RIFLE - INTEGRATED NIGHT VISION OPTICS WITH PORTABLE BATTERY

Suzuki's lips curled in distaste as he flipped through the design specifications submitted by Sony, Matsushita, and Fujitsu. Prime Minister Ino had billed the replacement rifle proposal as a 'next-generation competition,' but Suzuki had seen nothing worthy of that title among the candidates.

He scoffed at Sony's promise of adjustability and ammunition compatibility - fulfilling a non-existent need in Japan or its closest client militaries. It might be good for export, he supposed - but that hadn't even been in the Army's requirements.

As for Matsushita? The man had put together a dart gun. A focus on lightweight weaponry was useful at first glance, and fit Matsushita's emphasis on design well - but it would be a no-go for the exact opposite reason as Sony, creating a logistical nightmare where none existed.

And Fujitsu? While Suzuki admitted he was intrigued by the possibilities of improved night optics, he had nearly fallen out of his chair laughing when he saw the dimensions of the 'portable' battery - a car battery ripped out of an engine and strapped to a man's back!

He supposed he shouldn't have expected much - they were all newcomers to the needs of military equipment, and it showed. But all that mattered was picking one to submit to Tokyo...
strings.GNG_PTRG.1.a: ...to spare himself any further mental agony!
strings.GNG_PTRG.1.tt:
It is time to decide which experimental rifle project we will subsidize for advanced field testing.
The field-testing unit will then deploy, ready to be sent to Malaya.
To not run over budget, the PTRG in this and in all future projects has a deadline of 365 days before they are forced to pull out of the conflict.
To ensure that the PTRG is under control, it needs to have a general assigned to track progress.
strings.GNG_PTRG_Outcome_Preface_tt: Due to us fulfilling [?GNG_Missions_Success_Variable|Y0] combat missions, we gain following effects:
strings.GNG_PTRG.2.desc:
It appears that our entire manufacturing and design staff are idiots. There are a host of problems with the weapon we submitted to Tokyo - as our shareholders are all too willing to tell us - but the main ones are as follows:

The rifle either has not been tested, or the Product Testing Research Group was so horrifically incompetent, that having no tester fatalities in the process of firing counted as a pass.

Thanks to the back dealing of our associates, this “design” is still able to be reviewed by the Japanese government as a “potential” “candidate” for “use”. The truth of the matter is that this design was dead on arrival. The greatest aspiration that this design may genuinely live up to is as a middle manager's secondhand paperweight. Or maybe a homeless man might burn the discarded blueprints for a few, precious minutes of warmth? Or the back of said blueprint could even serve as children's doodling paper? The possibilities are endless, in that regard.

Regardless, the Prime Minister is displeased with our efforts, to say the very least. Calling it proof that “electronic firms do not belong in the presence of actual professionals,” it would be a miracle if we ever got to work in this line of the industry ever again. But no need to worry - the entire team has been fired. If only that term was literal.
strings.GNG_PTRG.2.a: Maybe they could use them as clubs?
strings.GNG_PTRG.3.desc:
Oh dear. The rifle was... not good.

On the upside, it at least was able to propel bullets out of its muzzle at a reasonably lethal velocity. The company is certain that it would generally maim anyone it points at a close distance. Most of the time.

The soldiers of the Product Testing Research Group have complained of a lack of “any contact with the design team whatsoever” with many saying that “they do not even know who's making the (EXPLETIVE CENSORED) thing.” Despite this discouraging feedback, our R&D Team still boasts of the best design that Asia has ever constructed, and that Guangdong will be making our Empire proud by handing our designs to the Japanese Army. They boast of being the next Da Vinci - visionaries ushering in a new age of technology!

It appears that our psychological background recruitment checks were not up to standard either.

Fortunately, the rifle is working in enough of a condition to at least make it into consideration. The Prime Minister has agreed to at least look at our designs and consider them, for a period of time. It might be a few seconds, but hopefully at least double-digit seconds. In comparison to others' designs - equipped with revolutionary techniques such as working optics, and the ability to leave its user unharmed - how can we stand a chance against them?
strings.GNG_PTRG.3.a: Can we call it a Proof of Concept?
strings.GNG_PTRG.4.desc:
Some good work here. Our rifles have proved themselves to be adequate weapons, in mortal combat. All that had to be done was to threaten to fire the entire engineering team if they did not incorporate the feedback of the Product Testing Research Group into the final product. While some areas could be improved, for a first design - a prototype - it is a good piece of weaponry. Even better, thanks to our allies within the Japanese government, the Chief Executive has procured a lucrative deal with the Prime Minister for some public trials within the Home Islands. While not a sure victory for our design, we have at least made progress into the reaper's domain that is arms manufacturing.

Already, our rifles have made for compelling reviews in the Army's professional journals, with the general feedback being our submission was “slightly above average” in quality. There are even rumours that the Chief Executive will approach our company with a demand for more weapons for “further study.”

If we play our cards right and shake the right hands, perhaps we will not simply be known as “that electronics company” - perhaps we will also be known as “that electronics company, that also produces guns as well.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.5.desc:
Surprisingly, the Product Testing Research Group's feedback indicates that our design was “better than expected.” General Nagano's soldiers spent hours laboriously dissassembling, firing and reloading the weapons and have become more acquainted with our guns - some even more so than their wives. Some choice feedback includes the gun being “easy to use,” “impressive firing rate” and “simple to reload” - mundane at face value, but a sign of what the soldiers actually care about.

What scant negativity that our gun has incurred has been taken in by the assigned engineering team and thoroughly implemented. What we have created is a weapon, suitable not only for the rifleman in the sweltering Malayan jungle, but for any elite force assaulting the hardest of enemy positions.

Thanks to our work, Guangdong's engineers - having received a heap of awards and praise - have been subject to innumerable iterations of presentations and speeches across the Empire to a whole host of wrinkled, depressed generals and army staff, with Guangdong's rifle in the final selection round. With every eye in the Empire on our design, we have to make sure that we're the ones accepting the final contract. Perhaps by the end of the year, every single army man in the Empire will complain about having to train with our design.
strings.GNG_PTRG.5.a: Not bad. Not bad at all.
strings.GNG_PTRG.6.desc:
It appears that batteries and radios aren't the only things our engineers are talented at building. Against all expectations, the Product Testing Research Group's weapon has blown away the competition! Our design harnesses both the technical skill and complexity of Guangdong's engineers and the ruggedness and reliability that the PTRG's testers have demanded from their weapons. Our design is the talk of every single IJA and IJN officer across the Empire - from the jungles of Burma to the icy winter steppes of Manchukuo, there is only one question on their lips.

“How do I get such a delightful tool of war and bloodshed to my men as soon as possible?”

Like the rest, they'll have to wait for our prized contract with the government to have its i's dotted and t's crossed before they use it on guerrillas in villages that need a reminder of their liberation under the Pan-Asian dream. For Guangdong, the contract promises further riches beyond our wildest expectations, while arming our forces with weapons that Washington and Germania did not think was even possible for this decade. Even if we lose this competition, no general will ever pass on our design entirely, and a place for our rifles in a niche role in the military is almost certainly guaranteed.

We have no remorse for the blood on our hands, given the thickness of our wallets. If someone complains, I'm sure we can offer them a discount - or a field demonstration.
strings.GNG_PTRG.6.a: Let's give ourselves a pat on the back.
strings.GNG_PTRG.6.b: We can do so much better...
strings.GNG_PTRG.6.tt:
We will receive the results of this further effort in 30 days
Effects of this rifle:
strings.GNG_PTRG.7.desc:
“Many doubted that our humble enterprises would be capable of producing a weapon fit to serve the needs of the sixties and beyond,” began the spokesman, either suppressing a grin or doing his best to appear to be. “Mad eccentrics, they called us. Scheming jackals, incapable of putting aside our differences for the sake of Japan and the sake of innovation.”

He moved towards the tarp. “How wrong they were.”

The cloth was whipped away to reveal a very odd-shaped machine. It certainly had something resembling a barrel and a trigger, though one complimented by so many attachments, knobs, and protrusions that one could be mistaken for assuming their brain was making assumptions solely on context. However, a projector soon fired into life, showing that the chimeric machine was indeed capable of throwing lead. The Japanese or Chinese kind. Or flechettes, should you prefer. Or grenades. In day or night vision. Whatever the customer desired, and whatever the foe dreaded.

The spokesman continued to list off specifications when one of the IJA staff members in the back interrupted.

“Very impressive, but I have concerns for its use in sustained campaigns. We can't take it into a shop in the middle of the jungle.”

The spokeman's grin did not falter. “Our ethos is to move fast and break things.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.7.a: “If you do the same, there will be no issue.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.8.desc:
“Watch how you carry that, Private!” shouted the lieutenant from the gangway. “Do you want to throw your back out?”

“How about we swap, sir?” came the reply from below. “I get the clipboard, and you carry these crates of junk all day.”

“Watch your tone, Private! That 'junk' is worth more than four years of your pay per unit. Keep the mouth up, and I'm sure we can bump it up to five.”

“For a gun, sir? We already have plenty of those. You're sure this isn't just the Diet pissing cash down Kōshū's mouth?”

“They're not just 'some gun', you imbecile!” yelled the liuetenant. “Weren't you listening during the presentation?”

“No, I was looking into the eyes of the crash test dummies opposite me,” said the private. “Whatever they went through, I don't want to follow.”

“You'll be singing a different tune if you ever use it in the field.”

“And will you be joining me in the field, Mr. Logistics Officer?”
strings.GNG_PTRG.8.a: “No, same way I won't be joining you on two weeks punishment detail.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.9.desc:
“...but a lack of weapon specifications is a weakness the ROC Armed Forces do not currently possess,” said the thin-cheekboned man in the green uniform. “Executive Vice President, I must admit that I am extremely skeptical of adding one more category for our logistics corps to sort through, easy to maintain or otherwise.”

“A fair point,” said the bespectacled young Cheung Kong man opposite the boardroom table from him and other Chinese military and political figures, himself flanked by fellow Cheung Kong and Sony executives. “However, this rifle was built specifically with addressing these issues in mind. I believe you are referring to the ongoing... lack of standardisation in ammunition between different units. However, as you can see here, the Modular Rifle is capable of supporting a variety of ammunition types commonly utilized in China. The cost offset in ammunition procurement alone makes the Modular Rifle not only a practical, but a profitable tool for the army of tomorrow.”

“That does sound promising,” chimed in one of the politicians.

“It would,” said another military man, “if not for the great achievements already made in improving equipment cohesion. You claim to speak for the army of the future, and of innovation generally, but you have made little but a solution for yesterday's problems.”

The executive bristled, then calmed. “Our yesterday, perhaps, but few would argue of the progress which still needs to be made. Progress we can circumvent immediately. When the world leaves yesterday behind...”
strings.GNG_PTRG.9.a: “...Guangdong will be ready with the new tomorrow.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.10.desc:
“As one can plainly see,” said the man in the white coat on the stage, “this is not your grandfather's rifle. We were told it would be impossible to have everything, but the jaded, incomplete views of the past now give way to...” An officer tapped him on the shoulder.

“Alas, my presence is needed elsewhere! Please welcome Kusanagi to the stage, and if I do not see you again this evening, my fondest farewells! It has been an absolute pleasure,”- the officer tugged at his arm- “Goodbye!”

A while later, the engineer was sat alone in a room full of army officers, with a difficult expression on their face. “This new weapon of yours goes far beyond the specifications of what the Imperial Japanese Army has asked you to produce.”

The engineer grinned for a second, but quickly let it drop. “We are aware, exceeding your expectations was our exact intention. What seems to be the issue?”

“The world outside the lab, for one thing,” said an officer. “Beyond the initial price of the weapon, which I can only assume is quite dear, one would have to bring half an electronics store to service this rifle in the field.”

“And why have you chosen to abandon the initial weapon you promised?” asked another officer. “We were satisfied with it as it already existed.”

The engineer sighed. “Well, if it is truly the wish of the IJA, the simpler weapon remains available for purchase. But we were of the understanding that you desired the best weapon that could be made by us, and I believe the tests shown today speak for themselves. It's a simple fact, my friends.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.10.a: “In commerce and war, premium goods command premium prices.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.15.desc:
TO: COMMANDER, IJA GUANGDONG FORMATIONS
FROM: GUANGDONG STATE GOVERNMENT, DAITŌASHŌ

THE GREATER EAST ASIA MINISTRY IS PLEASED TO ANNOUNCE THAT THE STATE GOVERNMENT OF GUANGDONG HAS VOLUNTEERED TO SEND A RESEARCH DIVISION TO INDONESIA TO HELP THE GREATER EAST ASIA CO-PROSPERITY SPHERE IN ITS FIGHT AGAINST THE FORCES OF WESTERN IMPERIALISM—“

General Nagano Shigeto put the paper down, dismayed. Anyone with a little bit of sense could tell why Guangdong had really 'volunteered' to send soldiers—his soldiers—out to that tropical hellhole. It was all to test some of those new technological horrors they called 'weapons'. Just wonderful, wasn't it?

Sure, the executives were happy to have an 'easy' opportunity to profit off the preservation of Imperial glory and get in Tokyo's good graces. But Nagano saw things differently. Money didn't mean anything to him.

To him, all this Indonesian volunteering nonsense was just a boondoggle—men being sent to fight a 'good' fight but with suspect weapons and even more suspect leadership. The hell of Malaya was proof enough of that.

But what choice did Nagano really have? None.

”Mine is not to question why, is it?“
strings.GNG_PTRG.16.desc:
“They've done it again, haven't they, Takashima? Tell me it isn't true.”

Takashima, Consul-General of Japan in the State of Guangdong, had nothing to offer but a sigh. “Yes, they've done it again, General.”

Nagano's head was in his hands, and he said, “Spell it out, then. What nonsense have they scribbled up this time?”

His interlocutor sighed and read it out: “The State of Guangdong has, in the interests of supporting the strategic goals of the Imperial Japanese Army and the Government of the Great Japanese Empire, declared the deployment of a volunteer-research division to the Colombian Civil War.” At that the general slammed his fist on the table.

“Infuriating! Imperial Japanese Army soldiers, my soldiers, are once again going to be sent to fight in a foreign war—a war of choice for us—without the equipment tried and tested for the cause! They're - they're guinea pigs for scientists who don't understand a single damned word of why they fight.”

The consul general sighed, and Nagano continued. “And I'm supposed to look these men in the eye as their rifles break down on them day in and day out, as their weapons and supplies prove all the more unreliable because some thrice-damned egghead 'scientist' made them without knowing how real combat works, and tell them they're 'doing the right thing' when all they're really doing is serving the Chief Executive's money-grubbing interests?” By now his voice had crescendoed into a shout.
strings.GNG_PTRG.16.a: “I hate this, Takashima, I hate it so much!”
strings.GNG_PTRG.17.desc:
“TO: COMMANDER, IJA GUANGDONG FORMATIONS
FROM: GUANGDONG STATE GOVERNMENT, DAITŌASHŌ

THE GREATER EAST ASIA MINISTRY IS PLEASED TO ANNOUNCE THAT THE STATE GOVERNMENT OF GUANGDONG HAS VOLUNTEERED TO SEND A RESEARCH DIVISION TO MIDDLE EASTERN TO HELP THE GREATER EAST ASIA CO-PROSPERITY SPHERE IN ITS FIGHT AGAINST THE FORCES OF WESTERN IMPERIALISM—”

General Nagano was in a depth of rage and despair he had never felt before.

He scribbled out 'fight against the forces of Western Imperialism', writing over it 'get Japan oil, and some oil for Guangdong too, and fucking grub some money selling bullshit bloody weapons to Arab imbeciles while we're at it'. Then he smashed the pen upon his knee, wincing in pain as he threw it in the garbage, and tore the paper to shreds.

What the hell was this? “They're asking soldiers to put their lives on the line as if they were mere mercenaries!
