Fighting for literal profit as a motivation—putting their lives on the line as, as, as mere sales representatives for the worthless corporations here! Is this the life of a soldier these days?”

As Nagano paced back and forth in anger, he yearned for the honourable (to him) service he had done in China forty years ago.

“This isn't what it means to be a soldier! This isn't!” the general cried out, as he realised just how impotent his rage was. Nagano sat down and put his head in his hands, knowing that no matter how strongly he despised what Guangdong made him do, that there was not a single thing he could do to stop it.
strings.GNG_PTRG.18.desc:
The Chief Executive's position in Guangdong is a busy one, with constant meetings to attend, reports to sort through, and orders to be authorize. On most days, the reporter talking on the TV, the conversation in the hallways surrounding his office, and the headlines on the daily paper were nothing more than just simple distractions. But {gng_getleader} noticed one country's name being said across all three mediums over the past week: Colombia.

And he began asking his closest advisors about Colombia. How there had been a stalemate for years, suddenly erupting into wide scale conflict. How the mainland government was expected to support one of the factions fighting in this conflict. How the IJA and IJN were constantly complaining about their outdated equipment. And just like that, he suddenly remembered one of Suzuki's old projects that had been defunct for a while now.

The Product Testing Research Group sounded like an ordinary research and development team from one of Guangdong's many companies, but it was instead a weapons development team working in tandem with the IJA and IJN to ensure that the Japanese military was always one step ahead of its adversaries. Companies would submit prototype weapon designs to the PTRG, and then the army and navy would actually go out and test the prototypes. The group had been put on the backburner since the Yasuda Crisis, but there were dozens of project ideas that had been considered after Indonesia.

The Chief Executive would spend the rest of the afternoon pitching the idea again to his contacts in the army and navy, who were excited to hear that the program was being restarted.

They always stressed their need for more reliable, more effective equipment, and if one of the Guangdong companies could provide it, the profits would make most other product launches look like failures. For {gng_getleader}, failure was never an option for surviving in Guangdong, and the PTRG would be no exception to that rule.
strings.GNG_PTRG.18.a: One country's loss is another's gain.
strings.GNG_PTRG.18.tt:
It is time to subsidize our experimental SPART project for advanced field testing.
The field-testing unit will then deploy, ready to be sent to Colombia.
The deadline for testing is 365 days.
To ensure that the PTRG is under control, it needs to have a general assigned to track progress.
strings.GNG_PTRG.19.t: A Test Site Close to Home
strings.GNG_PTRG.19.desc:
Had Indonesia always been that unstable? pondered {gng_getleader}, his fingers constantly tapping against his desk. He didn't remember it being on the verge of a civil war, yet the country had devolved into a mess right in front of his eyes, but also Japan's. It was certainly going to be a black eye on the Sphere, but fresh conflict meant new testing grounds for the PTRG.

He picked up the receiver, and dialed the number of several military commanders stationed back in Japan. Much to his expectation, the PTRG was given significantly more freedom and resources to operate with. Losing control of Indonesia was bad enough as is, but if the rebels managed to find a way to overthrow Sukarno's government, the fallout would be disastrous.

That is, for the Empire of Japan.

Guangdong has always been a state about turning a profit, and war was no different. The Chief Executive picked up several reports from the PTRG team, detailing new armor prototypes that the companies had sent in recently. With the expertise of the scientists in both the PTRG and the companies, and a little bit of luck to extend Indonesia's incoming civil war, Guangdong would be able to collect all the data it needed in order to make a decision on which product to support. If anything, he could use the comparison between the base IJA units and the PTRG unit to drive up the sale price even more when he sold the prototypes back to the mainland.

Failing to prove the prototypes' worthiness would negatively impact Guangdong's financial and political standing.
strings.GNG_PTRG.19.a: Thankfully, Guangdong has no tolerance for failure whatsoever.
strings.GNG_PTRG.19.tt:
It is time to decide which experimental tank project we will subsidize for advanced field testing.
The field-testing unit will then deploy, ready to be sent to Indonesia.
The deadline for testing is 365 days, and despite not ruling Guangdong, £GNG_Hitachi_texticon Hitachi has also chipped in, allowing us to subsidize them for temporary benefit.
To ensure that the PTRG is under control, it needs to have a general assigned to track progress.
strings.GNG_PTRG.20.desc:
{gng_getleader} had seen the reports regarding the new crisis facing his state. For the “Oil Crisis”, all of the news and internal signals he had been receiving over the past week were all bad. With the oil from the Middle East expected to dry up within the upcoming weeks, most of Guangdong's vital industries would also be forced to come to a grinding halt. And if that happened, the protests outside would surely turn into riots. Something needed to be done, and fast, but for once, he felt stumped. He slumped in his chair, his hand massaging the many new wrinkles that were covering his face.

He picked up another piece of paper with the PTRG stamp at the top. The report detailed several vehicle prototypes that were being adapted for desert and mountainous operations, given the current crisis. Prototypes were expected to be ready... within the month?! Surely Guangdong could get the rights to several oil sources in exchange for these nations to get an advantage in their conflicts with equipment devised by the PTRG.

The Chief Executive put on his jacket and prepared to leave his office. If this report was true, then it could very well be the solution that Guangdong needed to at least soften some of the effects of the current crisis. But first, he needed to verify the report he was given. One wrong move here, and his vision for Guangdong could be snuffed in an instant.
strings.GNG_PTRG.20.a: The lights in the labs come alive.
strings.GNG_PTRG.20.tt:
It is time to subsidize our experimental helicopter project for advanced field testing.
The field-testing unit will then deploy, ready to be sent to Middle East.
The deadline for testing is 365 days, and due to the multitude of conflicts, we need to decide in the £decision_icon_small decision tab which conflict to prioritize.
To ensure that the PTRG is under control, it needs to have a general assigned to track progress.
strings.GNG_PTRG.21.desc:
As a military cargoplane touches down in the rain at a base, PTRG scientists and military personnel deplane into the wet, humid night.

The former push around boxes worth of combat data and intelligence gained from the most recent deployment of the PTRG battalions, eager to discuss improvements and changes that need to be made to the weapons that they've been observing. They carry reports that their superiors will spend sleepless nights sifting through, making sure that every product that comes out of Guangdong's weapon development labs is not a failure by any and every metric, lest they want to be replaced. The data will be processed, with some of it being thrown out as useless, and other bits being prized as the gold standard. As the data is loaded onto their vans, they disappear into the neon cityscape that dominates the Guangdong night.

The latter stand in the rain, awaiting orders from their commanders to return to their barracks. They unload dozens of wooden coffins containing their fallen comrades, the soaked flags covering them offering little protection against the rain. There are no thanks, no rewards for having been the guinea pigs and lab rats for collecting the aforementioned data. The survivors know that as the next conflict breaks, they'll be sent to another foreign land to test equipment that was likely to malfunction and blow up in their face by their commanders. The same ones who watch as entire companies are torn apart in order to see if Guangdong's novel equipment could pass their high standards.

Both groups would return back to their daily duties, knowing that they would meet on the same airfield again at some point in the near future.
strings.GNG_PTRG.22.desc:
The following is a log of all incidents involving the experimental equipment that was assigned to the field team.

14/3 0900 - CA-1 begins a fire support mission, firing on grid K-6. 21 rounds are fired across 15 minutes, before the autoloader jams. CA-1 then spends an hour attempting to fix the autoloader, before realizing that they are missing critical parts that are necessary to complete the repair. CA-1 returns to base.

15/3 1400 - CA-1 completes repairs at FOB (REDACTED). A second SPG is added to CA-1 to increase combat effectiveness, designated CA-2. Team is able to make its way across the mountainous terrain in grid D-2, before stopping in grid D-4. However, ten minutes in, CA-1 notices a drop in round velocity, with observers reporting that rounds are falling short into grid K-3, killing eleven friendlies. CA-1 breaks off back to base, while CA-2 continues firing for another 30 minutes. Upon return to base, CA-1 notices that the protective coating on the barrels of the gun are melting, and installs a new barrel.

17/3 0800 - CA-2 is sent to grid E-1, but is spotted by enemy air reconnaissance while en route. A helicopter unit, likely belonging to (REDACTED), attacks CA-2 with small arms fire. Although the helicopter unit misses all anti-vehicle munitions, rifle fire is enough to penetrate the platform, and a bullet likely reaches either the ammunition belt or the gas tank, and CA-2 is lost. IJA unit (REDACTED) is tasked with ensuring the enemy does not recover the wreck.

Final Recommendation: Improve armor rating. Replace barrel coating. Ensure all crews have necessary parts to maintain repairs. Rate of fire is well above current IJA SPGs, so design can be salvaged if survivability and reliability can be improved.
strings.GNG_PTRG.23.desc:
Author: Lt. Masuzu, Colombian Expeditionary Force, Unit (REDACTED), edited by I-6, PTRG Scientist

Attached is a log of all incidents with equipment designated “MS”.

D2 0700 - CEF unit (REDACTED) in grid G-6 request air support in dealing with mass infantry and light vehicles, but are instead told to make do with several SPGs. IJA transport Torin-1 drops three MS platforms, with what it believes is sufficient ammunition. MS platforms fire 1.5 rounds per minute, driving enemy back into grid G-10. However, MS unable to reach grid G-10, and CEF loses 1/10th of fighting force when trying to push into grid G-8. (I-6: Gun too weak. At least idiotic IJA grunts can operate the gun without training.)

D4 1600 - Unit in grid B-7 request artillery fire, and PTRG authorizes deployment of four MS platforms, along with 500 hundred rounds. Limitations on available transports, however, mean that only 200 rounds are shipped with the MS platforms. B-7 shells position A-5, driving enemies back into grid A-2. Again, however, IJA units are unable to make an effective counterattack, due to fire support landing well short of desired targets.

D5 0300 - Defensive line Kiba-4 is attacked in the middle of the night by hostiles. 5 MS platforms are wheeled onto hill D-12 in under ten minutes, despite poor road quality and a steep uphill climb, and are able to relieve pressure on Kiba-4 by launching approximately 8 rounds per minute, driving hostiles back into grid B-4.

Performance Review: Acceptable. I do not believe that the platform has universal viability in terms of an artillery piece, given its current short range. It performs on par, if not worse, than standard IJA SPGs in everything except traversability. However, given the harsh environment we were fighting in, the MS platforms were effective.
strings.GNG_PTRG.24.desc:
D1 0500 - Flew into airbase (REDACTED) with Fujitsu's SPG, hereby designated as “FS”. FS caused quite a stir among the troops as soon as it landed, given that it requires a specialized train locomotive to lug around. Already logistics corps made a fuss about wasting fuel, but General (REDACTED) shut down concerns immediately, thankfully. FS likely to standout on actual battlefield, so I suggested to Lt. Shiromi that the unit act as more of a standing artillery piece, rather than a moving platform.

D3 0900 - Units in grids G-6 and G-7 are pinned down by enemy mortar crews. FS crew able to pinpoint exact location of mortar crews thanks to spotters, and are able to eliminate five mortar crews in just eight shots. However, FS unable to provide additional supporting fire, since the locomotive is unable to scale a (embarrassingly low) hill, allowing enemies to retreat and re-establish a defensive line.

D5 2000 - FS assigned to provide supportive fire in grid L-14, nearly 60 km away. Despite nighttime operation, IJA unit (REDACTED) reports enemy positions are thoroughly destroyed, and are incredibly impressed at both the rate of fire and the accuracy. However, a short circuit cuts FS' fire support mission short, and ordering replacement parts takes three days.

Final Recommendation: Accuracy and rate of fire may be enough to salvage this design, though it's hard to see it as anything but a stationary artillery piece with its awful maneuverability. Need to lower its weight somehow(shipping it here was bad, too), or this design is dead on arrival. Replacement parts can be easily sent with FS next time - not worried about that.
strings.GNG_PTRG.25.desc:
Author: G-3, PTRG Scientist

Attached is a log of all incidents involving experimental equipment “HS”.

D1 0900 - Two HS units are sent to grid C7 to provide fire support in grid C11, near Cali. Units in B11 call for a fire mission in grid B13, and HS fires 12 rockets, 10 of which land in B13, and 2 of which land in B15. Enemy positions in B13 are thoroughly wiped out with no survivors, thanks to the payload fired. Forces from New Granada inform us that over 40 civilians were found dead due to the errant missiles landing in grid B15, and request that we stop using the HS platform as fire support. Their request is denied.

D3 1200 - Four HS units are deployed to grid C10 to provide fire support. After firing three payloads, a request for additional ammo is sent back to HQ. Given their elevated location, three helicopters are sent to resupply the HS units. However, enemy combatants spot the resupplying helicopters in grid C12, and fire several RPGs, downing one of them. IJA unit (REDACTED) is tasked with salvaging the wreck, but fails to recover several missile pods. The HS units successfully retreat back into grid C6.

D6: 0800 - In response to the previous incident, HS units are now sent out with double their original missile allowance. Three HS units are tasked to provide fire support in grid K4, and begin their trip to grid H16, only to run out of fuel due to the extra weight of the additional ammunition. By the time resupply trucks arrive at 1000, the conflict in K4 has been resolved in the enemy's favor.

Final Recommendation: Extremely effective anti-infantry weapon. Missing missile pods could be a problem, given that they were most likely recovered by the OFN-aligned leftists. Accuracy leaves much to be desired; top brass will not like their own troops being hit by this gun, especially since it never leaves survivors. Need to document supply problems before handing the design off to IJA, given how difficult it is to resupply in combat zones.
strings.GNG_PTRG.26.desc:
Dai grimaced as he activated the newly installed infrared sight, which began transmitting a live feed of the dense jungle to the driver's seat of his tank. The first unit to use Sony's new technology, he was cheerfully informed that the tool could pinpoint any heat signature under 100 meters away. Naturally, the brief was coupled with orders to seize a settlement, far outside of normal operating range .

“They've got nowhere left to hide,” his commander said.

With annoyance, Dai realized that the tool was working perfectly, and was helpfully displaying a wall of orange light across the screen. He was shown every single heat signature in the jungle, at noon.

As the corps neared the village, Dai peered out from the hatch, seeing a deserted town and empty treeline. Returning to the infrared scanner, his environment was blanketed in uniform orange, revealing no distinct signatures but the corps' own vehicles, which were just beginning to enter the village. As the first tank passed the gate of the town, anti-tank fire shattered the tense silence as the forward vehicles were reformed into plumes of yellow on the monitor.

Dai hastily began retreating as the corps fired on the village, blanketing the screen with dozens of orange and yellow spots.

Watching from a distance, Dai watched as the unit continued to bombard the settlement, long after the last insurgent had fled.
strings.GNG_PTRG.27.desc:
Gota used to feel untouchable. He piloted a tank that the Indonesians could never pierce, while his gunner dealt retribution with hails of bullets. Then his corps was given the “privilege” of testing Matsushita's newest innovation, an autoloader and guided missile. This was vigorously lauded by an overexcited supervisor as a tremendous increase to a tank's firepower.

What he had neglected to mention was that the increased ammunition came at the expense of most of the armor. Although his gunner was delighted by the explosive spectacle, Gota watched a single stray shell immolate another tank in his unit. Gota tried to clear his mind of fear, knowing that loss of focus was now fatal.

As the dust settled, Gota breathed a sigh of relief. Another battle was over, and his tank - and life - were miraculously still intact. The enemy fortification was annihilated: only ash and rubble remained. He might have celebrated had he not glanced back and seen the charred steel remnants that littered the battlefield. Frowning, Gota returned to formation and began trundling back to base.

Back in his office, the corporate supervisor smiled with glee as he read the reports. Recent performance surpassed all expectations. By all metrics, the upgrade was a success. The higher-ups would be pleased.
strings.GNG_PTRG.27.a: The barracks were stifled by silence.
strings.GNG_PTRG.28.desc:
Of all the places he could have been deployed, Kaneko reflected, Indonesia had to be the worst. His lieutenant's uniform was not nearly prepared for the Indonesian heat, but he still had to stand and watch the vehicles in his platoon practice tactics every day. Every day he awoke to discover dozens of new mosquito bites across his arms and legs, which no amount of bug spray seemed to prevent. For all the talk of “serving his country” and “upholding the empire's honor”, Kaneko's deployment had mostly been spent finding ways to keep the soldiers, and himself, entertained. He longed for a frontline deployment, and a chance to finally prove himself in command.

Kaneko watched as the diminutive man exited his office, the “Fujitsu Limited” logo emblazoned on the man's suit staring back at him. In a strenuously long conversation, he was informed that his platoon had been selected to field-test Guangdong's newest armored technology. As he was repeatedly told, the tank was equipped with a gyroscopic turret, allowing it to fire accurately on the move. Glancing out the window, Kaneko frowned, seeing the thickly wooded rainforest bordering the base, and the narrow winding road that pierced it. What use was mobility in the forest? He cleared his head; he would find out soon enough.

Kaneko leaned forwards as his truck rounded a corner and their destination, a hostile village, came into clear view. As the convoy entered the clearing, Kaneko noticed a child run from the gates toward the village center. The village wasn't supposed to be inhabited. Kaneko failed to process his thoughts or make a complaint before gunfire resounded from the village, quickly reciprocated by the convoy. Kaneko watched in horror as the tanks circled around the village, laying waste to the settlement with uninterrupted fire. The representative's voice echoed over the radio, jubilant over the success of the upgrade. Struck silent, Kaneko stared as the platoon annihilated the town, home by home.
strings.GNG_PTRG.29.desc:
The ley lines of intercrossing roads were the lifeblood of the Japanese presence in Indonesia. Hundreds of packed-dirt veins and asphalt-paved arteries fed and armed the entire military across the archipelago. As a logistician, Magabe had the arduous task of maintaining maximum efficiency by ensuring that supply and personnel vehicles traveled with timely and orderly movements. He watched closely as a large tank - with two massive, screw-like cylinders in place of any treads - arrived from the brush of the rainforest, rejoining the column at the rear. As the convoy began to advance, Magabe blanched. The vehicle's strange propulsion method ripped chunks of the dirt road from the ground, leaving behind a minefield of potholes and indentations on the once smooth path. Magabe watched as the tanks, unknowing or uncaring about the devastation, trundled forward, carrying the “Hitachi Limited” logo proudly into view.

Riding near the middle of the convoy, Magabe struggled to find a solution to the issue. He knew better than to complain, especially about Guangdong's companies; mitigation was the only real option. Taking time to repack the roads was an open invitation to any partisans laying in wait, and alternative routes could add hours to a trip if they existed at all. Glancing at the vehicle's report, Magabe's frown grew deeper. The tanks would take an inordinate amount of fuel trucks to supply, wearing down the roads even more. The quartermaster was not going to be happy.

Back at home base, Magabe smirked as he overheard the soldiers discuss the wondrous feats of the new tank. The words “ambush”, “annihilated”, and “incredible” leapt out at him. He sighed in resignation, tepidly glad that the tank was strong in combat, at least. Magabe had already prepared his reports of “increased insurgent sabotage” when his superiors inevitably complained about the roads being unusable. It was the soldiers' problem now.
strings.GNG_PTRG.29.a: And they had a bumpy ride ahead of them.
strings.GNG_PTRG.30.desc:
Sony's new chopper had very responsive controls, as Takayanagi had found out the hard way. He'd nearly crashed the thing into the ground his first time out. The older models were big, bulky things that flew with all the grace of a walrus and took ages to move anywhere. This one, though, was lightweight, flexible, and supremely effective.

Takayanagi was a scout for his unit, bringing his chopper up just ahead of the front lines to spot enemy dispositions. He'd relay his report over the radio to the commander on the ground, and zip away before the fighting began.

If he was spotted, the chopper was usually agile enough to evade enemy SAM systems, and even had a few barrages of rockets for if fighting became necessary. Thermal imaging and night vision cameras meant Takayanagi was able to spot enemies in any weather conditions.

Most importantly - at least for the army procurement office - the chopper used only a fraction of the fuel of the older models, thanks to how light it was.
strings.GNG_PTRG.30.a: War has never been more sleek.
strings.GNG_PTRG.31.desc:
Nishimura watched as the new helicopters came back from their latest combat mission, carrying a few members of his company. As they disembarked, he noticed that the frame of one of the choppers was peppered with bullet holes. Some of the departing soldiers looked at the damage nervously as they got out.

Matsushita's new choppers were certainly welcomed by the men. They had dual attack-transport capability, so nobody had to worry anymore about being pinned down under fire with no air support.

That wasn't to say, of course, that there weren't issues with them. The pilots in particular were always complaining about how thin-skinned they were, and how flying one made them as easy to shoot down as someone piloting a hot air balloon. Jokes often went around about MPs sentencing undisciplined soldiers to ride shotgun in a chopper on their next mission.

You had to be crazy to fly one, so they said. But it wasn't like any of them had a choice. This was the military, after all.
strings.GNG_PTRG.31.a: And we do as we're told.
strings.GNG_PTRG.32.desc:
The latest consignment of Fujitsu helicopter gunships was certainly state of the art technology. Equipped with the latest in computerized guidance systems and an arsenal of high end rocketry, the gunship was a potent offensive weapon. Where artillery barrages or napalm runs were unavailable - most often when Japanese troops were too close to the enemy for it to be safe - Fujitsu's choppers would be out there, drowning the enemy in a sea of fire.

The upshot, though, was the cost. Field commanders knew that losing one of their gunships in combat would result in a frenzied hiding from their division's procurement office. Each one cost enough to outfit a few extra companies of troops, and the army budgetary office was not shy in reminding field commanders of that at any given opportunity.

With fiscal responsibility concerns so prominent, though, the gunship often saw only limited use in the field. Commanders unwilling to risk the displeasure of their superiors would use them only when the infantry had cleared out most of the opposition - ironically, this was a situation in which a helicopter gunship was least useful.
strings.GNG_PTRG.33.desc:
Pound for pound, missile for missile, the new Hitachi prototype helicopter was an invulnerable monster in the air. Its mobility was unmatched, its firepower overwhelming. It could shred American and German choppers in aerial combat, and obliterate a line of infantry within seconds with its laser-guided missiles.

However, all this ultra-modern tech came with some significant drawbacks. The things cost more than a city block, and so could never be combined in enough numbers to have a truly overpowering impact on the battlefield. Most units only had a couple, and they were jealously preserved by the procurement office.

Of greater concern to the soldiers, though, were the maintenance issues. The chopper was packed full of so many complex electronics and Hitachi-trademarked parts that the average army engineer could do no more than stare at it in dismay. Hitachi engineers had to be brought in to fix even the most minor of problems.

When it could be brought to bear, Hitachi's helicopter was an unmatched powerhouse. But therein lay the difficulty - it simply could not be brought to bear, at least not with current technology.
strings.GNG_PTRG.34.desc:
The first day that the new tanks rolled into the base, everyone was excited. These were the new marvels from the State of Guangdong, state-of-the-art tanks with innovative features to support the fighting men of Japan in their adventures abroad. To the IJA soldiers on this base, they looked like they came from the future: sleek and sturdy, with a design unseen from the more staid and traditional Mitsubishi. A smiling representative from Guangdong led the convoy, bearing a thousand sales pitches to throw at the impressed soldiers.

Then they got into those tanks, and the grumbling started.

“-swear, half this shit's in the wrong place. It's like they shuffled all the instruments around like playing cards. Why isn't the fuel reader near the-”

“-cameras mounted on the outside, without a lot of armour around it. Yeah, I guess he gets better visibility, but if someone gets a lucky shot with an RPG and knocks out a camera, the commander's deaf, dumb and-”

“-gun traversal's fine, but the shape looks off. It's a different design and a different material. And I swear I can hear scraping when I elevate the cannon. The boys down in maintenance are gonna need to double their warehouse space to fit all the spare parts-”

The representative from Guangdong lost his smile in the tidal wave of concerns, comments and queries. 'Overengineered' was the word of the day on the base; he had written that a hundred times in his notebook where he recorded what the soldiers told him of his tanks. As he drove back to his hotel, to catch some sleep before he took a plane back to Honkon, he wondered how the Chief Executive would respond to their remarks.

Well, he thought, that was his boss' problem.
strings.GNG_PTRG.34.a: “-and why is there a cup holder in this thing?”
strings.GNG_PTRG.35.desc:
“Sony believes that the Republic of China's needs for a next generation main battle tank are fulfilled by our product. To see and destroy your enemy before they can do the same to you - our infrared technology provides an unparalleled advantage to do just that.”

Section Chief Nagamori Eiji wrapped up his pitch to the Chinese generals and vice-ministers as the lights were turned back on, revealing the stony-faced expressions of the procurement committee. He tugged at his tie knot with a sweaty hand, subconsciously giving himself some breathing space before the inevitable barrage of questions.

“I see no material improvement in top speed - or, inversely, in armor protection,” said a stocky, muscled military man - clearly representing the combat arms of the Chinese military. “Survivability looks like a second priority.”

“I'd like to take a second look at the production schedules.” A suited, spectacled bureaucrat picked at the proposal with an exquisite, practiced fussiness. “For a supplier as young as yours, we need assurances there won't be any hiccups in a procurement order - or in regular maintenance.”

“Our factories are just across the border,” Nagamori countered. “Sony Armaments can deliver production anywhere in China, far quicker than shipping items from Japan.”

“With all due respect, we're all familiar with what the Japanese are selling, and less so with what Guangdong has to offer,” said the military spokesperson.

“Then rest assured,” Nagamori said, “that this product already reflects months of testing in live combat conditions - by the Imperial Japanese Army, no less. Where you once had to choose between reliability and novelty - ”
strings.GNG_PTRG.36.desc:
At first, the generals seemed quite happy with this new product. Some of them had served in Colombia (in a strictly advisory position) and seen it in action. Others had read the after-action reports, seen the specifications, and were quite impressed with its performance. Lightweight, durable, more accurate - and that was on its base performance, not taking into account the particular flair Guangdong added to the weapon. All that was left was the matter of cost.

At this, the representative from Guangdong hesitated. “Well, such intricate engineering does require greater investment than your average weapons manufacturer. We are developing batch production facilities to ensure a consistent output, but this will require initial investment and a mutual agreement on expected quantity to properly design and develop.”

“What you're saying,” said the one general who had been consistently unimpressed, “is that it's going to cost us an arm and a leg just to outfit one battalion, and you're asking us to buy for the whole army.”

“Maybe just an arm?” The representative stretched an awkward grin onto his face to match his poorly-advised joke. The mood in the meeting room had deflated. Suddenly, the generals seemed less keen, and the sceptic among them continued.

“With regards to maintenance, if you'd please open up page 39,” as he and his fellow generals turned the pages of the report in front of them, “you mention that certain care needs to be taken with their internal systems. I know the outer shell can take a beating, but some of these restrictions... we can't use these in dry heat? 'Build-up of foreign material such as coarse sand can interfere with the electrical components?' What happens if our boys need to fight in the desert?”
strings.GNG_PTRG.36.a: “I assure you, gentlemen, that'll be fixed in the next development cycle.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.37.desc:
The Sony howitzer let loose an ear-splitting roar, shaking the earth as it fired off the last shell of its fire mission on the practice range. The Sony scientist clicked his stopwatch, inspecting the total time elapsed: 63 seconds for six rounds. Even if the autoloader was doing most of the work, it still represented a material improvement on the part of the Chinese artillery crew - but there was still some room for improvement.

The Chinese crew - part of a battery of eight guns - smiled thinly as the scientist prattled on about the most optimal way to minimize the time between rounds loaded and to ensure the stability of their targeting solutions. Just four months ago, they had been part of a smaller battery of five towed artillery pieces, struggling to put three rounds on target in a minute and a half. Artillery was the king of the battlefield, and they were increasingly feeling like they lived up to the saying.

When the Sony representative had dismissed the crew for a break - and when he had conclusively disappeared out of eyeshot - they conferred amongst themselves.

“Finally feels like we're getting somewhere,” a clean-shaven corporal said. “But fuck me, feels wrong knowing it was made in Guangdong, of all places. What're they doing making guns, when they usually make TVs?”

The crew's spirits darkened at the mention of Guangdong, that rankling reminder of the unnatural split still dividing their families and their people. They fell silent for a second, looking at the ground beneath their feet - before the corporal opened his mouth again.

“If we ever take Guangdong back, I hope it's with this gun.”
strings.GNG_PTRG.37.a: The entire battery shared a knowing smile.
strings.GNG_PTRG.38.desc:
From the cockpit of his new helicopter, Hokazono Jun thought the world looked simpler than before. He was so used to the KH-4 that taking Guangdong's newest overengineered bird for a test flight was a disorienting experience. Sure, the fancy features of this beast were working as expected, but he could not understand why half of his flight controls needed to be reoriented. After struggling to find the right amount of pressure to put on these redesigned anti-torque pedals, he brought down the helicopter on the landing pad.

“So, what do you think?” called out the technician on the ground. Hokazono kills the engine; the blades slow down quicker than expected. He takes off his helmet and leaves the helicopter. “She's gonna be a bitch to maintain,” the technician continued. “Bet you anything that Guangdong's going to sell spare parts at a premium.”

“We're the IJA.” From his coat pocket Hokazono pulled out a cigarette. The technician lit it up for him. “If they think they can stiff us for parts, they can go fuck themselves.” He looked around at the empty base. There were other technicians milling around outside the helicopter pad, some taking notes with a representative from Guangdong. “Am I the only pilot here?”

“No, but they're all on other assignments. Looks like you got the new toys all to yourself.” The technician chuckled, slapped Hokazono on the back, but the pilot seemed uneasy about this new prospect. He'd been flying helicopters since '51, and he could not figure out where Guangdong's inventions could fit within their current fleet. They were simply too specialised, stuck out awkwardly in a squadron. He was on the schedule for more test flights, and he'd been told that he would pilot them going forward. Was this going to be his career from now on? Master of seldom-used aircraft, sold on a once-off basis, perhaps never to see action for fear of the repair costs?
strings.GNG_PTRG.38.a: Not all products immediately resonate with their intended audience.
strings.GNG_PTRG.39.desc:
Even if it had taken two months of training to become familiar with the dizzying array of flight surfaces, reconnaissance optics, and weapons controls, Lieutenant Sun couldn't deny the obvious: the Sony helicopter was worth its weight in gold and then some.

With a soft flick of his left wrist, the helicopter's body popped up above the hilltop, facing the firing range; Sun twisted a separate knob to the collective lever's side to adjust the high-definition camera's focus and zoom, before snapping three shots in quick succession. He twisted the flight stick to the right with his free hand, while pushing his left foot forwards to keep the helicopter's nose on target as he squeezed the flight stick's trigger.

The missile barrage that slammed home in a glorious explosion of dirt, flame, and smoke. Before the dust had settled, Sun had swung the helicopter back around, darting away from the target with the speed made possible by the lightweight chopper. Armor, the designers had reasoned, wasn't needed so long as the pilot didn't get hit; the fear of an instant death certainly gave Sun plenty of incentive to fly as Sony intended.

After the mission, looking at the Sony logo stenciled onto the fuselage, Sun realized two things: it galled him to no end that Guangdong was selling China weapons, and that said weapons were well worth the money. When asked for a comment by his superiors, he asked, “Can't we buy any more of these? It's not like Guangdong cares who we use these on.”

At that, his superiors balked.
strings.GNG_PTRG.39.a: “Do you know how much even one of these costs?”
strings.GNG_PTRG_end_result: The outcome of the product trials depend on how many of the research objectives we have fulfilled on the fields of battle.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.1.desc:
From the moment shots were reported in western Guizhou, Guangdong fell into shock. Reports came flooding in throughout the day, as a host of intelligence agencies and local administrators attempted to cobble together a timeline and plan of action. By the time it landed on {gng_getleader}'s desk, the report had grown into a mess, full of enough retractions and updates to strain the manila envelope it came in.

Still, the basics were clear. Long Yun, a Chinese warlord once reduced to playing second fiddle to his cousin's government, had reinstated himself and begun a campaign to remove China from the Sphere by force with the help of allied anti-Japanese armies in the West. Now, just a few hours away from Guangdong, a rebellious army threatened to destroy the stability of the entire Chinese region.

Despite himself, {gng_getleader} could not help but feel the weight of the threat. Yet his options were limited. The Product Testing Group and IJA Garrison needed to stay at home, in case the war worsened. Worse, a note from the Chinese government had been tucked into the envelope, ording Guangdong not to assist directly lest Nanjing be delegitimized further.

For now, the Chief Executive would have to wait, stick to putting out fires at home. It would be enough of a challenge alone. Investors, the IJA, the Corporations, all would be on high alert so long as the war roared. Until the war's end, every man and woman in Guangdong would see a plain truth: a violent end to the corporate experiment lay just around the corner.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.1.a: We stand inches from a fire, and cannot put it out.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.2.desc:
With the Western Insurrection only growing more deadly, reports of refugees had become a constant element of {gng_getleader}'s daily briefings. A mass of tent cities rose on practically every major road into Guangdong, and by his government's estimations some three thousand illegals had entered the nation in just the last months.

Clearly, a refugee policy would be needed in the short term. Yet the question of who to accept was murky. For the Chief Executive, it pitted two long-held industrial maxims against each other: quantity versus quality.

On the one hand, most refugees were completely unskilled, farmers and day-laborers that could do little for local industry that could not be done by your average citizen. A policy which limited new arrivals to only educated specialists may provide the best quality. It would require some expense to maintain a largely closed border, but for that cost, Guangdong could extract the best of China while maintaining a limited and effective population.

On the other hand, Guangdong always needed its share of labor. Refugees would not only make for acceptable factory workers, but would likely accept low pay and provisions without hesitation - after all, they were by definition low on options. For the cost of their housing and nourishment, an open-door policy could keep the factories staffed for years, without any need for direct recruitment.

Soon, {gng_getleader} called up his secretary. His decision had been made.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.2.a: The Chief Executive chose quantity, and let them in.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.2.b: The Chief Executive chose quality, and closed his doors.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.3.desc:
As the Mangyō truck rumbled across the express lane, Xue had to admire the roads it drove on. The pavement, the lights, and the trucks made this side of the border strikingly different, electrified and clean, from the moment one crossed over the border. This was a new world, Xue thought to herself. She prayed it was a better one.

From the moment Xue escaped into Guangdong, she and a dozen others had been shepharded into a truck headed to Kōshū. Supposedly, that was where the work was. For now, all it meant was a few more hours of standing, now shoulder to shoulder with a crowd of disparate refugees. Xue wished she could lie down. She had been on her feet for two days now.

As the last hour rolled around, Xue finally considered whether this new land would be any better. It seemed safer, perhaps, but she couldn't help but sense a carelessness to this process. What would she arrive at, when she landed? Was she about to be thrown to the wolves once more?

It wasn't a question worth litigating either way. No matter her fate, her old life was gone, and Guangdong was just a few hours away.

Finally, a few hours later, the back of the truck rolled open, and the crowd of refugees stumbled out into the streets of Kōshū. As Xue ducked down and jumped out of the truck, the driver turned to her with a flier in his hand.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.3.a: The first word on the paper: MITSUBISHI.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.4.desc:
Yan stared at the conveyor belt. If he stopped for just a few more seconds, the device before him would slip past before he had a chance to brand the tire, and his supervisor would come to soundly thrash him. He just needed a moment to catch his breath. To accept this life.

For a second, something had reminded Yan of his old life, of his old farm in Guangxi. It brought forth a thousand memories, big and small, powerful and pointless. A life that he once had.

And then came the insurrection, the razing, and Guangdong's open doors. The car that drove him down to Kōshū, and the shower of flyers for the Yokohama Rubber factory. The last memory came out bitter, ruined by every monotonous day that followed, but Yen knew those days had been filled with hope. He had felt like his life was starting over again.

Yet a life on the assembly line had a way of corroding your soul.

Once, the putrid smell of burning rubber felt like acid in his nostrils. Now, even as the stench lingered on his clothes, he barely sensed it. How long had it been since he had seen his wife, his daughter? How long until this machine beside him crushed his hand, and consigned him into the streets to rot once more?

Yan burned the logo onto the tire, and let it pass. It felt like he was branding himself.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.4.a: To survive, you must let everything burn.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.5.desc:
A torrential rain had descended upon the border camp a day earlier, and had carelessly remained since. It left the makeshift barricades slick and reflective, and turned the already soft ground into thick mud. By nightfall, those remaining in the snaking lines of checkpoints and patrols were left shivering and dirty, their clothes stuck to their bodies from the downpour, their shoes soaked through and inch-deep in sludge.

It was in these lines that Zeng Junfeng tried to cross into Guangdong. After four hellish, torturous hours, he was rejected - just like everyone else.

In all that time, he'd only seen a few men enter. He met just one - an engineer named Gan, who fled from Ningyuan when the NPA insurrection spilled across the border. Zeng had a similar story, down to his city of origin. Alas, Zeng was a merchant, not an engineer. Guangdong, it seemed, had more than enough merchants already.

Zeng never gave up hope, even as his feet began to lose feeling and his fellow refugees collapsed around him. There would be another way in, perhaps in Guangxi where border patrols were weaker. He'd be a little hungrier by the time he arrived, a little thinner, but he had lifeforce to drain. Better to burn that last bit of stamina searching for exits than to stay here and let it be snuffed out by NPA bullets.

All that mattered was escaping the front lines and escaping the border camps. In truth, the two were not so different. Even before the war arrived, the camps were already sinking into the dirt.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.5.a: In Guangxi, Zeng would find another answer - no matter how bitter.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.6.desc:
Even the bars of Guangzhou seemed alien to Gan. Since he arrived in the city, he had spent months searching for authentic chinese liquors, but every bar worth going to seemed to only provide Japanese imports, or a smattering of disgusting industrial wines. Even Purple Sun, the bar Gan finally settled on, served sake, not Huangjiu.

Gan didn't come here for the alcohol, not really. He came for the ritual - a beer, a newspaper from the box parked outside, and an hour of drinking and reading about Insurrection after work each day. Lonely as it was, the ritual provided a simple comfort for Gan. For an hour, Gan got to remember his past in China, and remind himself why he remained in Guangdong.

Occasionally, he would notice his Japanese co-workers as they crammed into a booth and drunkenly chatted about the firm - who was on the rise, who was making an ass of themselves. He listened, a few times, to see if they ever mentioned his name. It never seemed to come up.

The slight stung, but not too badly. In the last few months, Gan had come to accept how the Japanese saw him. It wasn't a cruel antipathy. The Japanese admired him and enjoyed him - They certainly paid him well. Yet he could feel the underlying beliefs behind their cheer. To the Japanese, a Chinese engineer was like a child prodigy. A credit to his people. An idle curiosity.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.6.a: Lost in a sea of co-workers.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.7.desc:
{gng_getleader} stared at the newspaper. The moment he entered his office in the morning, his secretary handed the paper to him, and told him to look it over in his office. “Good news”, she called it.

When he settled into his office and looked it over, he saw the words he had been waiting for -. Long Yun killed in action, and the last remnants of the Western Insurrection had been taken out by Chinese soldiers. One nightmare, at least, was over.

The Chief Executive sighed. There would be more to say, of course, and more to do. China, in its current state, could never promise the kind of complete stability that the Emperor had always asked of it, and even its loyalty might someday come into question. But these would be internal problems - as a rule, they were not the things which would harm Guangdong the most.

{gng_getleader} turned back to his work. For now, the time had come to focus inward once more.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.7.a: Guangdong had more than enough enemies already.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.8.desc:
No matter how much the Chief Executive might have wanted it, the fall of Nanjing could never have been dealt with calmly. The slow-moving catastrophe up north was an event no one could look away from, a horror which gripped Guangdong's consciousness more and more as reality set in. If the Republic died, the NPA's next targets were clear - Manchukuo and Guangdong. In a matter of weeks or days, Guangdong would be facing a fight for its life.

{gng_getleader} tried to be the calm one in the room. He had prepared with the cabinet a number of emergency directives, and in a matter of minutes each was put in place. The factories were mobilized. The IJA's Phoenix Division was sent to the front lines, side-by-side with the police and the Product Testing Group. If Guangdong had a man with a gun, he'd be there to fight.

Yet even the Chief Executive found it hard to reassure his allies, generals, and investors. Guangdong had, in all its years, been designed around the safety of the Sphere, a circle of security in which Guangdong was near the center. It had not been designed to face a threat like this.
strings.GNG_WI_PTRG_unit_tt: We will remobilize the Product Testing Research Group to defend our country against Long Yun.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.9.desc:
As the protestors neared the Lee home, the plates in the kitchen cabinets all began to shake, and a cup on the dining room table spun, slipped off the table, and shattered.

Leong played with Wai at the other side of the house. Wai was happy and smiling for now, but she seemed to already be catching on to what was happening outside. She had asked Mei who Long Yun was a few weeks earlier. Her mother didn't know how to answer.

Hei couldn't help but be annoyed, as he swept up the broken pieces of ceramic from the floor. Stupid protestors were forcing him inside, giving him more chores. They must have been so tired, marching out here from their farms just to get dispersed by an IJA battalion. Was it really worth it?

Mei took the kids into the kitchen once the protestors came by. She loved them, and they didn't need to see what might happen if the protests got out of control. Despite herself, she hoped they'd leave Leong's factory safe. Whatever happened to the NPA, the Lees still needed the work.

Chun just stared out the window, watching them go by. Even if his parents would not let him join them, he could still watch, no matter what they did. What a cause, he thought to himself. It seemed almost impossible.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.9.a: A person in Guangdong with something to fight for.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.10.desc:
Darkness had fallen in the far outskirts of Kōshū, and the division had stopped to eat and rest. One of his fellow officers turned to Lam. Their eyes met - Lam with a look of acknowledgement, and the other with a look of apology - before the officer vanished into the brush.

For the next few hours, Lam and two others searched the countryside for the runaway, stomping through the marsh in their galoshes and firing beams of light into the tall grass. It was a doomed venture, Lam knew - officers deserted into these marshes every day, protected by the foliage. If anything, his division had proven luckier than most. For many GPF divisions, more men left than stayed by the time they reached the front lines.

Those that remained weren't fundamentally any different. If he could have seen his fellow officers' faces in the dark, he would have seen the bags under their eyes, the looks of defeat. It seemed a hallmark of any GPF officer as he neared the front lines. Perhaps the ones who stayed were merely a little weaker.

Lam couldn't deny it - he felt for that man, and all the others like him. He didn't want to fight this war. He had never joined the GPF to “defend his nation” - he did it to protect himself, after Guangdong's cruel economic dealings left him no other option but to submit. Long Yun could not promise much better for a collaborator like himself, but he couldn't promise any worse.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.10.a: Guangdong was not his nation - he was merely in its employ.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.11.desc:
For those left adrift in the Three Pearls, perhaps only the journalists had been left better off. The invasion left everyone's eyes on the papers, listening to hear about every victory. Even as every other market fell, the market for words was booming.

Yoshiko had begun her own report, with a different angle. She based it on some rumors she had heard around town, disgruntled staff and middle managers complaining their employer was about to be whisked back to Tokyo. Though records in Guangdong were rarely publicly available, it seemed possible to follow the rush of money and people with the right sources. With the right calls, she managed to get herself a picture.

The results were horrifying. In a rush to escape the vortex in China, wealth was exiting Guangdong on scales that seemed truly unbelievable. Even the megacorporations were moving as many of their holdings out as they could, even as their executives said otherwise. Some twenty thousand Zhujin and Japanese had already departed for Taiwan or Tokyo, many among the richest in all of Guangdong.

Even as she wrote the last words of her report, she could barely stomach the meaning of her work. The rich and powerful had already given up on Kōshū. If Guangdong was a nation, it was a nation led by gamblers, a state locked in games of chance. It seemed with odds this bad, only the addicts were willing to stay at the table.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.11.a: Home, like everything else, lasts only for a moment.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.12.desc:
No matter how nice the day or good the news, the heart of Kōshū never truly sang. Dominated by massive Japanese architecture and small Chinese citizens, there was perhaps no miracle on Earth great enough to bring their two classes together in harmony. Yet today, if the people of Guangdong were not happy, they were at least calmed. Pacified, one might say.

{gng_getleader} noticed it on his walk to work, and a few hours after from the window outside his office. The people must have been reacting to the news - Long Yun was dead, and his revolt was over.

Since the head of the Product Testing Group first called the Chief Executive from a military line in Yunnan, {gng_getleader} had felt a great cleansing come through him, a sense of physical relief. Finally, he could sleep once more, regroup with his allies, and return to creating the fixes that Guangdong desperately needed. Guangdong no longer needed a commander-in-chief. {gng_getleader} was now a Chief Executive once more.

Yes, the streets had not returned to calm. Chinese workers still yearned for their insolent king - they grumbled about him on every street, murmured thoughts on the assembly line and around the local bars. The Japanese magnates still cowered in the Home Islands, waiting for more confirmation that the Guangdong market was stable. But in the Chief Executive's office, at least, things were better.
strings.GNG_Western_Insurrection.12.a: And someday, maybe this mess would be far behind him.
strings.GNG_WI_PTRG_unit_demobilize_tt: The PTRG has been thanked for its service, and has been demobilized accordingly.
strings.GNG_INS_progbar_tt_delayed: We have currently carried out [?INS.GNG_INS_progbar]% of our possible actions this month.
strings.GNG_INS_advisors_tt_delayed: Military advisors will be sent to aid the Indonesian military
strings.GNG_INS_engies_tt_delayed: Engineers will be sent to aid the Indonesian military
strings.GNG_CRR_top_info_tooltip_delayed:
The Next Chief Executive
--------------
With £GNG_Guangdong_texticon Suzuki's disappearance and £GNG_Yasuda_texticon Yasuda's collapse into ignominy, Matsuzawa Takuji has become Chief Executive - a poisoned chalice thrust upon him by the three remaining Tycoons of Guangdong. They - Morita Akio, Ibuka Masaru, and Matsushita Masaharu - know that when the dust settles, they are most likely to be chosen to fill the vacant Chief Executive's seat, and that the race to succeed Matsuzawa has already begun. With each filling a role in Matsuzawa's Executive Council, the decisions Matsuzawa makes will be critical in deciding who gets the all-important nomination by the£GNG_legco_texticon Legislative Council...
--------------
Yasuda's Auction
--------------
...And what becomes of £GNG_Yasuda_texticon Yasuda itself? Its mighty empire laid low by the economic crisis that bears its name, £GNG_Yasuda_texticon Yasuda's remaining assets are slated to be auctioned off to repay its creditors. For Guangdong's government, the auction will serve as a valuable source of income from commission alone; for the tycoons, it is an unprecedented opportunity to pick clean the carcass of their rival for a bargain. Whether at a fair price or not, someone will walk away with the lion's share of £GNG_Yasuda_texticon Yasuda's business empire - and with it, the loyalty of Yasuda's abandoned men in the£GNG_legco_texticon Legislative Council.
strings.GNG_CRR_Morita_leaning: At this rate, Morita Akio of Sony is on track for the position of Chief Executive.
strings.GNG_CRR_Matsushita_leaning: At this rate, Matsushita Masaharu of Matsushita is on track for the position of Chief Executive.
strings.GNG_CRR_Ibuka_leaning: At this rate, Ibuka Masaru of Fujitsu is on track for the position of Chief Executive.
strings.GNG_CRR_uncertain_leaning: It is too close to tell who shall hold the position of Chief Executive.
strings.GNG_CRR_Morita_Salute: We salute Chief Executive Morita Akio!
strings.GNG_CRR_Matsushita_Salute: We salute Chief Executive Matsushita Masaharu!
strings.GNG_CRR_Ibuka_Salute: We salute Chief Executive Ibuka Masaru!
strings.GNG_CRR_Morita_Akio_tt:
President Morita Akio of £GNG_Sony_texticon Sony
--------------
From nothing, to the cusp of everything - this is the arc of Morita Akio's life, as Guangdong ends its most uncertain hour.

Since establishing himself in Guangdong in the 1950's, Morita has struggled without end to ensure that Sony demonstrates that capitalism can work from local roots - winning first a seat among Guangdong's top executives in 1960, and now a seat next to the Chief Executive himself.

Perennially the outsider, yet always relevant, Morita makes no secret that he covets power - both for himself, and to prove that his program for the Zhujin of Guangdong has a future.
strings.GNG_CRR_Matsushita_tt:
President Matsushita Masaharu of £GNG_Matsushita_texticon Matsushita
--------------
Is now his hour? That is the question that Matsushita Masaharu asks himself, as Guangdong roils in the wake of the Yasuda collapse.

Having been adopted into the Matsushita Electric business empire, Masaharu has always been in the shadow of his adopted father, Matsushita Kōnosuke - the Tokyo transplant into the rough-and-tumble pace of Osaka's business world. Elation turned to puzzlement, then frustration - on both ends. Now, a few years after being dispatched to Guangdong to head Matsushita's operations in the China region, Matsushita has the opportunity of a lifetime to make a name for himself - but such a gamble could cost him everything.
strings.GNG_CRR_Ibuka_tt:
President Ibuka Masaru of £GNG_Fujitsu_texticon Fujitsu
--------------
A man with vision is bound to face resistance - and so it is incumbent on Ibuka Masaru to sweep every last obstacle aside.

Ibuka has spent his entire tenure at Fujitsu in pursuit of his vision - of a world made easier by technology, of the possibilities that can be unlocked with automation, calculation, and miniaturization. To not pursue this dream to its logical conclusion, he feels, would be to turn his back on the pledge he made when he agreed to fold Tokyo Telecommunications - that if he was giving up his company for access to resources, then he would never be content to serve at someone else's beck and call.

strings.GNG_arrest_non_compliant_GFT_protesters_: Some of the protestors at these rallies are getting aggressive and confrontational with the local police. Time to throw them into holding cells before they can do any serious damage.

strings.GNG_increase_nighttime_patrols_against_G: Attacks on our people and assets are growing increasingly common after nighttime curfews. We need to step up our nighttime patrols to snuff out this destructive activity.
strings.GNG_increase_nighttime_patrols_against_C: Attacks on our people and assets are growing increasingly common after nighttime curfews. We need to step up our nighttime patrols to snuff out this destructive activity.
strings.GNG_initiate_low_level_abuse_protections: We will sign some minor legislation that institutes some protections for Chinese workers in the hopes of making their worksites marginally more equal and safe.

strings.GNG_incorporate_minor_promises_GFT_desc: A token concession here and a promise about a minute detail there go a long way in terms of getting angry workers off the streets and back into the factories.

strings.GNG_deploy_riot_police_GFT_desc: Dispersing a riot with a loudspeaker usually goes nowhere. Dispersing a riot with a nightstick and a riot shield is proven to be far more effective. The current situation calls for the latter approach.
strings.GNG_deploy_riot_police_CCL_desc: Dispersing a riot with a loudspeaker usually goes nowhere. Dispersing a riot with a nightstick and a riot shield is proven to be far more effective. The current situation calls for the latter approach.
strings.GNG_increase_checkpoint_monitoring_GFT_d: Increasing checkpoint security to limit the flow of people in and out of certain districts will allow us to consolidate government control in potential hotbeds of dissident activity.
strings.GNG_increase_checkpoint_monitoring_CCL_d: Increasing checkpoint security to limit the flow of people in and out of certain districts will allow us to consolidate government control in potential hotbeds of dissident activity.
strings.GNG_strike_protest_logistics_hubs_GFT_de: State intelligence has identified several locations from which rioters are currently organizing. Raiding these will ease the strain on our security forces.
strings.GNG_strike_protest_logistics_hubs_CCL_de: State intelligence has identified several locations from which rioters are currently organizing. Raiding these will ease the strain on our security forces.
strings.GNG_arrest_abusive_executives_GFT_desc: Putting some of the bigwigs that oversaw systemic abuse in the local populace behind bars is sure to calm the current situation down. Just don't mind the fact that we let them operate with an iron fist for years before this crisis.
strings.GNG_arrest_abusive_executives_CCL_desc: Putting some of the bigwigs that oversaw systemic abuse in the local populace behind bars is sure to calm the current situation down. Just don't mind the fact that we let them operate with an iron fist for years before this crisis.
strings.GNG_onboard_GFT_leaders_as_advisors_desc: If we're committed to making Guangdong a more equitable state for the Chinese, putting several of their leaders on advisory positions is sure to be a hit and satisfy some of their demands.
strings.GNG_onboard_CCL_leaders_as_advisors_desc: If we're committed to making Guangdong a more equitable state for the Chinese, putting several of their leaders on advisory positions is sure to be a hit and satisfy some of their demands.
strings.GNG_direct_GFT_rioters_towards_right_loc: Politely pointing out that our government has done plenty of good for the local unions, and that the other companies have not, should be enough to put angry rioters in districts that we do not control, and therefore making them not our problem.

strings.GNG_dispatch_armored_patrols_GFT_desc: Bottles and rocks can certainly inflict serious wounds to our officers on foot. They cannot do the same damage to armored vehicles.
strings.GNG_dispatch_armored_patrols_CCL_desc: Bottles and rocks can certainly inflict serious wounds to our officers on foot. They cannot do the same damage to armored vehicles.
strings.GNG_enforce_lockdowns_GFT_desc: Putting entire buildings on lockdown will sap these riots of the manpower that's fuelling them. Unfortunately, it also saps our productivity in the factories, and trust among the populace.
strings.GNG_enforce_lockdowns_CCL_desc: Putting entire buildings on lockdown will sap these riots of the manpower that's fuelling them. Unfortunately, it also saps our productivity in the factories, and trust among the populace.

strings.GNG_redirect_the_police_to_GFT_desc: Giving our officers the right direction on which subset of rioters to target will buy us some time to handle the current crisis in a satisfactory manner.

strings.GNG_arm_the_police_against_GFT_desc: There's no telling what measures these hooligans on the street are willing to resort to. We need to protect our officers and ensure they're well equipped to handle any and all threats.
